hints.text: It was built in 1979–1984 next to an older neoclassical gallery.
Its centre is an open-top rotunda, crossed by a public footpath and ramp.
Travertine and sandstone contrast with green steel frames and bright pink and blue handrails.

summary.description: Designed by James Stirling and Michael Wilford after a 1977 competition and built from 1979 to 1984, the gallery echoes the neoclassical old gallery next door and alludes to the Altes Museum, the Guggenheim and the Pantheon. Its open-top rotunda is circled by a public footpath.
keyFeatures: Open-top central rotunda
Public ramp through the site
Travertine and sandstone
Green steel frames and pink and blue handrails
funFacts: It alludes to Stirling's earlier, unbuilt designs.

name: Sainsbury Wing
aliases: Sainsbury Wing of the National Gallery

architects.name: Robert Venturi
architects.bio: Architect and author of 'Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture' (1966), an anti-Modernist polemic; partner of Denise Scott Brown.

architects.name: Denise Scott Brown
architects.bio: Architect and planner, Venturi's partner.

hints.text: It is a 1991 extension to the west of a national art museum on a famous square.
It was designed by an American husband-and-wife partnership.
It is a significant example of Postmodernist architecture in Britain.

summary.description: Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown's extension to the west of the National Gallery opened in 1991. It was made possible by a donation in 1985 from Lord Sainsbury and his brothers, and it is a significant example of Postmodernism in Britain.
keyFeatures: Extension to the west of the main building
Postmodern design
Funded by the Sainsbury brothers
funFacts: The main National Gallery building was designed by William Wilkins.

architects.bio: American architect who, with John Burgee, designed the tower in the postmodern style.

hints.text: It was completed in 1984 as a telephone company's headquarters, and later housed an electronics company.
Its 37 storeys are faced in pink granite.
It is crowned by a broken pediment with a circular opening.

summary.description: Designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee and completed in 1984 as AT&T's headquarters, the 197-metre tower is faced in pink granite. A large entrance arch flanked by arcades faces Madison Avenue, and a broken pediment with a circular opening crowns the top. It later became Sony's American headquarters.
keyFeatures: Broken pediment crown
Large entrance arch with arcades
Pink granite facade
Sky lobby above the base
funFacts: Its ground-level lobby was originally a public arcade.

architects.bio: Los Angeles architect whose sculptural, metal-clad buildings are often associated with Deconstructivism, a label he does not accept.

hints.text: It was opened by a king on 18 October 1997.
Philip Johnson called it 'the greatest building of our time'.
Its curving forms of stone, glass and titanium unfold along a river in an old industrial city.

summary.description: Frank Gehry's museum on the Nervión river opened on 18 October 1997 and was immediately hailed as a masterpiece of the 20th century. Its titanium-clad curving volumes are organised around a light-filled atrium, nicknamed The Flower, with views of the estuary and hills.
keyFeatures: Titanium cladding
Atrium nicknamed The Flower
Interconnecting shapes of stone, glass and titanium
Riverside site
funFacts: A New Yorker critic called it 'a fantastic dream ship of undulating form in a cloak of titanium'.

architects.bio: Architect whose radical zigzag design was chosen from 189 entries.

hints.text: Its design was chosen from 189 entries and nicknamed 'Lightning' for its zigzag plan.
Before any exhibits were installed, more than 350,000 people visited the empty building.
It can be entered only through an underground passage from a Baroque building next door.

summary.description: Daniel Libeskind's zigzag building, chosen from 189 entries, was completed empty in 1999 and opened as a museum in 2001. Reached only underground from the Baroque Kollegienhaus, it is the largest Jewish museum in Europe and one of Germany's most visited.
keyFeatures: Zigzag plan
Underground entrance from the old building
Empty concrete voids
Three axes leading to the Garden of Exile and the Holocaust Tower
funFacts: It had over eleven million visitors from 2001 to 2017.

hints.text: Its glass structure sits on top of an old brick warehouse built in 1963.
Planned to cost €241 million and finish by 2010, it was completed in 2016 for €866 million.
At 108 metres it is the tallest inhabited building in its city.

summary.description: Resembling a hoisted sail, a wave or a crystal resting on the Kaispeicher A warehouse, the concert hall is the key project of the HafenCity district. Construction ended on 31 October 2016 at €866 million, far above its estimate, and it was inaugurated on 11 January 2017.
keyFeatures: Glassy superstructure on a brick warehouse
Wavy roofline and about a thousand curved windows
Public Plaza at the top of the warehouse
Vineyard-style hall for 2,100
funFacts: The first public test concert was held on 25 November 2016.

architects.name: Frank Gehry
architects.bio: Los Angeles architect whose sculptural, metal-clad buildings are often associated with Deconstructivism, a label he does not accept.

hints.text: It began with a $50 million gift in 1987 from the widow of a famous film producer.
It opened on 23 October 2003 and seats 2,265 people.
It is home to its city's philharmonic orchestra, and its acoustics by Minoru Nagata were widely praised.

summary.description: Funded by an initial $50 million gift from Lillian Disney in 1987, Frank Gehry's hall opened on 23 October 2003 as the fourth hall of the Los Angeles Music Center. Home to the Los Angeles Philharmonic, it seats 2,265, and its acoustics by Minoru Nagata and Yasuhisa Toyota were praised.
keyFeatures: Stainless-steel skin, replacing a planned stone exterior
Main hall with 2,265 seats
Acoustics by Minoru Nagata and Yasuhisa Toyota
Downtown site on Grand Avenue
funFacts: Gehry said being chosen was 'the least likely thing that I thought would ever happen to me in my life'.

architects.bio: Architect who began the work in 447 BC with Callicrates.

architects.name: Callicrates
architects.bio: Architect who worked with Ictinus; together they wrote a lost treatise on the building.

hints.text: Construction started in 447 BC, when an alliance of Greek city-states was at the peak of its power.
A Venetian bomb hit it in 1687, when the Ottomans were using it as a munitions store.
Many of its sculptures were removed to England between 1800 and 1803 and are named after an earl.

summary.description: Built on the Acropolis for the goddess Athena, the temple was begun in 447 BC by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates under the general supervision of Phidias, who also directed its sculpture. It was completed in 438 BC, with decoration continuing to 432 BC. A peripteral post-and-lintel temple, it was wrecked by an explosion in 1687.
keyFeatures: Peripteral colonnade carrying an entablature
Sculptural programme directed by Phidias
Cella for the colossal statue of Athena
Site on the Acropolis
funFacts: Its architects seem to have called it the 'hundred-footer'.
The colossal statue of Athena inside was by Phidias.

architects.name: Unknown Roman architects
architects.bio: The amphitheatre was built under the emperors Vespasian and Titus of the Flavian dynasty; its architects are not recorded.

hints.text: It was begun in AD 72 under one emperor and completed in 80 under his son.
It is the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built.
It could hold some 50,000 to 80,000 spectators for gladiatorial contests and animal hunts.

summary.description: Begun under Vespasian in AD 72 and completed under Titus in 80, the elliptical amphitheatre east of the Roman Forum is the largest ever built. Of travertine, Roman concrete and tuff, it held an average audience of about 65,000 for gladiatorial games, hunts, executions and even mock sea battles.
keyFeatures: Elliptical plan
Travertine outer wall
Roman concrete foundations, corridors and vaults
Tuff and brick secondary walls
funFacts: The name 'Flavian Amphitheatre' was given by later scholars; in antiquity it was simply 'the amphitheatre'.

architects.name: Abbot Suger
architects.bio: Abbot who rebuilt parts of the church in the 12th century with innovative structural and decorative features, creating what is called the first truly Gothic building.

architects.name: Pierre de Montreuil
architects.bio: Master builder who rebuilt the nave and transepts in the Rayonnant style in the 13th century.

hints.text: Its choir, completed in 1144, is widely considered the first structure to use all the elements of Gothic architecture.
Nearly every king of its country from the 10th century to the 19th was buried there.
It stands where the first bishop of a great city is believed to have been buried.

summary.description: Built over the burial place of Saint Denis, the abbey church was rebuilt by Abbot Suger, whose choir, completed in 1144, is considered the first fully Gothic structure. In the 13th century Pierre de Montreuil rebuilt the nave and transepts. It became the necropolis of the kings of France.
keyFeatures: Choir of 1144, the first fully Gothic structure
Rayonnant nave and transepts
Royal tombs
Crypts
funFacts: French queens were crowned there.
An earlier church was consecrated in 775 in Charlemagne's presence.

architects.name: Maurice de Sully
architects.bio: Bishop of Paris who began construction of the new cathedral in 1163.

architects.name: Eugène Viollet-le-Duc
architects.bio: Architect who supervised its restoration between 1844 and 1864.

A fire in April 2019 closed it until December 2024.

summary.description: Begun in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and largely completed by 1260, the cathedral pioneered the rib vault and flying buttress and has enormous rose windows. Victor Hugo's novel inspired its restoration by Viollet-le-Duc in 1844–1864. After the fire of 2019 it reopened in December 2024.
keyFeatures: Flying buttresses
Rib vaults
Large rose windows
Abundant naturalistic sculpture
funFacts: Its west rose window was completed in 1220.

architects.name: Unknown Umayyad builders
architects.bio: The mosque was built from 785 for Abd al-Rahman I and enlarged by his successors until the late 10th century; the builders are not recorded.

hints.text: It was begun in 785 on the orders of the founder of an Islamic emirate.
Its most famous innovation is rows of two-tiered arches over its prayer hall.
Since 1236 it has been a cathedral, with a Renaissance nave inserted in its centre in the 16th century.

summary.description: Begun in 785 for Abd al-Rahman I and enlarged until the late 10th century, the mosque's hypostyle hall repeats its signature two-tiered arches across many bays. Al-Hakam II added a richly decorated mihrab in 971. Converted to a cathedral in 1236, it received a Renaissance nave in the 16th century.
keyFeatures: Two-tiered arches in the hypostyle hall
Reused Roman and Visigothic columns
Mihrab and maqsura with interlacing multifoil arches
Renaissance cathedral nave inserted in the centre
funFacts: Abd al-Rahman III added a minaret, finished in 958.

architects.name: Unknown Nasrid builders
architects.bio: Begun in 1238 by Muhammad I, the complex was modified by later Nasrid rulers, above all Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the 14th century; its builders are not recorded.

hints.text: It is the only well-preserved palace from the medieval Islamic world.
Its building was begun in 1238 by the founder of the last Muslim state on the Iberian Peninsula.
After 1492 it became the court of Ferdinand and Isabella, and later an emperor built a Renaissance palace beside it.

summary.description: Begun in 1238 by Muhammad I on the Sabika hill, the palace and fortress complex received its defining royal palaces under Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the 14th century. After the conquest of 1492 it became the court of Ferdinand and Isabella, and in 1526 Charles V commissioned a Renaissance palace beside the Nasrid palaces.

Fortress on the Sabika hill
Royal palaces shaped by Yusuf I and Muhammad V
Renaissance Palace of Charles V
funFacts: Columbus received royal endorsement for his voyage there.

hints.text: It stands in a cloister beside a great Franciscan basilica.
It was paid for by a banking family whose wealth was second only to the Medici.
It closely resembles an earlier sacristy at San Lorenzo, which is why it is usually credited to that sacristy's architect.

summary.description: Funded from 1429 by Andrea Pazzi, the chapel in the first cloister of Santa Croce was begun about 1442 and completed in 1478. Commonly credited to Filippo Brunelleschi for its likeness to his Old Sacristy, it is an Early Renaissance masterpiece, though Giuliano da Maiano or Michelozzo have also been proposed.
keyFeatures: Early Renaissance design
Façade partly obscured by an added porch
Site in the first cloister of Santa Croce
Likeness to the Old Sacristy of San Lorenzo
funFacts: Brunelleschi was first named as its architect by an anonymous writer in the 1490s.

architects.name: Donato Bramante
architects.bio: Principal designer of the new basilica begun in 1506.

architects.name: Michelangelo
architects.bio: Sculptor, painter and architect, a principal designer of the basilica and its dome.

architects.name: Carlo Maderno
architects.bio: One of the three principal designers of the basilica, with Bramante and Michelangelo.

photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Wide classical church front with a row of giant columns, a statue-topped parapet and a great ribbed dome rising behind.

photos.credit: Photo: Jebulon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

Great ribbed dome rising above trees in a garden

Photo: NateBergin · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Construction began on 18 April 1506 and ended on 18 November 1626.
It is the largest church in the world by interior measure.
Its piazza and many fittings are by a Baroque sculptor-architect, and inside stands a famous Pietà.

summary.description: Begun in 1506 and completed in 1626, the basilica was designed principally by Bramante, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, with piazza and fittings by Bernini. One of the largest domes in the world rises over its central space, and its barrel-vaulted nave is the highest of any church.
keyFeatures: Great dome over the central space
Barrel-vaulted nave, the highest of any church
Four giant piers with colossal statues
Piazza by Bernini
funFacts: Michelangelo's Pietà stands in one of its chapels.

architects.name: Joseph Paxton
architects.bio: Designer of the Great Exhibition building, a cast-iron and plate-glass structure completed in thirty-nine weeks.

photos.credit: Photo: Dickinson Brothers · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Colour print of a huge iron-and-glass exhibition hall with a barrel-vaulted transept, seen across a park with a tall tree and strolling visitors.
Old photograph of a long glass-and-iron exhibition hall with a vaulted centre
photos.credit: Photo: William Henry Fox Talbot · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Joacolouzao · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a vast glass-and-iron building with a huge arched transept, standing in a bare open landscape.

photos.credit: Photo: J. McNeven · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Painting of a crowded glass-roofed hall with iron galleries, statues, fountains and exhibits displayed under a lattice ceiling.
Historic print of a vast glass-roofed hall crowded with visitors and exhibits
photos.caption: The interior, 1851 print.
photos.credit: Photo: Unknown artist, Library of Congress · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built in a park to house a great international exhibition held from May to October 1851.
It was made of cast iron and 293,000 panes of glass, and was built in thirty-nine weeks.
Rebuilt in a south London suburb, it was destroyed by fire in November 1936.

summary.description: Joseph Paxton's cast-iron and plate-glass building in Hyde Park housed the Great Exhibition of 1851. 564 metres long and 39 metres high inside, it was three times the size of St Paul's Cathedral and had the greatest area of glass ever seen in a building. Rebuilt at Sydenham, it stood until a fire in 1936.
keyFeatures: Prefabricated cast-iron frame
293,000 panes of glass
Interior height of 39 m
990,000 sq ft of exhibition space
funFacts: Its name may come from a Punch article about a 'palace of very crystal'.

architects.name: Lord Burlington
architects.bio: Aristocrat-architect who acquired a passion for Palladian architecture in Italy in 1719 and designed the villa himself.

architects.name: William Kent
architects.bio: Architect and landscape designer who created most of the garden, an early English landscape garden.

photos.credit: Photo: Michael Coppins · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Symmetrical white villa with a columned portico, a low dome behind it and twin stair ramps, across a wide gravel forecourt.
Pale Palladian villa with a temple portico, twin stairs and a low dome, in snow
photos.credit: Photo: Chivalrick1 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Tilman2007 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Low white villa with arched windows, a shallow dome and curved staircases, flanked by a stone wing, seen across a lawn.

photos.credit: Photo: Chivalrick1 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Small white garden temple with four Ionic columns, a pediment and a domed round body, standing among dark trees.
Richly painted and gilded ceiling with a central allegorical painting
photos.caption: A ceiling.
photos.credit: Photo: Mark Percy · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built after a fire in 1725 damaged an older Jacobean house on the estate.
Its designer was an earl who fell in love with an Italian architect's work during a trip in 1719.
Its garden is one of the earliest English landscape gardens.

summary.description: Designed by Richard Boyle, 3rd Earl of Burlington, and completed in 1729, the villa is a glorious example of Neo-Palladian architecture, inspired by Palladio and Scamozzi. William Kent created most of its garden, one of the earliest English landscape gardens.
keyFeatures: Neo-Palladian villa
Plan inspired by Palladio
Landscape garden by William Kent
26-hectare grounds
funFacts: Burlington relied on Palladio and Scamozzi rather than on drawings of Roman ruins.

architects.name: Hemiunu
architects.bio: Prince and vizier of Pharaoh Khufu, Hemiunu held the title 'Inspector of All Royal Buildings' and is believed to have been the architect of the Great Pyramid. His large mastaba tomb stands beside it at Giza.

architects.name: Khufu
architects.bio: Second pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty, Khufu commissioned the pyramid as his tomb and the centre of a vast funerary complex. He is remembered above all for this monument.

drawings.label: North–south section
drawings.alt: Section through a huge pyramid showing narrow passages, a large rising gallery and two chambers high inside, with a third chamber below ground
drawings.credit: F l a n k e r · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Huge stepped pyramid of rough stone blocks rising against a clear blue sky above desert sand
photos.credit: Photo: Douwe C. van der Zee · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ricardo Liberato · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Three large stone pyramids of decreasing size rising from a sandy plateau, with three small pyramids in the foreground.
Narrow, steeply rising corridor of stone with a corbelled, stepped ceiling
photos.caption: A corbelled corridor climbs towards the burial chambers.
photos.credit: Photo: Keith Adler · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: For almost four thousand years it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth.
It is the oldest of a famous ancient list of seven wonders, and the only one still largely standing.
It was once sheathed in smooth white limestone, which was stripped away over the centuries, leaving the rough core.

summary.description: Built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC, the pyramid rose to 146.6 metres and held the record as the world's tallest structure for more than 3,700 years. Some 2.3 million blocks of limestone and granite were assembled over about 26 years; inside are three chambers connected by narrow passages and a great sloping gallery. Hemiunu, the pharaoh's vizier, is believed to have been its architect.
keyFeatures: Roughly 2.3 million stone blocks
Original height of 146.6 metres, now 138.5 metres
Grand Gallery with a corbelled ceiling
Granite King’s Chamber and an unfinished chamber cut into the bedrock
funFacts: The smooth white casing came from Tura, while the granite for the King’s Chamber was floated down the Nile from Aswan.
It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

architects.name: Ustad Ahmad Lahori
architects.bio: Court architect of Shah Jahan, Lahori is usually named as the lead of the board of architects, artisans and supervisors who designed the tomb and its gardens.

architects.name: Shah Jahan
architects.bio: Fifth Mughal emperor and a great builder, Shah Jahan commissioned the mausoleum in 1631 for his wife Mumtaz Mahal and is buried there himself.

drawings.label: Floor plan of the mausoleum
drawings.alt: Symmetrical plan with a central octagonal chamber, four corner rooms and four great arched entrances
drawings.credit: Plan of the tomb · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: White marble tomb with a bulbous central dome and four slender minarets, seen down a long reflecting pool between gardens
photos.credit: Photo: Yann; edited by Jim Carter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Matthew T Rader · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Monumental red sandstone gateway with a tall pointed arch framed in white marble inlay and rows of small domed kiosks on top.

photos.credit: Photo: Gerd Eichmann · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: White marble wall with carved tulip reliefs and a border of inlaid semi-precious stones in floral patterns.
Octagonal screen of white marble pierced with delicate lattice, set around a tomb in a dim chamber
photos.caption: A carved marble screen surrounds the tombs.
photos.credit: Photo: Raphael Tuck & Sons · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a tomb by a grieving emperor for the wife who died giving birth to their fourteenth child.
Its four minarets lean slightly outward on purpose, so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb.
White marble inlaid with semi-precious stones sits at the centre of a garden laid out on a strict axis.

summary.description: Commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, the white marble mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the surrounding complex in 1653. It combines Persian, Islamic and Indian traditions in a perfectly symmetrical composition of tomb, mosque, guest house and gardens. More than 20,000 workers and artisans took part under a board of architects led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori.
keyFeatures: Symmetrical plan around a central dome
Four minarets leaning slightly outward
Pietra dura inlay of semi-precious stones
Charbagh garden with a long reflecting pool
funFacts: More than 20,000 workers and artisans were employed on the project.
Shah Jahan’s own tomb was added beside his wife’s after his death, breaking the symmetry of the chamber.

architects.name: Suryavarman II
architects.bio: Khmer king who commissioned the temple as his state temple and probable mausoleum. The architects are not recorded by name, so the king, who ordered and directed it, is credited.

drawings.label: Plan of the temple
drawings.alt: Plan of a vast square enclosure with nested galleries, a cross-shaped terrace and a central cluster of towers
drawings.credit: Baldiri · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Site plan with moat
drawings.alt: Aerial plan of a huge rectangular moat and wall with a long causeway leading to a central temple mound
drawings.credit: Baldiri · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Satdeep Gill · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Temple with five tall lotus-bud towers and a long low gallery, mirrored in a still pond with palms and blue sky.
Five tall towers shaped like lotus buds rising behind a long gallery, reflected in a lily pond

Photo: Charles J Sharp · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

Stone cloister with rows of balusters and carved doorways around an inner courtyard
photos.credit: Photo: Anandajoti · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It began as a temple to a Hindu god, later became a Buddhist monastery, and is still a place of worship.
Its five towers represent the peaks of a mythical mountain at the centre of the universe.
Unlike most temples of its kingdom it faces west, and its silhouette appears on a national flag.

summary.description: Built between 1113 and about 1150 for the Khmer king Suryavarman II, Angkor Wat was first a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later a Buddhist one. Within a vast moat and wall, three rising galleries lead to a central quincunx of towers that represents Mount Meru. It is often called the largest religious monument in the world and is decorated with extensive bas-reliefs.
keyFeatures: Temple-mountain with three rising galleries
Central quincunx of five lotus-bud towers
Vast moat and enclosing wall
Extensive bas-reliefs along the galleries
funFacts: It is oriented to the west, unlike most Angkorian temples.
It has remained in religious use ever since it was built, which helped it survive.

architects.name: Kuai Xiang
architects.bio: A carpenter who rose to lead the imperial building works, Kuai Xiang is traditionally credited as the master builder of the Ming palaces in Beijing.

architects.name: Yongle Emperor
architects.bio: Third Ming emperor, who moved the capital to Beijing and ordered the new palace city built between 1406 and 1420.

drawings.label: Plan of the palace
drawings.alt: Plan of a walled rectangular palace city, with halls and courtyards in rows along a central axis
drawings.credit: Unknown author · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Great yellow-tiled hall on a white marble terrace above a wide paved courtyard
photos.credit: Photo: N509FZ · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Han Zheng · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Overview from a hill of a vast palace of yellow-tiled roofs behind a red gate tower and a moat, with a city beyond.

photos.credit: Photo: Morio · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Huge red fortified wall with projecting wings and tiered tile-roofed pavilions around a wide empty paved courtyard.
Red-pillared hall with a gilded throne raised on steps beneath a carved canopy
photos.credit: Photo: Vaiz Ha · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Twenty-four emperors lived here over five centuries; ordinary people were forbidden to enter.
Legend gives it 9,999 rooms, but surveys count about 8,886.
It is the largest collection of preserved ancient wooden buildings in the world, and today it is a museum.

summary.description: Built between 1406 and 1420 for the Yongle Emperor, the palace city was the home of 24 Ming and Qing emperors and the centre of Chinese government until 1924. Its halls and courtyards are arranged symmetrically along a north–south axis, with the ceremonial buildings in front and the living quarters behind. It covers 72 hectares and is the largest collection of preserved ancient wooden structures in the world.
keyFeatures: Strict north–south axis of halls and courtyards
Yellow glazed roof tiles reserved for the emperor
Walled complex of about 8,886 rooms
Marble terraces and carved dragon ramps
funFacts: The Palace Museum has looked after it since 1925.
The 1987 film The Last Emperor was the first Western production allowed to film inside.

name: Temple of Heaven
aliases: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests

architects.name: Yongle Emperor
architects.bio: Third Ming emperor, who ordered the temple built in 1420 as part of his new capital, together with the Forbidden City. The designers are not recorded by name.

drawings.label: Plan of the temple grounds
drawings.alt: Old engraved plan of a long temple precinct with a round building at the north end and a circular altar at the south
drawings.credit: The British Library · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Shujianyang · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A round three-tiered hall with deep blue roofs and a golden finial stands on white marble terraces under a clear blue sky.
Round three-tiered temple with a deep blue tiled roof and a gilded finial, standing on white marble terraces
photos.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: xiquinhosilva · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A smaller round pavilion with a single blue-tiled conical roof, red walls and lattice doors, approached by white marble steps and balustrades.
Looking up at red and gold painted columns and a richly coloured circular ceiling
photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Emperors came here once a year to pray for a good harvest.
Its great hall is round under a blue roof, because ancient Chinese cosmology saw Heaven as round and Earth as square.
Its main hall is built entirely of wood, without nails, and was rebuilt after lightning burned the original in 1889.

summary.description: Founded in 1420 during the reign of the Yongle Emperor, the temple complex was where Ming and Qing emperors performed the annual rites of prayer for a good harvest. Its numbers, shapes and terraces symbolise the structure of the cosmos: round buildings for Heaven set on square grounds for Earth. The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, rebuilt after a fire in 1889, is a 38-metre-tall wooden building on three marble terraces.
keyFeatures: Circular halls under blue glazed tiles
Triple marble terraces
Echo Wall around the Imperial Vault of Heaven
Layout based on the sacred number nine
funFacts: A lightning fire destroyed the original Hall of Prayer in 1889.
The Echo Wall around the Imperial Vault carries whispers over long distances.

architects.name: Ikeda Terumasa
architects.bio: Lord of Himeji from 1600, Ikeda Terumasa completely rebuilt the castle between 1601 and 1609 on the foundations of Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s earlier keep, creating the vast complex seen today.

drawings.label: Plan of the castle grounds
drawings.alt: Plan of a spiral of walled enclosures winding around a central keep on a hill
drawings.credit: Fraxinus2 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Multi-storey white castle keep with gabled roofs above stone walls and a foreground of cherry blossom
photos.credit: Photo: Seattleite7 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Nikos Kitsakis · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A tiered white castle keep with stacked gabled roofs rises above a stone base and long low white walls, framed by green trees.

photos.credit: Photo: (Institute of Land Geography) 国土地理院 · Attribution · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a star-shaped castle complex ringed by moats and green grounds, surrounded by dense city blocks.

photos.credit: Photo: Luka Peternel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

Long wooden corridor inside a castle with dark timber beams, a polished floor and display cases
photos.credit: Photo: ScribblingGeek · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its brilliant white walls earned it a nickname after a bird.
It is almost 700 years old as a site, and it came through wartime bombing and a major earthquake almost undamaged.
The path to its keep winds back and forth through many gates, designed to lose and trap attackers.

summary.description: Himeji Castle dates to a fort built in 1333, and was remodelled by Toyotomi Hideyoshi and completely rebuilt between 1601 and 1609 by Ikeda Terumasa. Its white plastered keep and a network of 83 buildings with advanced defences make it the finest surviving example of Japanese castle architecture. It survived bombing in 1945 and the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake virtually undamaged.
keyFeatures: White plastered walls like a bird in flight
Network of 83 buildings
Winding approach through many gates
Complex of defences including loopholes and stone-drop openings
funFacts: A firebomb dropped on the top floor in 1945 failed to explode.
After the 1995 earthquake a bottle of sake on the keep’s altar was still standing.

architects.name: Emperor Shōmu
architects.bio: Devout Buddhist emperor who founded Tōdai-ji as the head of a network of state temples and commissioned its giant Buddha in 743. The present hall dates from a rebuilding in 1709.

photos.alt: Immense two-roofed wooden hall with golden ornaments on the ridge, seen from across a paved courtyard
photos.credit: Photo: ONO Masanobu · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: 663highland · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A long dark timber hall with a deep hipped roof and an open veranda stands on tall stilts above a grassy slope, with stone steps at the right.
Colossal dark bronze seated Buddha in a golden halo between red wooden columns
photos.credit: Photo: Zairon · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Chainwit. · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A red-pillared gate with a dark tiled roof and white panels seen along a paved path lined with stone lanterns and pine trees.

hints.text: It was founded as Japan’s answer to the great temples of Tang China.
Its great hall is among the largest wooden buildings in the world, yet today’s hall is only two-thirds the width of the original.
Inside sits the world’s largest bronze statue of the cosmic Buddha.

summary.description: Founded in 738 and opened in 752 in the old capital of Nara, Tōdai-ji was designed to imitate the great Tang temples of China. Its Great Buddha Hall houses the world’s largest bronze statue of the Buddha Vairocana. The hall was rebuilt in 1709, at about two-thirds of its original width, and was strengthened with steel framing between 1974 and 1980.
keyFeatures: One of the largest wooden buildings in the world
Colossal bronze Buddha Vairocana inside
Double roof with golden ridge ornaments
Complex of halls, gates and pagodas in Nara
funFacts: The present hall is about two-thirds the width of the original.
The hall was close to collapse in the late 19th century because of the weight of its roof.

architects.name: Gunadharma
architects.bio: Architect named in Javanese tradition as the designer of the temple for the Sailendra dynasty. The attribution rests on local legend, as no inscription names the builder.

drawings.label: Half cross section
drawings.alt: Old line drawing of a stepped, symmetrical temple mound in section, with a stupa on top and levels labelled in Sanskrit
drawings.credit: Short Guide to Borobudur, Mendut, and Pawon, diagram · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Huge stepped stone temple mound topped with a central stupa, set in a green park

photos.credit: Photo: Heri nugroho · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

Perforated bell-shaped stupas on a terrace with green hills in the haze behind

photos.credit: Photo: Photo Dharma from Penang, Malaysia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It lay abandoned for centuries until a colonial governor was told of its location in 1814.
Pilgrims walk up through nine stacked platforms past more than 1,400 narrative relief panels.
Seen from above it is a mandala: square terraces below, three circular platforms with perforated stupas above.

summary.description: Built around 825 under the Sailendra dynasty of Java, Borobudur is the largest Buddhist temple in the world. Nine stacked platforms, six square and three circular, rise to a central dome ringed by 72 Buddha statues in perforated stupas. Pilgrims climb through corridors lined with 1,460 narrative relief panels, a journey that mirrors the path to enlightenment.
keyFeatures: Nine stacked platforms topped by a dome
2,672 relief panels
72 Buddha statues in perforated stupas
Mandala plan symbolising the Buddhist cosmos
funFacts: Thomas Stamford Raffles, then British governor of Java, was told of the buried-in-jungle site in 1814.
The 1983 UNESCO-supported restoration took apart and rebuilt the monument.

architects.name: Itzá Maya builders
architects.bio: The pyramid was raised by the pre-Columbian Maya of Chichén Itzá as a temple to the Feathered Serpent, Kukulcán. No individual architect is recorded; the work is credited to the Itzá builders and their rulers.

photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Schwen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A square stepped stone pyramid with a stairway on each side and a small temple on top, standing on a flat grassy plaza under a blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Luka Peternel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A corner view of a stepped stone pyramid, with a wide stairway on one face and the small temple on top, against deep blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Kos Nina · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a stepped stone pyramid in a clearing, with another colonnaded building nearby and dense forest stretching to the horizon.
Carved stone serpent head with open jaws at the foot of a pyramid stair
photos.credit: Photo: Frank Kovalchek · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Red jaguar-shaped stone throne with jade-inlaid spots in a dark chamber, behind a carved reclining figure
photos.caption: A red jaguar throne sits inside the older pyramid within.
photos.credit: Photo: Unknown author · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Twice a year, at the equinox, the setting sun makes a shadow that looks like a serpent crawling down its stair.
It is a stepped pyramid with a stairway on each of its four sides, topped by a small temple.
A smaller, older pyramid is hidden inside it, containing a red throne shaped like a jaguar.

summary.description: Built by the pre-Columbian Maya sometime between the 8th and 12th centuries, this step pyramid was a temple to Kukulcán, the Feathered Serpent. A series of square terraces rises to a temple on top, with a stairway up each side. Around the spring and autumn equinoxes the late sun casts triangular shadows on the northwest balustrade that look like a serpent crawling down the stair. An earlier pyramid, with a red jaguar throne, survives inside.
keyFeatures: Stepped square terraces with four stairways
Plumed serpent heads at the foot of the north stair
Equinox shadow effect on the balustrade
Older temple and jaguar throne enclosed within
funFacts: Thousands of people gather at the equinox to watch the serpent shadow.
It is not known whether the shadow effect was planned.

architects.name: Aretas IV
architects.bio: Nabataean king under whom the Treasury is thought to have been carved as a royal tomb. The names of the sculptors and designers are not recorded.

drawings.label: Restoration of the façade
drawings.alt: Engraved elevation of a two-storey classical façade with columns and statues, beside a plan and architectural details
drawings.credit: Jacques Ignace Hittorff, engraving, 1830s · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Jorge Láscar from Australia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A tall columned facade with a pediment and a round central pavilion is carved into a pink sandstone cliff face, with a dark doorway at the base.

photos.credit: Photo: David Berkowitz from New York, NY, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: An oblique view of a rock-cut columned facade rising from a sandy forecourt between towering red cliffs, with small visitors at its foot.
Tall rock-cut façade with columns, a pediment and a round tholos, glimpsed through a narrow gorge
photos.credit: Photo: Azurfrog · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Bare square chamber cut into banded orange and red sandstone, with a small doorway in one wall
photos.credit: Photo: Michael Gunther · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Rose-red carved façade in a canyon at night, with rows of candles on the ground in front
photos.credit: Photo: Susanahajer · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was carved straight out of a sandstone cliff, not built up from blocks.
Its name means "treasury", from a legend that a pharaoh hid his riches in the urn on its façade.
You approach it through a long, narrow gorge, and it appears suddenly at the end.

summary.description: Carved out of a rose-red sandstone cliff around the 1st century AD, probably for the Nabataean king Aretas IV, the Treasury is one of the most elaborate tombs of Petra. Its two-storey façade mixes Hellenistic columns, pediments and a central tholos with Nabataean details. Behind the grand front is only a plain chamber. The name comes from a legend that treasure lay in the urn above, whose bullet marks show how far the myth was believed.
keyFeatures: Two-storey façade carved from the cliff
Corinthian columns and a central tholos
Hellenistic and Nabataean details combined
Plain, unadorned chambers behind the front
funFacts: The urn is solid sandstone, but Bedouin firing at it hoped to release treasure.
The Bedouin named it Khaznat el-Far’oun, the Pharaoh’s Treasury.

architects.name: Raja ibn Haywa
architects.bio: A scholar and adviser to the Umayyad caliphs, named by tradition as one of the two men in charge of the building, together with Yazid ibn Salam.

architects.name: Abd al-Malik
architects.bio: Umayyad caliph who ordered the shrine built in 691–692 over the Foundation Stone, in the first major monument of Islamic architecture.

drawings.label: Plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a double octagon around a central circle of piers and columns, with an entrance at each side
drawings.credit: Georg Dehio and Gustav von Bezold, 1887 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Section
drawings.alt: Engraved section of a domed octagonal building with two arcaded rings of arches and columns under a large dome
drawings.credit: Georg Dehio and Gustav von Bezold, 1887 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the oldest surviving major work of Islamic architecture in the world.
It is not a mosque for congregational prayer but a shrine, built around a sacred rock.
Its golden dome and blue tiles are among the most recognisable sights of a city sacred to three religions.

summary.description: Built in 691–692 on the orders of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik, the Dome of the Rock is an octagonal shrine over a sacred rock on the Temple Mount. A dome about 20 metres wide, mounted on a drum standing on 16 supports, rises over two concentric octagonal ambulatories. Its plan and original mosaics follow nearby Byzantine churches, and it carries the earliest inscriptions proclaiming Islam. The blue tiles were added by Ottoman rulers and the gold roof in the 20th century.
keyFeatures: Octagonal plan around a central dome
Two ambulatories for circling the rock
Gold-plated dome about 20 metres wide
Ottoman Iznik-style tiles on the walls
funFacts: It is the world’s oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture.
Its present gold roof dates only from 1959–64, redone in the 1990s.

architects.name: Fifth Dalai Lama
architects.bio: Spiritual and political ruler of Tibet who ordered the present palace begun in 1645 and moved his government there. The master builders are not named.

hints.text: For three centuries it was the winter home of a spiritual leader, and the seat of his government.
It sits on a hill at almost 3,700 metres, and its slanting walls are poured with copper at the base against earthquakes.
It has 13 storeys, a white part for government and a red part for worship.

summary.description: Begun in 1645 on the orders of the 5th Dalai Lama on the hill Marpo Ri, the Potala was the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas and the seat of the Tibetan government from 1649 until 1959. Built in the dzong style at about 3,700 metres, it is 13 storeys and 119 metres high, with more than 1,000 rooms and some 200,000 statues. Sloping stone walls average three metres thick, and copper was poured into the foundations as protection against earthquakes. It is now a museum.
keyFeatures: 13 storeys on a rocky hill
White Palace for government and Red Palace for worship
Walls 3–5 metres thick
More than 1,000 rooms and 10,000 shrines
funFacts: Copper was poured into the foundations to guard against earthquakes.
Its name comes from Mount Potalaka, the mythical home of the bodhisattva of compassion.

architects.name: Pedro I of Castile
architects.bio: King of Castile who commissioned the Mudéjar palace in the 1360s, employing craftsmen from Seville, Toledo and the Nasrid court of Granada.

hints.text: It is still used by a royal family, and the oldest parts began as an Islamic citadel.
Its most famous palace was built for a Christian king by craftsmen working in an Islamic style.
Its delicate plaster arches, tiles and courtyards echo a famous palace in Granada.

summary.description: The Alcázar began as a 10th-century Islamic citadel, later enlarged by the Abbadids and Almohads, and was rebuilt after the Castilian conquest of 1248. Its heart is the Mudéjar palace built by King Pedro I in the 1360s, with courtyards such as the Patio de las Doncellas, richly carved plaster, tiles and wooden ceilings. Later Gothic and Renaissance additions and large gardens complete one of the finest examples of Mudéjar style in the Iberian Peninsula. It is still an official residence of the Spanish royal family.
keyFeatures: Mudéjar palace of Pedro I
Courtyards with scalloped arches and carved plaster
Later Gothic and Renaissance parts
Extensive gardens
funFacts: The upper floors are still used by the Spanish royal family when they visit Seville.
Craftsmen from Granada’s Nasrid court worked on the palace.

architects.name: Adrian Smith
architects.bio: Design partner at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, who led the design of the Burj Khalifa and shaped its three-lobed, spiralling form.

architects.name: Bill Baker
architects.bio: Structural engineer at SOM who devised the buttressed-core system that lets the tower rise to 828 metres.

hints.text: It is the tallest structure in the world, at almost 830 metres.
Its plan is based on a desert flower, and its three wings spiral away as the tower rises.
It was renamed just before opening, after the president of the country that bailed out its developer.

summary.description: Designed by the Chicago office of SOM, the Burj Khalifa rises 829.8 metres and has been the world's tallest structure since its opening in 2010. Its Y-shaped plan, inspired by a desert flower, steps back in spirals, which reduces wind forces on the tower. The primary structure is reinforced concrete around a buttressed core, and the tower is named after Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed, then president of the UAE.
keyFeatures: Y-shaped plan with three wings
Buttressed core structure
Stepped, spiralling set-backs
Total height of 829.8 metres
funFacts: Some structural steel came from the demolished Palace of the Republic in East Berlin.
It was called Burj Dubai until its inauguration.

name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque
aliases: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque Abu Dhabi

architects.name: Yusef Abdelki
architects.bio: Syrian architect who led the design team, drawing on Mamluk, Ottoman, Mughal and Moorish models for the mosque.

style: Modern Islamic (Mughal, Moorish and Mamluk influences)

hints.text: It is the largest mosque of its country, and its founder is buried in its courtyard.
It has 82 domes and more than a thousand columns, mostly in white marble.
Its prayer hall holds what is claimed to be the largest hand-knotted carpet in the world.

summary.description: Built between 1994 and 2007, the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque was launched by the first president of the UAE, who is buried in its courtyard. The complex measures about 290 by 420 metres and has 82 domes, more than 1,000 columns, gilded chandeliers and the world's largest hand-knotted carpet. Its design draws on Mamluk, Ottoman, Mughal and Moorish models, and it combines them in a modern composition of white marble.
keyFeatures: 82 domes of varying sizes
More than 1,000 columns in white marble
Floral inlays of semi-precious stones
Vast hand-knotted carpet and gilded chandeliers
funFacts: Its main axis is rotated about 12 degrees to point to Mecca.
A smaller replica stands in Surakarta, Indonesia.

architects.name: César Pelli
architects.bio: Argentine-born American architect who won the competition to design Kuala Lumpur’s landmark towers and drew their plan from Islamic geometry.

hints.text: They were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
Their plan is based on an eight-pointed Islamic star motif, with round lobes added to give more office space.
A two-storey bridge joins them partway up, and it is not rigidly fixed so that the towers can sway.

summary.description: Designed by César Pelli and completed in 1998, the 88-storey Petronas Towers rise to 451.9 metres and were the world's tallest buildings until 2004. They remain the tallest twin towers in the world. The plan is based on a Rub el Hizb, an eight-pointed Islamic star, with circular lobes added to provide office space, and the steel and glass façades echo Islamic motifs. A skybridge links the towers at the 41st and 42nd floors.
keyFeatures: Eight-pointed star plan based on Islamic geometry
Tube-in-tube structural system
Steel and glass cladding
Two-level skybridge between the towers
funFacts: They surpassed the original World Trade Center towers as the tallest twin towers.
Their structural design uses a tube-in-tube system invented by Fazlur Rahman Khan.

name: Tower of London (White Tower)
aliases: Her Majesty’s Royal Palace and Fortress of the Tower of London

architects.name: Gundulf of Rochester
architects.bio: Bishop of Rochester and a skilled builder, Gundulf was placed in charge of constructing the White Tower for William the Conqueror.

architects.name: William the Conqueror
architects.bio: The Norman duke who conquered England in 1066 and had the keep begun around 1078 as a symbol of his power over London.

hints.text: It began as a symbol of conquest, built by a king who had just taken a country by force.
Over the centuries it has been a palace, a prison, an armoury, a zoo and a mint, and it still guards a famous set of royal jewels.
Folklore says that if its resident black birds ever leave, the kingdom will fall.

summary.description: Begun around 1078 by William the Conqueror after the Norman conquest, the White Tower is a great keep of pale stone that gives the whole fortress its name. It was supervised by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester, and stands at the heart of a complex of buildings set within two rings of walls and a moat. Over the centuries the Tower has served as a royal residence, armoury, treasury, menagerie and prison, and it holds the Crown Jewels.
keyFeatures: Thick-walled Norman keep with corner turrets
Chapel of St John in the south-east corner
Two concentric rings of defensive walls
Home of the Crown Jewels
funFacts: It was begun in 1078 and was at first a resented symbol of oppression.
Kings Richard I, Henry III and Edward I expanded it in the 12th and 13th centuries.

name: Westminster Abbey
aliases: Collegiate Church of Saint Peter at Westminster

architects.name: Henry of Reynes
architects.bio: Master mason of Henry III, who began the present Gothic church in 1245 on the model of 13th-century French cathedrals.

architects.name: Henry III
architects.bio: King of England who ordered the church rebuilt from 1245 as a coronation church and a shrine for Edward the Confessor.

architects.name: Nicholas Hawksmoor
architects.bio: Baroque architect who, with John James, designed the Gothic-style western towers that were completed in the 1740s.

hints.text: Forty monarchs have been crowned here since 1066.
Its present church was begun in 1245 by a king who wanted a worthy shrine for a royal saint, and who took French cathedrals as his model.
Its two western towers were added only in the 1740s, in a Gothic style, by Baroque-trained designers.

summary.description: The present church was begun in 1245 on the orders of Henry III, who wanted a coronation church and a shrine for Edward the Confessor. Its Gothic architecture draws chiefly on 13th-century French and English styles, The Lady Chapel was added by Henry VII, and the western towers were built in the 1740s by Nicholas Hawksmoor and John James. It has been the site of the coronations of 40 monarchs since 1066.
keyFeatures: Tall French-inspired Gothic nave
Fan-vaulted Henry VII Chapel
Cosmati pavement before the high altar
Western towers by Hawksmoor and James
funFacts: At least 16 royal weddings have taken place here since 1100.
The abbey is a "royal peculiar", answerable to the sovereign rather than to a bishop.

architects.name: Master Gerhard
architects.bio: First master builder of the cathedral, who drew up the French-inspired Gothic plan and directed the work from 1248.

architects.name: Ernst Friedrich Zwirner
architects.bio: Prussian architect who led the 19th-century completion of the cathedral until his death, using modern iron roof girders.

hints.text: Work began in 1248, stopped for about three centuries, and was finally completed in 1880.
It is the tallest twin-spired church in the world, and its façade is the largest of any church.
It was finished in the 19th century according to its original medieval drawings, and it stood remarkably intact among the ruins of a bombed city in 1945.

summary.description: Begun in 1248 under Master Gerhard, Cologne Cathedral was left unfinished for about 300 years from around 1560. Construction resumed in the 19th century to the original medieval plan, with modern iron roof girders, and was completed in 1880. At 157 metres it is the tallest twin-spired church in the world, and its two towers give it the largest façade of any church. It shelters the reliquary of the Three Kings.
keyFeatures: 157-metre twin spires
Largest façade of any church
French High Gothic plan
Reliquary of the Three Kings
funFacts: Its medieval façade drawings survived and made the 19th-century completion possible.
It was declared a World Heritage Site in 1996.

name: Milan Cathedral
aliases: Metropolitan Cathedral-Basilica of the Nativity of Saint Mary

architects.name: Simone da Orsenigo
architects.bio: First chief engineer of the cathedral works, who planned to build in brick in the Lombard Gothic style.

architects.name: Nicolas de Bonaventure
architects.bio: French master appointed chief engineer in 1389, who brought the Rayonnant Gothic of northern Europe to Milan.

hints.text: It took nearly six centuries to complete, and its last details were finished in 1965.
It was begun in brick in a local style, but its patron wanted the newest northern Gothic, and a French master was called in.
Its roof is a forest of spires and statues, crowned by a gilded figure of the Virgin.

summary.description: Begun in 1386, Milan Cathedral took almost six centuries to finish, with the last details completed in 1965. Under its first chief engineer, Simone da Orsenigo, it was planned in brick in Lombard Gothic style, but its patrons soon adopted the northern Rayonnant Gothic brought by Nicolas de Bonaventure in 1389. It is the largest church in Italy, and its roof is covered with a forest of spires and statues. In 1805 Napoleon ordered the façade to be completed.
keyFeatures: Largest church in Italy
Rayonnant Gothic influenced by France
Forest of spires and thousands of statues
Five-aisled nave with giant clustered columns
funFacts: Napoleon ordered the façade completed before his coronation as King of Italy in 1805.
The gilded Madonnina on the highest spire became a symbol of the city.

architects.name: Bonanno Pisano
architects.bio: Sculptor and bronze caster of Pisa, long credited with the design of the tower, although the attribution is now disputed.

architects.name: Diotisalvi
architects.bio: Pisan architect of the Baptistery and the bell tower of San Nicola, proposed by a 2001 study as the original architect of the tower.

hints.text: It began to lean while it was still being built, because it stands on soft ground.
It is the bell tower of a cathedral, and it stands in a famous green square beside a baptistery.
A rescue in the 1990s reduced its tilt by about a degree and a half so that it would not topple.

summary.description: Begun in 1173 as the bell tower of Pisa's cathedral, the tower started to lean during construction because of the soft ground, and the work stretched over almost two centuries. Its eight tiers of arcades are built of white marble. It is 55.86 metres high on the low side, with 294 or 296 steps. After remedial work between 1993 and 2001 its tilt was reduced from 5.5 to 3.97 degrees.
keyFeatures: Eight tiers of marble arcades
Cylindrical tower with a bell chamber at the top
Tilt reduced to 3.97 degrees
Part of the Piazza dei Miracoli with the cathedral and baptistery
funFacts: The identity of its architect is still disputed.
The remedial work between 1993 and 2001 reduced its tilt from 5.5 to 3.97 degrees.

architects.name: Antonio Rizzo
architects.bio: Veronese sculptor and architect who rebuilt the east wing of the palace after the fire of 1483 and brought the Renaissance language into it.

architects.name: Francesco Foscari
architects.bio: Doge of Venice who decided in 1424 to extend the Gothic rebuilding to the wing overlooking the Piazzetta.

hints.text: It was the home of the elected ruler of a maritime republic, and also held its government offices and a prison.
Its upper floors are heavy and patterned, and rest on lighter open arcades, the opposite of what you would expect.
It is linked by a famous covered bridge to the prisons across a canal.

summary.description: The palace of the Doge, the elected ruler of the Republic of Venice, was rebuilt in the Venetian Gothic style from about 1340. In 1424 Doge Francesco Foscari ordered the works extended to the wing facing the Piazzetta, and after a fire in 1483 Antonio Rizzo brought the new Renaissance language into the reconstruction. It held the government offices, law courts and a prison. It became a museum in 1923.
keyFeatures: Venetian Gothic arcades and loggia
Pink and white patterned masonry on the upper floors
Renaissance courtyard façade by Rizzo
Great Council hall with huge paintings
funFacts: A fire in 1483 forced a major reconstruction of the canal-side wing.
It has been a museum since 1923.

architects.name: William of Volpiano
architects.bio: Italian-born Benedictine abbot and architect, builder of Fécamp Abbey, who was chosen by Richard II of Normandy to design the Romanesque abbey church, placing its crossing at the very top of the mount.

hints.text: It is an island only at high tide, and the sea here can rise and fall by about 14 metres.
A Benedictine abbey crowns its summit, with the church built right on the top of the rock.
It was never captured during the Hundred Years’ War, and it later served as a prison.

summary.description: On a rocky tidal island in Normandy, the abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel was begun in the 11th century, when William of Volpiano designed the Romanesque church at the very top of the mount, supported by crypts and chapels built beneath it. In the early 13th century the Gothic Merveille was added on the north side. The island was never conquered during the Hundred Years' War, and later served as a prison. It is today seen as a building of Romanesque architecture.
keyFeatures: Romanesque abbey church at the summit
Gothic Merveille buildings
Fortifications and a walled village
Tidal island with a 14-metre range
funFacts: The island was linked to the mainland by a raised causeway in 1879.
A small garrison beat off an English attack in 1433.

name: Saint Basil’s Cathedral
aliases: Cathedral of the Intercession of the Most Holy Theotokos on the Moat

architects.name: Postnik Yakovlev
architects.bio: Russian master builder traditionally credited, with the builder named in chronicles as Barma, with the cathedral. The identity of the architect is uncertain.

hints.text: It commemorates the capture of two cities by a feared tsar.
It is a cluster of separate chapels around a central tower, each topped by a differently patterned dome.
Legend says the tsar had its architect blinded so that he could never build anything like it again.

summary.description: Built from 1555 to 1561 on the orders of Ivan the Terrible, the cathedral commemorates the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan. It consists of a cluster of chapels around a central tent-roofed church, each crowned with a differently patterned dome; the bright colours were completed only in 1683. It has been called a prime example of Russian Renaissance architecture, and historians note that nothing similar exists in Russian building.
keyFeatures: Cluster of chapels around a central tent-roofed church
Onion domes in different patterns and colours
Brick walls with decorative detail
Stands on Red Square beside the Kremlin walls
funFacts: The colourful painting of the domes was completed only in 1683.
The architect’s identity is unknown; tradition names Postnik Yakovlev and Barma.

architects.name: Pierre Lescot
architects.bio: French Renaissance architect who designed the Lescot Wing from the late 1540s, the oldest standing part of the palace, on the orders of Francis I.

architects.name: Claude Perrault
architects.bio: Physician and architect credited, with Louis Le Vau and Charles Le Brun, with the classical east façade of the Cour Carrée, with its great colonnade.

architects.name: I. M. Pei
architects.bio: Architect of the glass pyramid added to the Cour Napoléon in 1989 as the main entrance to the museum.

hints.text: It began as a medieval fortress, became a royal palace, and is now one of the most visited museums in the world.
Its oldest standing wing, from the 1540s, brought the French Renaissance to a royal court.
A glass pyramid, added in 1989, now marks its main entrance in the middle of a courtyard.

summary.description: Built as a fortress in the late 12th century under Philip II, the Louvre was converted by Francis I in 1546 into a royal residence and redesigned and extended many times. Pierre Lescot's wing from the late 1540s is its oldest section above ground, while Claude Perrault's colonnade closes the east front of the Cour Carrée. Louis XIV moved to Versailles in 1682, leaving the palace to display the royal collections, and it became the national museum. I. M. Pei's glass pyramid was added in 1989.
keyFeatures: Lescot Wing of the French Renaissance
Classical east colonnade by Perrault
Cour Carrée and Cour Napoléon
Glass pyramid entrance by I. M. Pei
funFacts: Remains of the medieval fortress are visible in the basement.
Louis XIV chose Versailles over the Louvre in 1682.

architects.name: Jean-François Chalgrin
architects.bio: French Neoclassical architect who designed the arch in 1806 and led the work until his death in 1811. It was inspired by the Arch of Titus in Rome.

architects.name: Louis-Robert Goust
architects.bio: Architect who took over the work after Chalgrin’s death, and who built the arch up to its completion under the Bourbon Restoration and the July Monarchy.

hints.text: It was commissioned by an emperor after his greatest victory, but he did not live to see it finished.
The names of victories and generals are engraved on its inner and outer surfaces.
Twelve avenues meet at its feet, and an eternal flame burns beneath its vault.

summary.description: Commissioned in 1806 by Napoleon I after his victory at Austerlitz, the Arc de Triomphe was designed by Jean-François Chalgrin and inspired by the Arch of Titus in Rome. Work continued under Louis-Robert Goust after Chalgrin's death in 1811 and was completed only in 1836. It stands 49.54 metres high at the centre of the star-shaped Place Charles de Gaulle, at the western end of the Champs-Élysées. Beneath its vault lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
keyFeatures: Single huge opening between two massive piers
Sculpted groups and relief friezes
Names of victories and generals on its walls
Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath the vault
funFacts: A wooden mock-up of the arch was built to welcome Napoleon’s new bride in 1810.
It is at the centre of a star of twelve radiating avenues.

architects.name: Gustave Eiffel
architects.bio: Engineer whose company designed and built the tower from 1887 to 1889 as the centrepiece of the Exposition Universelle, and who gave it his name.

architects.name: Maurice Koechlin
architects.bio: Senior engineer at Eiffel’s company who made the first sketch of a great pylon of four lattice girders in 1884; the design is attributed to him and Émile Nouguier.

architects.name: Stephen Sauvestre
architects.bio: Head of the architectural department of Eiffel’s company, who added decorative arches at the base, a glass pavilion on the first level and other embellishments.

hints.text: It was built as the entrance arch of a world’s fair that celebrated a revolution’s centennial.
For 41 years it was the tallest human-made structure in the world, until an American skyscraper passed it in 1930.
Its wrought-iron lattice was shaped by wind-resistance calculations, and decorative arches were added at the base.

summary.description: Built from 1887 to 1889 by the company of the engineer Gustave Eiffel as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair and the centennial of the French Revolution, the tower is a 330-metre lattice of wrought iron. Its design is attributed to the engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, to which Stephen Sauvestre added the decorative arches and the glass pavilion. Initially criticised by many artists, it became the global symbol of France and the most visited paid monument in the world.
keyFeatures: 330-metre wrought-iron lattice
Four curved legs joined by arches
Decorative arches and a glass pavilion by Sauvestre
Three public levels
funFacts: It was the tallest structure in the world for 41 years, until the Chrysler Building in 1930.
Many of France’s leading artists and intellectuals protested against it before it was built.

name: Sacré-Cœur Basilica
aliases: Basilica of the Sacred Heart of Montmartre

architects.name: Paul Abadie
architects.bio: Architect and restorer of historic buildings, whose neo-Byzantine-Romanesque design was chosen from 77 proposals. After his death in 1884 the work was carried on by four other architects.

hints.text: It crowns the highest hill of its city, and its white domes can be seen from far away.
It was proposed as an act of penance after a military defeat and a civil uprising.
It took forty years and five architects to build, and it was consecrated only after a world war.

summary.description: Begun in 1875 on the summit of Montmartre, the basilica was proposed after France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune. Paul Abadie's neo-Byzantine-Romanesque plan was chosen from 77 proposals, and work went on for forty years under five architects. It was completed in 1914 and consecrated in 1919, after the First World War. Its white stone domes and bell tower make it one of the most recognisable silhouettes in Paris.
keyFeatures: Romano-Byzantine domes on a stone hill
Tall campanile
Three arched porches on the façade
Great apse mosaic
funFacts: It is the second most popular tourist destination in Paris, after the Eiffel Tower.
Its hilltop site overlooks where the 1871 uprising began.

architects.name: Imre Steindl
architects.bio: Architect who won the international competition for the new parliament in 1883 with a neo-Gothic design that resembled the Palace of Westminster. He went blind before it opened and died in 1902.

hints.text: It sits on the bank of a great river, and it has been the largest building in its country since it was finished.
Its Gothic Revival style recalls the parliament of another capital, which its architect’s plans resembled.
Its central dome crowns a hall where the national crown is displayed.

summary.description: Designed by Imre Steindl after an international competition won in 1883, the Parliament stands on the eastern bank of the Danube in Pest. Its neo-Gothic design resembles the Palace of Westminster, and it opened in 1902 as the largest building in Hungary. A central domed hall flanked by two symmetrical assembly chambers organises the plan. Steindl lost his sight before its completion and died the same year it opened.
keyFeatures: Neo-Gothic façade on the Danube
Central dome over the main hall
Symmetrical plan with two assembly chambers
Rich interiors with gilding and stained glass
funFacts: It has been the largest building in Hungary since its completion.
Steindl’s plans resembled the Palace of Westminster, which helped to win him the job.

architects.name: William Thornton
architects.bio: Physician and amateur architect whose late entry to the 1792 competition was chosen in 1793, drawing on the east front of the Louvre and the Panthéon in Paris. He served as the first Architect of the Capitol.

architects.name: Thomas U. Walter
architects.bio: Fourth Architect of the Capitol, who added the wings of the 1850s and designed the great cast-iron dome that was completed around 1866.

hints.text: Its design was picked in a competition, from a late entry by a physician who was an amateur architect.
Its massive iron dome was finished around 1866, just after a civil war.
British troops burned it in 1814, and it was rebuilt and extended with new wings for a growing legislature.

summary.description: The building where the United States Congress meets was designed by the amateur architect William Thornton, whose plans were approved in 1793. It was partly destroyed in 1814 by British forces and restored within five years, then extended with new wings in the 1850s, with the Senate in the north wing and the House in the south. The massive cast-iron dome by Thomas U. Walter was completed around 1866, just after the Civil War.
keyFeatures: Great cast-iron dome
Central rotunda under a fresco canopy
Symmetrical wings for the Senate and the House
East front portico
funFacts: Thornton took inspiration from the east front of the Louvre and the Panthéon in Paris.
The east front portico was extended in 1958.

architects.name: James Hoban
architects.bio: Irish-born architect who won the competition for the President’s House in 1792, modelling it on Leinster House in Dublin, and who rebuilt it after the fire of 1814.

hints.text: Its architect was an Irish immigrant who won a design competition in 1792.
It was burned by invading troops in 1814 and then rebuilt.
Its sandstone walls are painted white, and it was first called the President’s House.

summary.description: Designed by the Irish-born architect James Hoban, the residence and workplace of the American president was built between 1792 and 1800 in the Neoclassical style, modelled on Leinster House in Dublin. Its exterior walls are Aquia Creek sandstone painted white. It was set on fire in 1814 by British forces and rebuilt. The North Portico and South Portico were added later, and its wings have been extended repeatedly.
keyFeatures: Neoclassical front of the Georgian type
Aquia Creek sandstone painted white
Curved South Portico
State rooms such as the Red Room
funFacts: John Adams was the first president to live there, in 1800.
It is modelled on Leinster House in Dublin.

name: Reichstag Building

architects.name: Paul Wallot
architects.bio: Architect of the Neo-Renaissance parliament building, constructed between 1884 and 1894 for the German Empire.

architects.name: Norman Foster
architects.bio: British architect who redesigned the ruined building from 1995 to 1999 for the reunified German parliament, adding a glass dome that opens the roof to the public.

style: Neo-Renaissance with a modern glass dome

photos.alt: Heavy stone palace with corner towers, a columned portico and a glass dome, beside a river

hints.text: Its glass dome lets visitors look down into the debating chamber, a symbol of open government.
It was damaged by a famous fire in 1933 and stood without a parliament for decades before being rebuilt in the 1990s.
Behind an imperial stone exterior, a British architect added a futuristic dome in 1999.

summary.description: The Neo-Renaissance building was constructed between 1884 and 1894 on the River Spree to plans by Paul Wallot, to house the legislature of the German Empire. Severe damage in the fire of 1933 prevented its further use, and it was left in ruins after the Second World War. From 1995 to 1999 it was fundamentally redesigned by Norman Foster for the reunified German parliament, who crowned it with a glass dome open to the public.
keyFeatures: Neo-Renaissance stone exterior with corner towers
Glass dome with a spiral ramp
Mirrored cone that lights the debating chamber
Rebuilt by Foster between 1995 and 1999
funFacts: The 1933 fire was a pivotal event in the entrenchment of the Nazi regime.
Soviet soldiers left graffiti on its walls in 1945, which was kept in the rebuilding.

architects.name: Renzo Piano
architects.bio: Italian architect who, with Richard Rogers, won the 1971 competition for the cultural centre with a radical design that put its structure and pipes on the outside.

architects.name: Richard Rogers
architects.bio: British architect and a leader of high-tech architecture, who designed the Pompidou Centre with Renzo Piano, Gianfranco Franchini and Su Rogers.

architects.name: Gianfranco Franchini
architects.bio: Italian architect who was the third principal partner of the team that won the Pompidou Centre competition.

hints.text: It was designed to be turned inside out: its structure, stairs and service pipes are all on the outside.
Its pipes are colour-coded, with blue for air, green for water, yellow for electricity and red for movement.
It was named after a president, and it caused a scandal in an old district of its capital when it opened.

summary.description: Designed by Richard Rogers, Su Rogers and Renzo Piano, with Gianfranco Franchini, the Pompidou Centre is a landmark of high-tech architecture. It stands in the Beaubourg district of Paris and was named after Georges Pompidou, the president of France from 1969 to 1974. Its structure, escalators and service ducts are placed on the outside and painted in bright colours, leaving large open floors free inside for changing uses. It opened in 1977 and houses a modern art museum and a public library.
keyFeatures: Structure and services expressed on the outside
Colour-coded pipes and ducts
Glass-enclosed escalator running up the façade
Large, flexible open floors
funFacts: It was named after Georges Pompidou, president of France from 1969 to 1974.
The team won an international competition in 1971 with a design that many critics found shocking.

architects.name: Louis Kahn
architects.bio: Philadelphia architect known for monumental, light-filled buildings in concrete and brick, who designed the Salk Institute between 1959 and 1965 with the advice of the Mexican architect Luis Barragán.

photos.credit: Photo: Cristina Bejarano · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Wide travertine plaza with a central water channel running between two rows of concrete laboratory blocks toward the sea and a clear blue sky.
Two parallel stepped concrete and timber buildings facing each other across a bare stone court on a bluff

hints.text: It was built for a scientist who wanted a place where a Picasso might be at home, on a cliff above the ocean.
Two laboratory blocks frame a stone plaza, split by a thin channel of water that points to the horizon.
A Mexican architect advised leaving the court between them bare, as a façade to the sky.

summary.description: Built between 1959 and 1965 on a bluff above the Pacific, the Salk Institute was commissioned by the polio vaccine pioneer Jonas Salk and designed by Louis Kahn. Two laboratory blocks of concrete and teak face each other across a travertine plaza, divided by a thin channel of water that leads the eye to the horizon. Each laboratory floor is free of columns, with service floors in between, so the spaces can be changed as research changes.
keyFeatures: Two mirrored laboratory blocks
Central travertine plaza with a water channel
Column-free laboratory floors
Concrete, teak and glass
funFacts: Kahn first planned the central court with gardens, then followed the advice of Luis Barragán to leave it bare.
Blackboards were set into the walkway walls in place of concrete facing, for impromptu discussion.

architects.name: Herzog & de Meuron
architects.bio: Swiss architecture firm founded in Basel in 1978 by Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron. It won the 2003 competition for the stadium with a design of interwoven steel.

architects.name: Ai Weiwei
architects.bio: Chinese artist who was the artistic consultant on the stadium design, before later publicly distancing himself from the Olympics.

Huge oval stadium wrapped in a web of crossing steel members, standing on open land

hints.text: It was designed for an Olympic Games, by a Swiss practice working with a famous artist.
Its walls and roof are one interwoven web of steel, like twigs woven into a basket.
It can hold about 80,000 people, or 91,000 with temporary seating.

summary.description: Designed by the Swiss firm Herzog & de Meuron after a competition won in April 2003, the National Stadium was built between 2004 and 2008 for the Beijing Summer Olympics. Its structure and its façade are the same thing: a web of interlaced steel members that looks like a bird's nest. It covers about 204,000 square metres and holds 80,000 spectators, or 91,000 with temporary seating, and it hosted the opening ceremony in 2008 and the 2022 Winter Games.
keyFeatures: Self-supporting steel lattice
Façade and structure are one
Seating for 80,000 spectators
Used for both the 2008 and 2022 Olympics
funFacts: It was used for the 2008 Summer Olympics and again for the 2022 Winter Olympics.
Ai Weiwei served as the artistic consultant on the design.

architects.name: Warren and Wetmore
architects.bio: New York firm that designed the Beaux-Arts station house and its sculpted façade, in partnership with Reed and Stem, which handled the engineering and the train shed.

architects.name: Reed and Stem
architects.bio: St. Paul firm that won the 1903 competition and designed the multi-level plan of the terminal, with its ramps and separate levels for long-distance and suburban trains.

Its great hall has a ceiling painted with the constellations, though it is shown as seen from outside the sky.
It was nearly demolished in the 1960s, and its rescue made a landmark law.

summary.description: Opened in 1913 at 42nd Street and Park Avenue, Grand Central Terminal is a commuter rail terminal known for its Beaux-Arts station house and its vast main concourse. The architecture was a joint work of the firms Reed and Stem and Warren and Wetmore. Its multi-level plan separates trains and pedestrians with ramps, and it is the southern end of three Metro-North lines. It is the third-busiest station in North America.
keyFeatures: Beaux-Arts station house
Vast main concourse with arched windows
Multi-level plan with ramps
Celestial ceiling
funFacts: It is the third-busiest train station in North America.
Grand Central Madison, a 16-acre addition under the tracks, was built from 2007 to 2023.
