It honours a president, and a huge marble figure of him fills its central room.

summary.description: Dedicated on 30 May 1922, the Lincoln Memorial honours Abraham Lincoln, the 16th president of the United States, at the western end of the National Mall in Washington, D.C. Its architect, Henry Bacon, built it as a neoclassical temple in the form of a classical temple with Doric columns around the exterior. Inside, a large statue designed by Daniel Chester French and carved in marble by the Piccirilli brothers sits in front of murals by Jules Guérin.

Large seated marble statue by Daniel Chester French
Interior murals by Jules Guérin
Placed at the end of the Reflecting Pool
funFacts: It has often been used as a symbolic centre for civil rights gatherings.
The statue was carved from marble by the Piccirilli brothers.

It is said to have about 1,500 rooms, 1,886 doors and 1,945 windows.
Its pale green and white front is Baroque, and it now houses one of the world’s great art museums.

summary.description: The present Winter Palace, the fourth on its site, served as the official residence of the Romanov emperors from 1732 to 1917 and was built and altered almost continuously between the late 1730s and 1837, when a fire severely damaged it and it was immediately rebuilt. Its Baroque design is the work of Bartolomeo Francesco Rastrelli. It contains about 1,500 rooms, 1,886 doors and 1,945 windows, and now houses the Hermitage Museum.

Pale green façade with white and gold detail
About 1,500 rooms and 117 staircases
Now part of the Hermitage Museum
funFacts: It was rebuilt immediately after the fire of 1837.
The storming of the palace in 1917 became a symbol of the October Revolution.

It is said to have 1,441 rooms, and its enormous garden is part of the same design.
It is a Baroque palace that was remodelled in the Rococo style for an empress who had sixteen children.

summary.description: Schönbrunn was the main summer residence of the Habsburg rulers, located in the 13th district of Vienna. The 1,441-room Baroque palace, one of the most important architectural, cultural and historic monuments in Austria, grew over more than 300 years, reflecting the changing tastes of successive monarchs. Its plans were first drawn by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach, and it was remodelled for Empress Maria Theresa by Nikolaus Pacassi. It has been a major tourist attraction since the mid-1950s.
keyFeatures: 1,441 rooms
Baroque and Rococo interiors
Great Gallery with ceiling paintings
Vast formal gardens with the Gloriette
funFacts: Emperor Franz Joseph was born here and died here in 1916, aged 86.
The name means "beautiful spring", after an artesian well.

A giant golden steel ball hangs inside its upper floors to keep it steady in typhoons and earthquakes.

summary.description: Taipei 101, formerly the Taipei World Financial Center, is a 508-metre, 101-storey skyscraper in Taipei, Taiwan. Its postmodernist and neo-futurist design evokes traditional Asian aesthetics in a modern structure, with stacked, flared segments like a pagoda or bamboo. It was officially the tallest building in the world from its opening on 31 December 2004 until it was surpassed by the Burj Khalifa in 2009. A tuned mass damper in the upper floors counters wind and earthquake sway.

Tuned mass damper sphere

Shopping mall with the world’s largest ruyi symbol
funFacts: It was the tallest building in the world from 2004 to 2009.
It is the setting of a famous New Year’s Eve fireworks display.

summary.description: Adolf Loos designed this villa in Prague for František Müller, co-owner of a reinforced-concrete construction company, and it was completed in 1930. Its plain white cubic exterior follows Loos's essay on ornament, while the interior is richly finished in marble, wood and silk. Inside, the rooms are arranged at different levels in what Loos called the Raumplan, a design of spaces rather than of floor plans, facades and sections. The architect Karel Lhota also contributed because of Loos's poor health.

funFacts: Loos celebrated his 60th birthday in the house with a few friends after it was finished.
Communists seized the villa in 1948; it was restored in 1998 and reopened as a museum in 2000.

summary.description: Built in 1910 in Vienna, the Steiner House is one of the major works of Adolf Loos. Because only one storey could rise above street level on the street side, Loos gave the house a quarter-round roof facing the street, which hides the two further floors that look onto the garden. The raised living area is separated from the private rooms, and the service spaces sit in the basement and attic. Its stucco facade is smooth and unornamented, and reveals nothing of the interior.

funFacts: The curved roof was a way to build within the street-side height limit while keeping two more floors toward the garden.
Loos used stucco as a protective skin over brick, not as a cheap imitation of stone.

summary.description: Designed in 1907 by Adolf Loos and finished in 1908, this cocktail bar in central Vienna fits into about 290 square feet, yet feels expansive thanks to mirrors above mahogany panelling and tiles of onyx, which are echoed by green and white marble on the floor. There is no ornament beyond the materials themselves, which are left unaltered. The street front carries an illuminated mosaic of a national flag above four green marble columns. Loos published Ornament and Crime four years later, and it is likely that he developed its ideas while working on the bar.

Floor of green and white marble
Illuminated flag mosaic on the street front
funFacts: Its materials are all left in their original state, without dye or added decoration.
The bar was the subject of several recreations and an exhibition in Los Angeles.

summary.description: Designed by Alvar Aalto in 1962 and built between 1967 and 1971, the hall was inaugurated on 2 December 1971 with a concert that included Sibelius's violin concerto played by Isaac Stern. It was the only part of a grand plan for a new monumental centre around Töölö Bay in Helsinki to be built. Its tower-like section with a sloping roof, hidden by a lattice ceiling, gives the main hall a deep post-echo, and Carrara marble is set against black granite. Aalto designed every detail, from lamps to furniture, as a total work of art.

Lattice ceiling hiding the high space above the audience

funFacts: A black trapezium on the white tower makes the National Museum look as if it rises from the hall when seen from across Töölö Bay.
The Congress Wing was designed in 1970 and built in 1973–1975.

summary.description: Alvar Aalto won the commission in a 1949 competition, and the building was completed in December 1951 for the small factory town of Säynätsalo, which merged with Jyväskylä in 1993. A U-shaped council chamber and town hall and a community library with flats surround a raised central courtyard, inspired by the Italian Renaissance. The palette is limited to brick, timber and copper, and a glass-enclosed walkway borders the courtyard like an arcade. The double-height council chamber is crowned by Aalto's butterfly trusses.

Palette of brick, timber and copper
Glass-enclosed circulation space like an arcade
Council chamber with butterfly trusses, reached by a ramp
funFacts: Aalto had already been commissioned in 1944 to design a town plan for Säynätsalo, a wood-processing mill town.
He wanted the large public space and the public sections to express the relationship between democracy and government.

summary.description: Aino and Alvar Aalto designed this L-shaped house in the Helsinki suburb of Munkkiniemi as their home and workspace, and it was completed in August 1936, roughly at the same time as the Viipuri Library. Living quarters are on the upper floor and the studio at ground level. The street front is closed and harsh, softened by climbing plants and a slate path. With plentiful wood and four brick fireplaces, the house anticipates Villa Mairea and shows a more romantic functionalism.

summary.description: Alvar Aalto designed this office in 1955–56 in the Tiilimäki neighbourhood of Munkkiniemi, Helsinki, when his practice outgrew his home. The facade is plain white-painted, lightly rendered brick, and the closed mass conceals an inner courtyard garden shaped like an amphitheatre, with slate steps. Large windows light the upstairs workspace on both sides. An extension in 1963 added a kitchen and dining space known as the taverna.

summary.description: Alvar Aalto designed this Lutheran church in Kaukopää, Imatra, and it was completed in 1958; it is said to be his most original church design. Three consecutive halls can be separated by sliding walls, which lets parts of the church be used for parish activities during the week. The exterior is white with copper roofing. Docomomo lists it as a significant example of modern architecture in Finland.

summary.description: Frank Lloyd Wright bought the site in the McDowell Mountains in 1937, and his apprentices raised the first structures between 1938 and 1941 as a winter home and studio. The buildings are arranged on a 45-degree grid and connected by courtyards and walkways, with walls of desert masonry, a mixture of local rocks and concrete, originally topped by wood-and-canvas roofs. The main building has a drafting room, kitchen, dining room, garden court and the family residence, and the complex also has a kiva room and two performance venues. It is a National Historic Landmark and a World Heritage Site.

summary.description: After the Unity Church of Oak Park burned down in 1905, the trustees hired Frank Lloyd Wright. Construction began in May 1906, Unity House opened in 1907, the auditorium was finished in October 1908 and the church was dedicated in 1909. The building is made of reinforced concrete, with a facade of Portland cement washed to expose the gravel and recessed clerestory windows near the top. Instead of a spire it has flat, overhanging roof slabs, and it is decorated with abstract motifs rather than religious imagery. It is cited as an early example of modern architecture.

summary.description: Frank Lloyd Wright designed this house for the heiress Aline Barnsdall, who had planned a theatrical complex since 1915 on a hill she acquired in 1919. The house and its outbuildings, completed in 1921, were the only parts of the complex built. Its three wings, with the living and music room, the dining and kitchen wing, and the gallery and bedroom wing, surround a central courtyard. The walls are hollow clay tile, wood frame and stucco sloping inward at the top. Rudolph Schindler, Richard Neutra and Wright's son Lloyd Wright helped design it, and it became the first World Heritage Site in Los Angeles.

summary.description: Harold C. Price Sr., head of a pipeline-construction firm, hired Frank Lloyd Wright in 1952 to design the headquarters in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, and the nineteen-story, 221-foot tower opened in February 1956. It derives from a 1929 proposal for apartment buildings in New York City. The plan is laid out on a grid of parallelograms with 30-60-90 triangles around a pinwheel-shaped structural core with four piers, and the reinforced-concrete floors cantilever outward from it. The facade combines embossed copper spandrels and louvers with tinted glass and poured stucco. It received the AIA's Twenty-five Year Award in 1983.

summary.description: S. C. Johnson's chief executive, Herbert Fisk Johnson Jr., hired Frank Lloyd Wright in 1936 to design the Administration Building, which was completed in April 1939; the 15-story Research Tower followed in November 1950. The Administration Building is a variation of the streamlined Art Moderne style, with a curved brick facade and Pyrex glass-tube windows. Its main interior space is a great workroom with concrete shell columns topped by large calyxes, and offices on a mezzanine and penthouse hold furniture designed by Wright. The tower alternates square floors with circular mezzanines cantilevered from its core.

summary.description: Built between 1887 and 1889 by Adler & Sullivan, the partnership of Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan, this early skyscraper in Chicago's Loop is 240 feet tall, mostly ten storeys with a 17-storey tower to the south. It was a multi-use complex of theatre, offices and hotel, financed by a syndicate led by Ferdinand Peck, and the theatre opened on 9 December 1889. Its iron and steel frame rises on grillage foundations, and the theatre occupies much of its volume, with 4,200 seats on four levels. Roosevelt University took over the building in 1946 and turned the offices and hotel into classrooms.

summary.description: Built in 1908 in Owatonna, Minnesota, the bank was the first of Louis Sullivan's "jewel box" bank designs, with decorative elements by George Elmslie. The building is clad in red brick with green terra-cotta bands, and two large arches mark its street-facing facades. Single-storey wings that housed bank offices extend along each side. Inside are two stained-glass windows by Louis J. Millet, a mural by Oskar Gross and four huge cast-iron electroliers designed by Elmslie. Sullivan's plan included a farmers' exchange room, a women's consultation room, a board room and the president's office.

summary.description: Louis Sullivan designed this twelve-storey building at State and Madison streets in Chicago for the retailer Schlesinger & Mayer, overseeing the original 1899 building and a 1903 annex. It was Sullivan's last large commercial building. On each elevation, piers divide the facade into bays with wide Chicago windows, and a curved corner joins the two. The lowest two storeys are clad in decorative cast iron, and the upper windows are framed by white terra-cotta bands. The superstructure is cast iron and steel columns supporting terra-cotta floor slabs, and the interior was planned with open spaces between the columns to maximise selling space.

summary.description: Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru asked Le Corbusier to build a new capital for Punjab, a city free of the traditions of the past, and the Palace of Assembly became the centre of its Capitol Complex. Construction began in 1951 and ended in 1962, and the building was inaugurated on 15 April 1964. It houses the Punjab and Haryana legislative assemblies and has a circular assembly chamber, a forum for conversation and stair-free circulation. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

summary.description: Designed between May 1953 and 1960 by Le Corbusier, his final building, this Dominican priory stands on a hillside at Éveux-sur-l'Arbresle, 25 km from Lyon. Four heavy rectangular wings form a closed interior space: the church and its sacristy occupy the compact block at the edge of the hill, while the other three wings, raised on pilotis of many shapes, hold the living and working spaces. The building is reinforced concrete, with undulating glass surfaces on three faces designed by Iannis Xenakis. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

summary.description: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed the museum and its sculpture gardens, which opened on 15 September 1968 in West Berlin south of the Tiergarten. The upper story is an entrance hall and the main special-exhibition gallery, under a square black steel roof plate 1.8 metres thick carried by eight cruciform columns, with an 18-metre cantilever and floor-to-ceiling glass 8.4 metres high on a 3.6-metre grid. The lower story, three-quarters below ground, houses the permanent collection, a library, offices, a shop and a café. David Chipperfield Architects renovated it, and it reopened in August 2021.

summary.description: Completed in 1956 on the campus of the Illinois Institute of Technology, S. R. Crown Hall was designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe for the College of Architecture, which he led for two decades. A glass curtain wall in three tiers of panes, between steel columns and mullions, wraps a rectangular building of 120 by 220 feet. Four girders on four pairs of columns hold the roof 18 feet above the main level, leaving an open plan with half-height partitions. The main level is raised six feet and reached from a porch on the south side. It is a Chicago Landmark and a National Historic Landmark.

summary.description: Peter Zumthor designed this spa over the thermal springs of Vals, in Graubünden, on the site of a failed 1960s hotel complex that the village had bought in 1983. Built between 1993 and 1996 from locally quarried Valser quartzite, it is made of 15 table-like units 5 metres high, with cantilevered concrete roofs supported by tie-beams and 8 cm gaps covered with glass. The concept is an interpretation of a stone quarry, with a constant change between very small intimate spaces and the large meandering bath. Since 2012 the hotel and spa have been privately owned and renamed 7132 Therme & Hotel.

hints.text: It stands on the site of a Romanesque church destroyed in World War II, and wraps around its ruins.
A perforated grey brick facade wraps around the museum and the old church like a cloak.
Its sixteen exhibition rooms differ in daylight, size, proportion and pathways.

summary.description: Built from 2003 to 2007 for the Archdiocese of Cologne, the museum was designed by Peter Zumthor, whose atelier won the competition in 1997, and it was consecrated on 15 September 2007. It sits on the site of the Romanesque church of St. Kolumba, destroyed in World War II, and shares it with the Gothic ruins and the 1950 chapel 'Madonna of the Ruins' by Gottfried Böhm. A perforated cloak of light grey brick, specially fired for the project, wraps the museum and the old church. The sixteen exhibition rooms have walls of light grey brick and clay plaster, floors of Jura limestone and terrazzo, and ceilings of poured mortar.
keyFeatures: Perforated light grey brick facade made of specially fired bricks
Built on the foundations and remains of St. Kolumba
Sixteen exhibition rooms with varying daylight
Includes the 1950 chapel "Madonna of the Ruins" by Gottfried Böhm
funFacts: The museum was founded by the Society for Christian Art in 1853 and taken over by the Archdiocese in 1989.
Until April 2007 the collection was housed near Cologne Cathedral.

architects.name: Peter Zumthor
architects.bio: Swiss architect who won the Pritzker Prize in 2009. He works slowly and on few commissions, with a close attention to materials, light and atmosphere, in buildings such as the thermal baths at Vals, the Kunsthaus Bregenz and the Kolumba museum in Cologne.

hints.text: It opened in July 1997 with an exhibition by James Turrell.
It was conceived as a "daylight museum", and from outside the glass-sheathed cube looks like a lamp.
Its architect won the Mies van der Rohe Award for European Architecture in 1998.

summary.description: Commissioned by the State of Vorarlberg and designed by the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor, the Kunsthaus Bregenz was built between 1990 and 1997 on the shore of Lake Constance and opened in July 1997 with an exhibition by James Turrell. It is made of glass, steel and a cast concrete mass that gives texture and spatial composition to the interior. From outside the building looks like a lamp, absorbing and reflecting the light of the sky and the haze of the lake. Conceived as a daylight museum, it is a fine example of architectural minimalism that presents temporary exhibitions of international contemporary art.
keyFeatures: Glass-sheathed cube on the shore of Lake Constance
Cast concrete interior mass
Conceived as a daylight museum
Temporary exhibitions of international contemporary art
funFacts: Edelbert Köb was the first director, from 1997 to 2000.
Zumthor was also the 2009 Pritzker Prize laureate.

hints.text: It commemorates 91 people tried and executed for witchcraft in 1621.
It has two buildings: a 120-metre wooden structure framing a fabric cocoon, and a square smoked-glass room.
One of its two buildings holds the last major installation of a French-American artist.

summary.description: The memorial in Vardø, in Finnmark, Norway, commemorates the trial and execution in 1621 of 91 people for witchcraft. It was designed by the artist Louise Bourgeois and the architect Peter Zumthor, began in 2006 and opened on 23 June 2011 in the presence of Queen Sonja. It comprises a 410-foot wooden structure framing a fabric cocoon that holds Zumthor's installation, and a square smoked-glass room, 39 feet on each side, that holds Bourgeois's work. Bourgeois died in 2010, and The Damned, The Possessed and The Beloved was her last major installation.
keyFeatures: 120-metre wooden structure framing a fabric cocoon
Square smoked-glass room with Louise Bourgeois's installation
Commissioned by the town, county, museum and national roads administration
Linked to the Norwegian National Tourist Routes
funFacts: Finnmark had the highest rate of witchcraft accusations in Norway and an unusually high proportion of executions.
The memorial was built 348 years after the peak of the trials in 1662–1663.

architects.name: Tadao Ando
architects.bio: Self-taught Japanese architect and former boxer, winner of the Pritzker Prize in 1995. Ando is known for poured-in-place concrete, with a smooth finish, that frames light, water and nature in quiet, geometric spaces, from the Church of the Light to the museums of Naoshima.

hints.text: It is a privately owned wedding chapel on the island of Hokkaido.
A large floor-to-ceiling window frames a reflecting pool, in the Japanese tradition of "borrowed scenery".
Its architect designed it in 1985 and completed it a few years later.

summary.description: Designed by Tadao Ando in 1985 and completed in 1988, this privately owned wedding chapel stands in Tomamu, Shimukappu, on the island of Hokkaido. The chapel faces a large reflecting pool visible through a floor-to-ceiling window, in the Japanese architectural tradition of shakkei, or borrowed scenery. Concrete and glass frame the water, the cross and the surrounding trees.
keyFeatures: Floor-to-ceiling glass wall facing a reflecting pool
Cross standing in the water
Concrete box with a glass cube on the roof
Use of shakkei, or borrowed scenery
funFacts: It is also known as the Chapel on the Water, and in Japanese as Mizu no Kyokai.
It is a notable project of the Japanese modernist architect Tadao Ando.

Its building opened to the public on 14 December 2002, after a five-year design process.
Three long pavilions are set into a reflecting pond, beside two other famous museums in the same cultural district.

summary.description: The Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth, founded in 1892, has been housed since 14 December 2002 in a building designed by the Japanese architect Tadao Ando. Michael Auping, the museum's chief curator, worked closely with Ando during the five-year design process to ensure that the interior spaces met the needs of curators and artists. The building features three long pavilions set into a reflecting pond and provides 53,000 square feet of gallery space. In 2019 it was selected as the Best Designed Building in Texas by Architectural Digest.
keyFeatures: Three long pavilions set into a reflecting pond
53,000 square feet of gallery space
Concrete and glass galleries lit from above
Located in the Cultural District beside the Kimbell Art Museum and the Amon Carter Museum
funFacts: The permanent collection has more than 3,000 works of international modern and contemporary art.
The museum holds works by Picasso, Rothko, Pollock and Richter, among many others.

architects.name: Zaha Hadid
architects.bio: Iraqi-British architect who in 2004 became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize. Hadid's flowing, fragmented forms, first explored in drawings and paintings, grew from deconstructivism into a fluid, curved style seen in buildings around the world.

hints.text: All its functions and entrances are folds of a single continuous surface.
In 2014 it won the Design Museum's Design of the Year, making its architect the first woman to win it.
It spreads over eight floor levels and holds a 1,000-seat auditorium, exhibition spaces, workshops and a museum.

summary.description: Zaha Hadid was appointed design architect in 2007 after a competition for this 57,500-square-metre complex in the centre of Baku. Its flowing form emerges from the folding of the landscape's natural topography and the wrapping of individual functions, with entrances and all functions represented by folds in one continuous surface that eschews sharp angles. It extends over eight floor levels and houses a 1,000-seat auditorium, temporary exhibition spaces, a conference centre, workshops and a museum. The building had a soft opening on 10 May 2012.
keyFeatures: Single continuous folded surface with no sharp angles
Eight floor levels
1,000-seat auditorium
Conference centre, workshops and a museum
funFacts: It won the Design Museum's Design of the Year Award in 2014, despite concerns about the site's human rights record.
In 2013 it held the first exhibition in Azerbaijan of over a hundred works by Andy Warhol.

It has a 50-metre competition pool, a 25-metre diving pool and a 50-metre warm-up pool.
The spectator wings were not in the original design; they were added to fit the estimated audience.

summary.description: Designed by Zaha Hadid in 2004, before London won the bid for the 2012 Summer Olympics, the centre was built opposite the Olympic Stadium on the opposite bank of the Waterworks River. It is 45 metres high, 160 metres long and 80 metres wide, under a wave-like roof. Its 50-metre pool is 3 metres deep, with a floor that can be moved and booms to change its size. The diving pool has platforms at 3, 5, 7.5 and 10 metres and three 3-metre springboards. The spectator wings were added later, and after significant modification it opened to the public in March 2014.
keyFeatures: Wave-like roof over three pools
50-metre competition pool with a movable floor
Diving platforms at 3, 5, 7.5 and 10 metres
Temporary spectator wings for the Games
funFacts: The IOC president Jacques Rogge described it as a "masterpiece".
The revised 2006 design was much smaller than the first, which would have doubled its estimated cost.

It was completed in 2005 for 67 million euros, after just over four years of construction.
Its exhibition of about 9,000 square metres has no prescribed route.

summary.description: The science centre in Wolfsburg was designed by Zaha Hadid with the Lörrach firm Mayer Bährle, cost 67 million euros and opened its permanent exhibition on 24 November 2005, after just over four years of construction. More than 350 interactive experiment stations, around 40 designed by artists, fill the roughly 9,000-square-metre exhibition, which is divided into the themes Life, Vision, Energy, Dynamics, Sense and Maths. The entrance area, the ideas forum and the science theatre are on the ground floor, with the main exhibition floor above.
keyFeatures: Interactive exhibition of about 9,000 square metres
More than 350 experiment stations
Science theatre with live demonstrations
Workshops for schoolchildren and teachers
funFacts: There is no prescribed course: simple experimental arrangements invite visitors to work out the functions for themselves.
Text panels at each station explain the process in German and English.

architects.bio: American architect and theorist, a leading figure of deconstructivism. Eisenman's work plays with grids, shifts and abstract rules rather than conventional composition, from early houses numbered in Roman numerals to the Wexner Center in Ohio and the Holocaust memorial in Berlin.

summary.description: Designed by Peter Eisenman with Buro Happold, this memorial in Berlin covers 1.9 hectares with 2,711 concrete slabs arranged in a grid pattern on a sloping field, a block south of the Brandenburg Gate. The slabs are 2.38 metres long and 0.95 metres wide and range from 0.2 to 4.7 metres in height. Long, straight, narrow alleys run between them along ground that undulates. Building began on 1 April 2003 and finished on 15 December 2004, and it was inaugurated on 10 May 2005. An underground information centre holds the names of about 3 million Jewish victims of the Holocaust.
keyFeatures: 2,711 concrete slabs in a grid on a sloping field
Slabs from 0.2 to 4.7 metres high, set slightly askew
Narrow alleys between the slabs along undulating ground
Underground "Place of Information" with the names of about 3 million victims
funFacts: The original plan was for nearly 4,000 slabs, but only 2,711 could legally fit the site.
It stands on the former location of the Berlin Wall's "death strip" and cost about 25 million euros.

It stands on the bank of Guaíba Lake, designed by a Pritzker Prize–winning Portuguese architect.

summary.description: The headquarters and museum of the Iberê Camargo Foundation, dedicated to preserving and promoting the work of the Brazilian painter Iberê Camargo (1914–1994), were designed by the Pritzker Prize–winning Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza. The foundation was created in 1995, a year after the artist's death, and it also aims to stimulate reflection on contemporary art through displays, courses, seminars and meetings. Before the building was inaugurated in May 2008, it operated in the artist's own home, also in Porto Alegre. The new building stands on the bank of Guaíba Lake.
keyFeatures: Curved concrete ramps and balconies wrapped around a tower
Skylit white galleries crossed by wide passages
Site on the bank of Guaíba Lake
Headquarters, museum and study centre for one painter
funFacts: The honorary president of the foundation is the painter's widow, Maria Coussirat Camargo.
The foundation offers courses, seminars and meetings as well as exhibitions.

summary.description: The contemporary art museum of the town of Chaves was inaugurated in July 2016 in a building designed by Álvaro Siza Vieira. A municipal museum, it permanently shows the work of the painter Nadir Afonso, and also presents other contemporary art in temporary exhibitions. The core of the collection is fifteen works on canvas and chipboard that Nadir Afonso donated to the municipality in 1982. The building holds a foyer, a library, an auditorium for about a hundred people, a bar and four exhibition rooms.
keyFeatures: Foyer, library, auditorium for about a hundred people and a bar
Four exhibition rooms
Permanent display of the painter Nadir Afonso
Logo designed by the architect in 2016

In 2019 part of the collection of the Museu Nacional de Arte Contemporânea was announced to move here, as a "pole of the Museu do Chiado".

summary.description: Designed by Álvaro Siza Vieira, the Bouça housing complex on Rua da Boavista in Porto was built under the SAAL programme. Its difficult site beside an elevated railway embankment forced the construction of a large wall to block the sound of the trains, which are now metro trains. The complex has four longitudinal blocks organised by repeating a module, joined at the ends and by the wall. The dwellings, from one to four bedrooms, fit into each other in both plan and section.
keyFeatures: Four long blocks linked by a large noise wall
Repetition of a single module
Dwellings of one to four bedrooms fitted together in plan and section
Part of the SAAL social housing programme

The parallel arrangement of the homes creates an internal environment that is potentially problematic, according to the programme's documentation.

It was abandoned in 1834, when male religious orders were abolished, and its project for a new use was presented in 1989.
It has been classified as a Property of Public Interest since 1958, and an inn opened in it in 1997.

summary.description: Part of an old monastery in the municipality of Amares, in northern Portugal, was converted into an inn, the Pousada de Santa Maria do Bouro. The project of the architect Eduardo Souto de Moura for adapting the monastery's buildings was presented in 1989, work began in 1994 and the inn was inaugurated in 1997. The monastery was given by Afonso Henriques to the Benedictines in 1148 and followed the Cistercian rule from 1195. It was rebuilt from the late 16th century, with new decoration in carved wood and tiles, and abandoned in 1834, when male religious orders were abolished. It has been classified as a Property of Public Interest since 1958.

Church of three naves and a central cloister
Restoration from 1994 to 1997
Classified as a Property of Public Interest in 1958

summary.description: Designed by Eduardo Souto de Moura, who also designed the Porto Metro's Trindade station, this underground station on Avenida da França was inaugurated on 7 December 2002, with commercial services beginning on 1 January 2003. It was built on the site of the old Avenida da França station on the Porto to Póvoa and Famalicão railway line, which closed in 2001 to enable the metro's construction. It is one of the main underground stations of the network, and is already prepared for a future line to be installed under it. The station takes its name from the nearby concert hall.

summary.description: Designed by the Italian architect Renzo Piano, the 95-storey pyramid-shaped skyscraper in Southwark rises 309.6 metres, making it the tallest building in the United Kingdom and Western Europe. Construction began in March 2009, it was topped out on 30 March 2012 and inaugurated on 5 July 2012, with practical completion in November 2012. The glass-clad tower has 72 habitable floors, with a viewing gallery and an open-air observation deck on the 72nd floor, which opened to the public on 1 February 2013. It was developed by Sellar Property Group and is owned 95% by the State of Qatar.

summary.description: The California Academy of Sciences, a research institute and natural history museum in Golden Gate Park, began in 1853 as a learned society and is California's oldest operating museum and research institution for the natural sciences. Its primary building, completely rebuilt in 2008 to a design by Renzo Piano, covers 400,000 square feet. It includes the Kimball Natural History Museum, the Morrison Planetarium with a 90-foot digitally controlled dome, and a rainforest enclosed in a 90-foot glass dome. Research and administrative facilities occupy nearly half of the building.

summary.description: The Whitney Museum of American Art, founded in 1930 by Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, moved in 2015 to a new building at 99 Gansevoort Street in the Meatpacking District, designed by Renzo Piano. It closed its former home on Madison Avenue, designed by Marcel Breuer and Hamilton P. Smith, in October 2014 and opened here on 1 May 2015, expanding the exhibition space to 50,000 square feet. The museum focuses on collecting and preserving 20th- and 21st-century American art and holds more than 25,000 works by more than 3,500 artists.

summary.description: Designed by Norman Foster with Ove Arup & Partners, this 47-storey, 178.8-metre tower is a steel suspended structure completed on 18 November 1985 and opened on 7 April 1986. The bank had outgrown its 1935 headquarters and decided in 1978 to replace it with a building that would symbolise modernisation. It took seven years from concept to completion, and was then the most expensive building in the world at about HK$5.2 billion. A modular design of five steel modules, prefabricated in the UK, allowed rapid on-site assembly and large open interior spaces, an example of high-tech architecture.

summary.description: Sage Gateshead, now officially The Glasshouse, is an international centre for musical education and concerts on the Gateshead bank of the Quayside. It was developed by Foster and Partners, who were unanimously chosen as the winner after a competition launched in 1997 managed by RIBA Competitions, where over 100 architects registered interest, 12 were invited to prepare concept designs and six were shortlisted. It cost over £70 million, mainly from National Lottery grants, with Laing O'Rourke as contractor, and opened over the weekend of 17–19 December 2004. The design won the RIBA Inclusive Design Award and the Civic Trust Award.

summary.description: The art museum on the campus of the University of East Anglia was one of the first major public buildings designed by Norman Foster and Wendy Cheesman, designed between 1974 and 1976 and opened in 1978. It sits on sloping, turfed ground beside the River Yare as a large cuboid, clad steel structure, one face of which is almost entirely glazed with its prefabricated skeleton visible. Inside, a regular structure embraces all functions in a single, flexible enclosure, a 'universal space', with no internal divisions to interfere with the interplay of natural and artificial light. It became Grade II* listed in December 2012.

summary.description: The airport's main passenger terminal, which opened in 1991, was designed by Foster Associates, founded by Norman Foster, with structural engineering led by Peter Rice at Ove Arup & Partners. The plans were approved in 1985 and construction by the John Laing company took place between 1988 and 1991 at a cost of £100 million. The terminal originally comprised a square structure of 11 bays by 11 bays. It is regarded as influential for airport architecture, and has three passenger satellites containing the departure gates.

summary.description: Philip Johnson built the house in 1948–49 as his weekend retreat, behind a stone wall at the edge of a crest overlooking a pond, and used it for 58 years. The structure is 56 feet long, 32 feet wide and 10.5 feet high, in charcoal-painted steel and glass on a brick floor raised 10 inches above the ground. The interior is open, divided by low walnut cabinets, and a brick cylinder holds the bathroom. It is an example of minimal structure, geometry, proportion and transparency, and the estate includes other buildings by Johnson from across his career. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1997.

summary.description: Pennzoil Place is a pair of 36-storey towers in downtown Houston designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee from a concept by Eli Attia. Completed in 1975, the two trapezoidal towers, each 495 feet high, stand ten feet apart and are sheathed in dark bronze glass and aluminium. They are mirror images, and a 115-foot glass pyramid-shaped atrium encloses the street-level plaza that joins them. Deliberately designed as an optical illusion, the building looks different from every angle. It broke the modernist glass box made popular by followers of Mies van der Rohe and helped introduce postmodernism.

summary.description: Designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee for the minister Robert H. Schuller's congregation in Garden Grove, the Modern-style reflective glass church seats 2,248 people. After its completion in 1981 it was described as 'the largest glass building in the world'. Its congregation went bankrupt, and the Diocese of Orange bought the building and campus in February 2012 for $57.5 million. After a two-year renovation to convert it for Catholic liturgy it was consecrated as Christ Cathedral on 17 July 2019. It houses the Hazel Wright Organ, one of the largest musical instruments in the world.

summary.description: The Sesc Pompeia is a culture and leisure centre in the Vila Pompéia area of São Paulo that brings together theatres, sports courts, swimming pools, snack bars, restaurants, exhibition spaces, a beer hall, workshops, a reading area and free internet. Its architectural project was developed by Lina Bo Bardi in 1977. Its inauguration in 1982 featured performances by São Paulo punk bands of the time, such as Inocentes, Ratos de Porão, Cólera and Olho Seco. The New York Times chose it as one of the 25 most important architectural works built after World War II.

summary.description: The Louvre Abu Dhabi is an art museum on Saadiyat Island, designed by Jean Nouvel. It runs under an agreement between the UAE and France, signed in March 2007, that lets it use the Louvre's name until 2047. About 24,000 square metres in size, with 8,000 square metres of galleries, it is the largest art museum in the Arabian Peninsula, showing artworks from around the world with the stated intent of bridging Eastern and Western art. By 2019 it had attracted 2 million visitors. It was one of the first completed projects of the Saadiyat Cultural District.

summary.description: Designed by the Japanese architect Shigeru Ban, the museum of modern and contemporary art in Metz, a branch of the Pompidou arts centre of Paris, was inaugurated by President Nicolas Sarkozy on 12 May 2010. It is a large hexagon structured around a central spire reaching 77 metres, three rectangular galleries weave through it at different levels and jut out through the roof with picture windows angled toward landmarks such as the Gothic cathedral. Its roof, a 90-metre-wide hexagon of sixteen kilometres of glued laminated timber, was inspired by a Chinese hat. It offers 5,000 square metres of space across three galleries, a theatre and an auditorium.

summary.description: La Seine Musicale is a music and performing arts centre on Île Seguin, an island on the Seine between Boulogne-Billancourt and Sèvres. In July 2009 Jean Nouvel was named lead coordinating architect for the project, and the first buildings, designed by the team of Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines, opened in April 2017. The complex includes an elevated egg-shaped theatre-in-the-round, the 1,150-seat Patrick-Devedjian Auditorium, a larger modular concert hall, Grande Seine, for up to 6,000, rehearsal rooms and an extensive roof garden. It was inaugurated on 22 April 2017.
keyFeatures: Egg-shaped auditorium with 1,150 seats
Grande Seine hall for up to 6,000
Mobile curved solar panel array
Extensive roof garden
funFacts: Bob Dylan held the first concert there, in the 6,000-seat Grande Seine, in the inauguration week.
It hosted Junior Eurovision 2021, the first Eurovision event held in France since 1999.

summary.description: Built from 1964 to 1966 as the third home of the Whitney Museum of American Art, 945 Madison Avenue, now commonly called the Breuer Building, was designed by Marcel Breuer and Hamilton P. Smith, with Michael H. Irving as consulting architect and Paul Weidlinger as structural engineer. It was Breuer's most significant design in New York and his first museum commission. Faced in variegated granite with exposed concrete and stark angular shapes, with cantilevered floors extending above the entry like an inverted ziggurat, it is often described as Brutalist. It later became the Met Breuer and the Frick Madison, and in 2023 Sotheby's bought it.
keyFeatures: Variegated granite and exposed concrete faces
Cantilevered floors above the entry
Site of 13,000 square feet on Madison Avenue
Breuer's first museum commission
funFacts: The site was once occupied by six 1880s rowhouses.
The Whitney occupied the building until 2014.

Its front has a broken gable and a purely ornamental applied arch, an open challenge to Modernist orthodoxy.
A historian called it the biggest small building of the second half of the twentieth century.

summary.description: The Vanna Venturi House, one of the first prominent works of postmodern architecture, stands in the Chestnut Hill neighbourhood of Philadelphia. Robert Venturi designed it for his mother, Vanna Venturi, and it was built between 1962 and 1964. The five-room house stands only about 30 feet tall but has a monumental front facade, an effect achieved by manipulating the elements that indicate scale. Elements such as a non-structural applied arch and "hole in the wall" windows were an open challenge to Modernist orthodoxy, as described in Venturi's 1966 book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture. Architectural historian Vincent Scully called it "the biggest small building of the second half of the twentieth century."
keyFeatures: Broken gable and a purely ornamental applied arch on the front
Central chimney and stair competing for the middle of the plan
Pitched roof and closed ground floor instead of Modernist glass and columns
A stair that seems to lead to a non-existent third floor
funFacts: Venturi called it "Mother's House" and redesigned it at least five times in fully worked-out versions while writing his book.
Venturi compared the front facade to "a child's drawing of a house".
Along with Guild House, it was Venturi's first work as an independent architect.

summary.description: Guild House is a residential building in Philadelphia, built in 1960–63 for low-income senior citizens, and was the first major work by Robert Venturi. Along with the Vanna Venturi House it is considered one of the earliest expressions of postmodern architecture. It was commissioned by a Quaker organization, the Friends Neighborhood Guild, and designed by Venturi and Rauch with Cope and Lippincott. Using red clay brick and ordinary double-hung windows, it combined ordinary commercial architecture with ironic historical references and rejected Modernist ideals. It was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2004.
keyFeatures: Six-storey red-brick block with a symmetrical, stepped facade
Monumental classical entrance bay with a polished black granite column
Large arched window opening onto the common room
91 apartments with winding interior corridors
funFacts: The roof was originally crowned with an oversize, nonfunctional television antenna, a sculptural nod to the residents' chief pastime.
It was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2004, despite being barely 40 years old.

summary.description: Luis Barragán House and Studio, also known as Casa Luis Barragán, is the former residence of the architect Luis Barragán in the Miguel Hidalgo district of Mexico City. Built in 1948, it remained his home until his death in 1988, and during this time it underwent many modifications and served as a kind of laboratory for his ideas. The Jalisco state government and the Fundación de Arquitectura Tapatía acquired it in 1993 and turned it into a museum in 1994, preserving the original furniture, personal objects and a mostly Mexican art collection. In 2004 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site because it is one of the most influential and representative examples of modern Mexican architecture.
keyFeatures: Plain street front hiding a private garden
Original furniture and personal objects kept in place
Mixes traditional and vernacular elements with mid-century modernism
Only private residence in Latin America on the UNESCO list
funFacts: It has been named one of the ten most important houses built in the twentieth century.
It is owned by the Fundación de Arquitectura Tapatía and the Government of the State of Jalisco, and is open mostly by appointment.

They appear in Alejandro Jodorowsky's surrealist film The Holy Mountain.

summary.description: The Torres de Satélite (Satellite Towers) are a group of sculptures in the Ciudad Satélite district of Naucalpan, State of Mexico, and one of Mexico's first urban sculptures of great dimensions. Planning began in 1957 with the ideas of the architect Luis Barragán, the painter Jesús Reyes Ferreira and the sculptor Mathias Goeritz. The project was originally planned as seven towers, the tallest 200 metres, but a budget reduction left five, the tallest 52 metres and the shortest 30. Goeritz wanted shades of orange, but it was finally decided to have one tower each in red, blue and yellow, and two in white. They were inaugurated in the first days of March 1958 as the symbol of the new Ciudad Satélite.
keyFeatures: Five prismatic towers between 30 and 52 metres tall
Painted red, blue and yellow, with two left white
One of Mexico's first large urban sculptures
Symbol of the new Ciudad Satélite
funFacts: Goeritz originally wanted the towers in different shades of orange, but changed his mind under pressure from constructors and investors.
In The Holy Mountain, the hero is hoisted up the red tower and enters through a circular hole painted on for the film.

summary.description: The Bonnefanten Museum is a museum of historic, modern and contemporary art in Maastricht, Netherlands. Founded in 1884 as the historical and archaeological museum of the Dutch province of Limburg, it moved in 1995 to a former industrial site named Céramique, into a new building designed by the Italian architect Aldo Rossi. With its rocket-shaped cupola overlooking the river Maas, it is one of Maastricht's most prominent modern buildings. Its name derives from the French "bons enfants", the popular name of a former convent that housed the museum from 1951 to 1978.

Old masters on the first floor, contemporary art above
Built on the former industrial site of Céramique
Museum since 1884; art museum only since 1999
funFacts: Since 1999 the museum has been exclusively an art museum, and its historical and archaeological collections are housed elsewhere.
Its contemporary collection focuses on American Minimalism, Italian Arte Povera and Concept Art.

summary.description: Monte Amiata Housing is a residential complex in the Gallaratese district of Milan, designed by the architects Carlo Aymonino and Aldo Rossi in the late 1960s. It is sometimes called the "Red Dinosaur", referring both to the reddish colour of the buildings and the oddity of their design. The complex comprises five red buildings, grouped around a central area with a yellow open-air theatre and two small triangular plazas. It was conceived as a utopian micro-city within the city, and Rossi took inspiration from Giorgio de Chirico's paintings for the smaller slab. It is regarded as one of the projects that best represent Aymonino's vision of "fragmentism".
keyFeatures: Five red buildings around a yellow open-air theatre
Passages, decks, balconies and bridges linking the blocks
Conceived as a micro-city within the city
Rossi's block inspired by de Chirico's paintings
funFacts: The complex is named after Mount Amiata and covers about 120,912 square metres between Via Francesco Cilea and Via Enrico Falck.
In its early years it was occupied by homeless families, then deserted in 1974, and was later converted into a middle-class condominium.

summary.description: The Gustavo Capanema Palace, architecturally known as the Ministry of Education and Health Building, is a government office building in downtown Rio de Janeiro. As the first modernist project in Brazil, it is historically important to the country's development of modernism and is on its UNESCO tentative list. It was designed in 1935–36 by a team led by Lucio Costa, with Affonso Eduardo Reidy, Ernani Vasconcellos, Carlos Leão, Jorge Machado Moreira and Roberto Burle Marx, and Le Corbusier was invited to oversee the project. Construction began in 1939 and finished in 1945. The 15-storey building is raised three floors on pilotis, and employs azulejos in modern wall murals and adjustable Corbusian brises-soleil, the first of their kind in the world.
keyFeatures: Raised three floors above the pavement on pilotis
Adjustable brise-soleil sun-shades on the glass facade

Roof gardens by Roberto Burle Marx
funFacts: It was the first modernist public building in the Americas and far larger than anything Le Corbusier had built until then.
Le Corbusier suggested siting it beside the sea, but the government declined.

It plays with classical orders in stainless steel and neon, and was sometimes called the first "postmodern ruin".

summary.description: The Piazza d'Italia is an urban public plaza behind the American Italian Cultural Center at Lafayette and Commerce Streets in downtown New Orleans. Completed in 1978 to a design by the postmodern architect Charles Moore and Perez Architects, it debuted to widespread acclaim. Moore, with Ron Filson, Malcolm Heard and Allen Eskew, conceived a fountain in the shape of the Italian peninsula, surrounded by hemicyclical colonnades, a clock tower, and a campanile and Roman temple in abstract space-frame fashion. Because the development around it was never realized, the plaza rapidly deteriorated and was sometimes called the first "postmodern ruin" before being fully restored by 2004.
keyFeatures: Fountain in the shape of the Italian peninsula
Hemicyclical colonnades appropriating classical orders
Stainless steel, neon and water jets in place of stone
Clock tower gate on Commerce Street
funFacts: Water jets were used to suggest the acanthus leaves of traditional Corinthian capitals.
The restoration of the plaza was done by 2004, together with the conversion of the adjacent Lykes Center into the Loews Hotel.

summary.description: The Centro Galego de Arte Contemporánea (CGAC) is an arts centre in Santiago de Compostela that promotes culture in Galicia through the exhibition and study of contemporary art. It was established in 1993 and has had a stable programme since the end of 1994. The building, on the edge of the city next to the Convento de San Domingos de Bonaval, was designed by the Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza Vieira. Work began to take shape in 1988, the project was presented in 1992 and construction was completed between 1993 and 1994. It has three floors with an entrance porch, auditorium, coffee shop, library, offices and exhibition halls, and an accessible terrace.

Accessible terrace over the old quarter

funFacts: Santiago de Compostela is the only city outside Portugal with two works by Siza, the other being the Faculty of Journalism.
Its collection of about 1,300 works focuses on art from the second half of the twentieth century to the present.

summary.description: The Tidal Pools of Leça da Palmeira are a public swimming pool on the beach of Leça da Palmeira in Matosinhos, in the district of Porto. The structures consist of two natural pools filled with fresh sea water, designed and built between 1960 and 1973 by the Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza Vieira. It is one of his early projects and his second design in Leça da Palmeira, after the Boa Nova tea house a kilometre to the north. In 2011 the pools were classified as a national monument, and since 2017 they have been considered for UNESCO World Heritage together with the tea house and six other projects. The pools are open seasonally between June and September.

funFacts: The final design left out a restaurant in the north area that had been included in a 1961 plan.

summary.description: The Municipal Library of Viana do Castelo was designed by Álvaro Siza Vieira and stands at the eastern end of the Praça da Liberdade, on the riverfront of Viana do Castelo. Since its foundation in 1888 the library had six addresses. The new building began construction in January 2004 and was inaugurated on 20 January 2008, within the celebrations of the 750th anniversary of the town's charter; it cost about 4.5 million euros. It has 3,130 square metres on two floors, with a central void at ground level that lets people north of the building see the river Lima. It is built of white concrete covering a complex iron structure, on a granite base.

White concrete over an iron structure, granite base
Space of its own for children with a story room

The collection holds around one hundred thousand books and municipal documents.

summary.description: The Centro Cultural de Viana do Castelo, or Coliseu de Viana do Castelo, is a multi-purpose centre for cultural, musical, sporting and leisure events in Viana do Castelo, on the riverfront at the mouth of the Lima. Designed by the architect Eduardo Souto de Moura, it was inaugurated on 14 July 2013, after delays in finishing the work. It cost about 13 million euros, including 1.1 million euros of outdoor works. It has three floors and a total area of 3,792 square metres, using 900 tonnes of reinforcing steel and a 1,200-tonne metal structure. It seats 2,000 people, or 2,700 for standing concerts. Its first stage performance was by the fado singer Camané.
keyFeatures: Three floors with a metal structure of 1,200 tonnes
Seats 2,000 (2,700 for standing concerts)
Large silver ducts running along the roof
Riverside site on the Foz do Lima
funFacts: At its opening 32 cultural and sports associations took part, with more than 700 artists performing.
The work cost around 13 million euros, including outdoor works, accesses and a car park.

summary.description: The Municipal Market of Santa Maria da Feira is a market designed by the architect Fernando Távora in 1953 and classified as a monument of public interest. It is a seminal work in the history of Portuguese architecture, unanimously considered the first attributable to the Porto School. It was one of Távora's first works after finishing his studies at the Porto School of Fine Arts. It sits in the historic centre of Santa Maria da Feira, keeping visual relations with the castle and the Church and Convent of the Lóios. The market is fragmented into four volumes of different character, distributed around a courtyard with a fountain, with roofs designed as protective "wings" and a structure of reinforced concrete and granite walls.

He set out his 'five points of a new architecture', devised the Modulor proportion system and planned the Indian city of Chandigarh. His late work in raw concrete helped shape Brutalism. Seventeen of his works are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

summary.description: The Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts at Harvard University, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is the only building designed primarily by Le Corbusier in the United States and one of only two in the Americas, the other being the Curutchet House in La Plata. Le Corbusier designed it with the Chilean architect Guillermo Jullian de la Fuente, while the on-site construction plans were handled by the office of Josep Lluís Sert, then dean of the Harvard Graduate School of Design. It was completed in 1962. Because it was to be his only building in America, he made it a synthesis of his Five Points of architecture. The compact, roughly cylindrical mass is bisected by an S-shaped ramp on the third floor, which brings pedestrians through the building so they see the artistic activities within.

Applies Le Corbusier's Five Points of architecture
Studios and exhibition spaces seen through glass from the ramp

summary.description: Row House in Sumiyoshi, also called Azuma House, is a personal residence in Sumiyoshi-ku, Osaka, designed by Tadao Ando early in his career. It was designed without exterior windows, reflecting the owner's desire to feel that he was not "in Japan", and to compensate for the lost light an interior courtyard with a cross walkway was created. Its raw concrete style, typical of Ando, inspired the set design for the music video of Jamiroquai's "Virtual Insanity".

One of its most distinctive features is a group of 100 flower beds on an incline, with 1,575 steps and 235 flights.

summary.description: The Awaji Yumebutai is a complex comprising a conference centre, hotel and memorial in Awaji, Hyōgo, Japan, built near the epicentre of the 1995 Great Hanshin Awaji earthquake. It was designed by Tadao Ando, who had begun planning the project as a park before the earthquake. Yumebutai means "Dream Stage", metaphorically "a place in which to dream", and refers to the aim of restoring the ecology of the island, whose soil had been partly removed for land reclamation in Osaka. One of its most distinctive features is Hyakudan'en, the "hundred stepped gardens". The hotel is operated as the Westin Awaji Island Resort.

Hyakudan'en: 100 flower beds in grids across several levels
Built on land eroded by reclamation works, to restore its ecology
Raw concrete terraces, walkways and stairs
funFacts: The "hundred" in Hyakudan'en refers to the number of mini-gardens, not the steps; there are 1,575 steps and 235 flights.
Ando had begun planning the project as a park before the earthquake struck.

summary.description: The Casa de Vidro (Glass House) was designed by the Italian-born architect Lina Bo Bardi and built between 1950 and 1951 in the Morumbi district of São Paulo, the first house built in what became Jardim Morumbi. It was her first work in Brazil, built for herself and her husband Pietro Maria Bardi, who lived there for over forty years. The house takes its name from its large glass facade and sits in a garden of about 7,000 square metres on a site of Atlantic Forest, with the back of the building resting on concrete walls. Le Corbusier was one of her influences, in the mix of transparency and opacity. It has been listed by Condephaat since 1987 and houses the Instituto Lina Bo e P. M. Bardi.

summary.description: The Parque Guinle Residential Complex consists of three buildings in Parque Eduardo Guinle, in Rio de Janeiro. It began to be designed in the 1940s by the Brazilian architect Lucio Costa and is considered an icon of modern architecture in Brazil. The original project included six buildings, but only three were built: Nova Cintra (1948), Bristol (1950) and Caledônia (1952). The buildings are blocks raised on pilotis, with balconies whose facades use brises, cobogós and trellises to protect the flats from the afternoon sun without blocking the view of the park, and are marked by blue, pink, yellow, white and natural ceramic. The gardens were designed by Burle Marx. The project won Costa the Collective Housing Prize at the 1951 São Paulo Biennial and was listed by IPHAN in 1986.

summary.description: The Atelier-Museu Júlio Pomar in Lisbon preserves and promotes the work of the painter Júlio Pomar (1926–2018) through exhibitions, events and educational activities. It stands between the Bairro Alto and Madragoa neighbourhoods, in a former warehouse on Rua do Vale bought by Lisbon City Council in 2000 and intended as Pomar's studio. The building was designed by the architect Álvaro Siza Vieira, winner of the 1992 Pritzker Prize. With an austere design and clean lines, discreetly integrated into the fabric of the neighbourhood, it has two floors with a central exhibition area, two storage rooms, service areas, an office and a reception, around an exterior courtyard. Its holdings include about 1,500 works by Pomar and artists close to him.

summary.description: The Sines Arts Centre, inaugurated on 20 August 2005, is a modern facility designed by the practice Aires Mateus & Associados (Manuel Aires Mateus and Francisco Aires Mateus) in the historic zone of Sines. A single building holds four facilities: an exhibition centre, the new municipal library, a 191-seat auditorium and the municipal historical archive. It stands where the Vasco da Gama cine-theatre and the Teatro do Mar once stood. Its monumental scale is that of the historic centre, and its play of transparency and opacity suggests the openings and arrow slits of the castle walls. On Rua Marquês de Pombal it presents a very robust lioz stone facade, while along Rua Cândido dos Reis it is lit by glazed facades; inside, natural light reflects off smooth white marble ceilings and walls.

Much of what visitors see is the work of later kings, military engineers and Victorian restorers.
