architects.name: Unknown Almoravid and Castilian builders
architects.bio: Built by the Almoravids on Roman foundations, then rebuilt and extended by Castilian kings, including John II in the 15th century and Philip II in the 16th.

photos.alt: Castle with slender slate-roofed turrets on a rocky outcrop at dusk, shaped like the prow of a ship
photos.credit: Photo: Rafa Esteve · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ángel Sanz de Andrés · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A sandy-coloured fortress palace with slate-roofed turrets and a crenellated keep perches on a rocky cliff above autumn woodland.

photos.credit: Photo: Jumk18 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Front view of a tall crenellated tower with rounded corner turrets, flanked by pointed slate-roofed towers, above a stone terrace with visitors.
Hall with a coffered wooden ceiling, glass chandeliers and painted frieze above portraits
photos.credit: Photo: Ministrillo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a castle-palace perched on a rocky crag where two rivers meet, shaped like the prow of a ship.
In 1474 a princess took refuge here and was crowned queen of Castile the next day.
Its fairy-tale spires, added in the 16th century, are said to have inspired an animated princess film's castle.

summary.description: First mentioned in 1120, the fortress was built by the Almoravids on a Roman castrum. After a fire in 1258 it was rebuilt over centuries, and Isabella was enthroned here on 13 December 1474. In the 16th century Philip II added the sharp slate spires, and from 1764 it housed the Royal College of Artillery.
keyFeatures: Ship-shaped crag site
Tower of John II
Hall of the Galley with ceiling like an inverted hull
Slate spires added under Philip II
UNESCO listing with the Old City, 1985
funFacts: Its silhouette inspired the castle in Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs.
A fire on 6 March 1862 destroyed the ceilings of the private rooms.

architects.name: Frederick II
architects.bio: Holy Roman Emperor and King of Sicily who had Castel del Monte built in the 1240s on lands inherited from his mother, Constance of Sicily.

photos.alt: Pale limestone octagonal fortress with a tower at each corner and a single ornate doorway, on a scrubby hill
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Oblique view of an octagonal limestone castle with tall corner towers, a carved portal and a few small pointed windows under a bright sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Carsten Steger · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of an octagonal stone castle with eight corner towers on a wooded hilltop encircled by a path.

photos.credit: Photo: Sailko · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Rough limestone walls of an inner courtyard rise to the sky, with small arched windows and a framed doorway above.
Eight-sided courtyard seen from below, with stone walls rising to an octagonal opening of sky
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a hilltop fortress whose plan is built entirely on the number eight.
Historians still debate its purpose, because it has no moat, no drawbridge and little sign of defence.
Soil near it gave bacteria used to make cancer drugs, and it appears on a euro coin.

summary.description: Built in the 1240s for Frederick II, this citadel is an octagonal prism with an octagonal tower at every corner around an eight-sided courtyard. Its purpose is debated: once called a hunting lodge, it is now thought to have been a citadel. It later served as a prison, was looted in the 18th century and was bought by the Italian state in 1876.
keyFeatures: Octagonal plan with eight octagonal towers
Eight-sided central courtyard
Eight rooms on each floor
Originally marble walls and columns
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996
funFacts: It appears on the Italian one-cent euro coin.
In the Second World War the US 15th Army Air Force ran a secret navigation station here.

name: Malbork Castle
aliases: Castle of the Teutonic Order in Malbork

architects.name: Unknown Teutonic Order builders
architects.bio: Master builders of the Teutonic Order, who raised the castle between 1274 and 1406.

photos.credit: Photo: DerHexer; derivate work: Carschten · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A huge red-brick fortress with steep tiled roofs and a tall tower stands behind long walls across a calm river in clear light.

photos.credit: Photo: Aneta Pawska · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Low sun lights long red-brick walls and tiled roofs of a vast castle, with a square tower above bare trees and a green lawn.

photos.credit: Photo: Kapitel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a brick castle complex with tall tower, walls and moat beside a wide river, surrounded by trees and fields.

photos.credit: Photo: Aneta Pawska · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Cobbled courtyard enclosed by red-brick galleries with pointed arches, a small well house and a tall tower against a blue sky.
Hall whose slender central pillar fans out into a palm-like ribbed vault above Gothic windows
photos.credit: Photo: Aneta Pawska · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the largest castle in the world by land area, built of brick.
A military religious order made it its headquarters in 1309, and Poland took it in 1457.
More than half of it was destroyed in 1945, and rebuilding has continued since 1962.

summary.description: Built by the Teutonic Order mainly between 1274 and 1406, this castle became the Order's headquarters in 1309 when Grand Master Siegfried von Feuchtwangen moved there. It has three parts, the High, Middle and Lower Castles, separated by moats and towers. Fighting in early 1945 destroyed more than half of it, and most has since been rebuilt.
keyFeatures: Largest castle in the world by land area
High, Middle and Lower Castles
Grand Master's Palace in the Middle Castle
Great Refectory with palm vaulting
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997
funFacts: It was under German rule for over 170 years, from the First Partition of Poland in 1772 to 1945.
In 1457 King Casimir IV entered it after Bohemian mercenaries sold it to Poland.

architects.name: James of Saint George
architects.bio: Military engineer, probably the architect of Caernarfon and several other castles built for Edward I in Wales.

photos.alt: Grey stone castle with polygonal towers and turrets beside a harbour full of boats
photos.credit: Photo: Herbert Ortner · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Nilfanion · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Polygonal grey stone towers with battlements rise above a stone quay and a rippling estuary under a cloudy sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Steve Collis from Melbourne, Australia · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Wide view of a battlemented gatehouse tower with a deep arched entrance and a stair, linked by long curtain walls.

photos.credit: Photo: Albertistvan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Inside the walls, grass lawns and stone paths lie below ruined battlemented towers, with a pale estuary in the distance.
Narrow stone spiral staircase inside a tower, with a rope as handrail
photos.credit: Photo: Martinvl · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was begun in 1283 by an English king to hold down a conquered country.
Unlike many castles of its kind it has polygonal towers and bands of coloured stone, perhaps echoing the walls of Constantinople.
It staged the investitures of two Princes of Wales, in 1911 and 1969.

summary.description: Edward I began replacing an earlier motte-and-bailey fort here in 1283, probably under Master James of Saint George. Polygonal towers and banded masonry set it apart from the round towers of other Edwardian castles. Work stopped in 1330 with parts unfinished, and the interior buildings survive only as foundations.
keyFeatures: Polygonal towers
Banded coloured stone
Eagle Tower with three turrets
King's Gate left unfinished
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986
funFacts: Owain Glyndŵr's forces besieged it unsuccessfully in 1401–1404.
Its Royalist garrison surrendered in 1646, the last fighting it saw.

architects.name: Friedrich August Stüler
architects.bio: Prussian architect who designed the Gothic Revival third castle on Mount Hohenzollern, built 1846–1867 for Frederick William IV of Prussia.

photos.alt: Fairy-tale castle with many pointed turrets and bastions crowning a wooded hilltop in autumn
photos.credit: Photo: A. Kniesel (= User:-donald-), Lauffen · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Olga Ernst · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a Gothic Revival castle with many pointed slate turrets and bastion walls on a wooded hilltop.

photos.credit: Photo:  · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Castle courtyard with a steep-roofed chapel, round corner tower and ivy-covered stone walls under blue sky and clouds.

photos.credit: Photo: Olga Ernst · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: A turreted castle crowns a conical forested hill above a field of bright yellow flowers beneath dark stormy clouds.
Chapel vault painted blue and gold with ribs and pointed stained-glass windows
photos.credit: Photo: Zairon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on a 855-metre hill at the edge of the Swabian Jura.
The first castle here was destroyed in 1423, and the present one is a 19th-century memorial to a royal family.
It was built from 1846 to 1867 in the Gothic Revival style for a Prussian king.

summary.description: The present castle is the third on Mount Hohenzollern. The first, built around 1040, was destroyed in 1423, and a second was completed around 1461. The third was built in 1846–1867 as a family memorial for Frederick William IV of Prussia, designed by Friedrich August Stüler in Gothic Revival style.
keyFeatures: Gothic Revival design
Hilltop at 855 m
Third castle on the site
Chapel with Frederick the Great's coffin until 1991
Crown of Wilhelm II on display
funFacts: The coffins of Frederick William I and Frederick the Great rested in the chapel from 1952 to 1991.
A 1978 earthquake damaged its turrets, and repairs lasted into the mid-1990s.

architects.name: Unknown Moorish and Portuguese builders
architects.bio: Moorish builders raised the fortifications in the 10th century; Portuguese kings, including Denis around 1300, later turned the alcáçova into a royal palace and extended the walls.

photos.alt: Honey-coloured stone fortress with a tall crenellated keep and curtain walls behind a stone bridge on a sunny day.
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Sandstone fortress walls with square crenellated towers and sloping bastions under a blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: NorbertNagel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A stone bridge with brick arches crossing a dry moat toward towering battlemented walls and a corner tower.
photos.credit: Photo: Peter K Burian · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Weathered stone battlements with a person leaning on the merlons under a grey sky
photos.credit: Photo: Simon Lee from London · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a medieval fortress on the highest hill of a capital that stands beside a wide estuary.
A knight is said to have jammed a gate with his own body so that Christian troops could enter in 1147.
Its tower holds a camera obscura, and in 1498 a king received Vasco da Gama here.

summary.description: Moors fortified this hill in the 10th century, and Afonso Henriques took the castle in 1147. King Denis turned the Moorish alcáçova into a royal palace around 1300, and in 1498 Manuel I received Vasco da Gama here. The 1755 earthquake badly damaged it, and major renovations followed in the 1940s.
keyFeatures: Hilltop citadel with ten towers
Moorish walls from the 10th century
Former royal palace
Camera obscura in the Tower of Ulysses
Monument to Afonso Henriques, 1947
funFacts: Royal records were kept in the Torre do Tombo here until the 1755 earthquake.
Legend credits Martim Moniz with holding the gate open in 1147.

name: Castelo de Guimarães

architects.name: Unknown medieval builders
architects.bio: Built on the orders of Countess Mumadona Dias in the 10th century, expanded by Count Henry in the late 11th century and remodelled by King Denis around 1300.

style: Late Romanesque with early Gothic elements

photos.alt: Granite castle with a tall rectangular keep and crenellated corner towers rising above low battlemented walls under a grey sky.
photos.credit: Photo: John Samuel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A gravel path climbs a grassy hill toward a stone castle with crenellated towers among trees under a blue sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Krzysztof Golik · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Roofless granite palace wall with rows of rectangular window openings against the sky
photos.credit: Photo: Béria Lima de Rodríguez · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a small granite fortress in northern Portugal, first mentioned in a 10th-century codicil.
It is traditionally said to be the birthplace of the country's first king.
A nearby battle in 1128 led to the independence of the county that became a kingdom.

summary.description: A codicil of 968 mentions this castle as newly built under Countess Mumadona Dias to protect a monastery's community. Count Henry expanded it as his residence, and Afonso Henriques was born here in 1111. King Denis gave it its present form around 1300, and a restoration from 1937 to 1940 followed a failed demolition proposal in 1836.
keyFeatures: Pentagon-like wall circuit
Eight rectangular towers
Central keep
Late Romanesque with early Gothic elements
Part of the Historic Centre of Guimarães, UNESCO 2001
funFacts: It withstood sieges in 1369 and 1385.
It was declared a national monument in 1910 and re-inaugurated on 4 June 1940.

architects.name: Victor Horta
architects.bio: Born in Ghent, Horta designed a series of Brussels town houses in the 1890s that made him the pioneer of Art Nouveau architecture, with open plans, exposed iron and whiplash ornament. Four of them, including the Hôtel Tassel and his own house, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

photos.alt: Narrow stone town house front with curved bay windows, wrought-iron balconies and an arched wooden door at street level.
photos.credit: Photo: Aleksa Aleksi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Narrow town house façade with curved bay windows, wrought-iron balconies and slender wooden window frames
photos.credit: Photo: Fred Romero from Paris, France · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Close view of a first-floor balcony with a swirling wrought-iron railing below tall wooden-framed windows set in pale stone.
photos.credit: Photo: Fred Romero from Paris, France · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stair hall with a whiplash-curved iron balustrade, a stained-glass skylight and a large pointillist mural
photos.credit: Photo: Brigade Piron · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Panelled salon with curving wooden glass cabinets, a round table with chairs, a chandelier and tall windows hung with sheer curtains.
photos.credit: Photo: Brigade Piron · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A narrow Brussels town house built for a wealthy industrial family, whose architect designed every detail down to the doorbell.
Its stair hall is lit by a stained-glass skylight, and a pointillist painter collaborated on the decoration of the staircase.
It was built between 1895 and 1900 and is one of four town houses by the same architect that UNESCO listed in 2000.

summary.description: A town house on Avenue Louise built for Armand Solvay, son of the chemist and industrialist Ernest Solvay. Victor Horta designed it in total: furniture, carpets, light fittings, tableware and even the doorbell, in marble, onyx, bronze and tropical woods.
keyFeatures: Façade with curved bays and wrought-iron balconies
Stair hall under a stained-glass skylight
Total design down to the furniture and doorbell
Marble, onyx, bronze and tropical woods
funFacts: The pointillist painter Théo van Rysselberghe collaborated on the staircase decoration.
The house stayed private until it opened as a museum on 23 January 2021.

architects.name: Henri Sauvage
architects.bio: French architect whose first project, at the age of 24, was the Villa Majorelle in Nancy.

photos.alt: Stone house with a steep gabled roof, a large arched window and a balcony with green metalwork
photos.credit: Photo: cliché Damien Boyer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Pale stone house with steep slate gables, a canopy over the entrance and a white iron railing along the street wall.
photos.credit: Photo: SiefkinDR · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Tall stone wall with arched windows and a curving wrought-iron ornament sweeping across the upper storey, beside a green drainpipe.
photos.credit: Photo: SiefkinDR · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Pale stone façade with irregular carved window frames and a curved wrought-iron canopy
photos.credit: Photo: Audesome · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as a showcase for a furniture maker's work, with a studio on its top floor.
It was the first project of a 24-year-old architect and is among the earliest and most influential Art Nouveau houses in France.
It stands in Nancy and was first called after the client's wife, Jitka.

summary.description: A house built in 1901-1902 for the Nancy furniture maker Louis Majorelle, as a showcase for his furniture and for other decorative artists. It was the first project of the 24-year-old Henri Sauvage and is among the first Art Nouveau houses in France.
keyFeatures: Carved oak staircase
Ceramics by Alexandre Bigot
Stained glass by Jacques Gruber
Wrought-iron front grille and mosaic vestibule floor
funFacts: L'Illustration called it "a house made by an artist for an artist".
It was declared a historical monument in January 1975.

architects.name: Josep Puig i Cadafalch
architects.bio: Catalan architect who redesigned Casa Amatller for the chocolatier Antoni Amatller in 1898-1900.

photos.alt: Façade with a stepped tiled gable, rows of small windows and carved stone window frames over patterned plaster
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stair court with a red-carpeted marble stair, a stencilled wall and a window with a wrought-iron grille set with coloured glass
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Entrance hall with twisted stone columns, pointed arches, a tiled wainscot and a few small café tables on a patterned floor.
photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Looking up a stair court at a rectangular stained-glass skylight in warm yellow and red geometric patterns, with carved stone walls.
photos.credit: Photo: Eli Beckman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A wealthy chocolatier and amateur archaeologist had an 1875 house remodelled into a new home.
A tile-covered stepped gable crowns the façade, whose sculpture includes a rat with a camera.
It stands on a famous block of three celebrated houses on one of the city's grandest boulevards.

summary.description: A house on Passeig de Gràcia, built in 1875 and redesigned between 1898 and 1900 by Josep Puig i Cadafalch for the chocolatier and amateur archaeologist Antoni Amatller. It stands on the Illa de la Discòrdia beside Casa Batlló and Casa Lleó-Morera.
keyFeatures: Stepped gable covered in tile
Sculptural compositions on the façade
Entrance foyer with large stained-glass doors
Stair court with a stained-glass ceiling
funFacts: One façade sculpture shows a rat with a camera.
Continuous family ownership until 1960 kept the 1900 interior largely intact.

architects.name: Le Corbusier
architects.bio: Born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in Switzerland, Le Corbusier became one of the most influential architects of the 20th century. He set out his 'five points of a new architecture', devised the Modulor proportion system and planned the Indian city of Chandigarh. His late work in raw concrete helped shape Brutalism. Seventeen of his works are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

photos.alt: Tall rough concrete slab end wall with a zigzag external stair, raised on massive tapering supports
photos.credit: Photo: Gatotienesueño · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Roof terrace edge with a mesh-fenced concrete ventilation stack overlooking a city and distant hills
photos.credit: Photo: Anapuig · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A postwar housing block raised on large concrete legs, with wide internal corridors it called streets in the sky.
It holds 337 apartments in 23 layouts, plus shops, a hotel and a communal roof with a running track and paddling pool.
It was built between 1947 and 1952 in the south of a French port city and joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2016.

summary.description: A 12-storey housing block built between 1947 and 1952 with Shadrach Woods and George Candilis, in rough-cast concrete (béton brut), raised on large pilotis. It holds 337 apartments in 23 layouts and is often cited as an inspiration for Brutalist architecture.
keyFeatures: Raised on large pilotis
337 apartments in 23 layouts
Internal corridors every third floor
Communal roof terrace
Shops, hotel and restaurant inside
funFacts: Walter Gropius reportedly said any architect who did not find it beautiful should put down his pencil.
It joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2016 with 16 other works by the same architect.

architects.name: William Pereira
architects.bio: American architect whose firm, William L. Pereira & Associates, designed the main library of UC San Diego, opened in 1970.

photos.alt: Stepped glass tiers of a concrete building rising from splayed concrete legs, seen from a corner beside a low concrete wall.
photos.credit: Photo: Stephen Bay · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stepped glass tiers of an eight-storey concrete building held aloft on splayed concrete legs
photos.credit: Photo: Gankbank789 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Overcast view of a stepped glass-and-concrete tower on angled concrete supports behind dry shrubs and eucalyptus trees.
photos.credit: Photo: Jami (Wiki Ed) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Study floor with curved bookcases, armchairs and tall windows looking over a wooded hillside
photos.credit: Photo: FASTILY · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A concrete library on a university campus on the Pacific coast, described as a nexus between brutalism and futurism.
Its floors are numbered 1, 2, then 4 to 8, because the missing third floor is an open outdoor forum.
Opened in 1970 and renamed in 1995, it holds a collection of about 8,500 items from a famous children's author.

summary.description: The main library of UC San Diego, a reinforced-concrete tower of eight floors, about 34 m tall and 61 m wide, designed by William L. Pereira & Associates. Construction began in 1968 and it opened in 1970; it was renamed in 1995 after Audrey and Theodor Seuss Geisel (Dr. Seuss).
keyFeatures: Eight stepped floors of concrete and glass
Reinforced-concrete construction
Underground expansion completed in 1993
Dr. Seuss Collection of about 8,500 items
funFacts: The third floor is an open outdoor forum, not a sealed floor.
A 560-foot slate path, Snake Path by Alexis Smith, winds around the building.

architects.name: Ernő Goldfinger
architects.bio: Architect of Trellick Tower, commissioned by the Greater London Council; it was his last major project.

photos.alt: Tall concrete residential slab with rows of balconies beside a separate slim service tower, rising behind a line of dark evergreen trees.
photos.credit: Photo: Trellick · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Tall concrete residential slab with balconies beside a separate narrow service tower topped by a glazed boiler room
photos.credit: Photo: Edwardx · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Looking up between two concrete towers at rough-aggregate walkways with small windows that bridge the gap between them.
photos.credit: Photo: stevecadman · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A dense grid of concrete balconies and windows across a high-rise wall, with satellite dishes and laundry hanging out.
photos.credit: Photo: Steve Cadman · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Distant view of a tall concrete slab and tower above low houses and trees along a street under a blue sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Paul The Archivist · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A London council-housing tower whose lift and service shaft stands apart from the main slab.
In the 1970s it earned the nickname Tower of Terror before a residents' association and a concierge turned its reputation around.
It was finished in 1972, rises 98 metres over 31 floors, and is Grade II* listed.

summary.description: A Brutalist residential tower in Kensal Town, completed on 28 June 1972 for the Greater London Council. It is 98 m tall with 31 floors and 217 dwellings, and a separate tower holds the lifts and plant room.
keyFeatures: 31 floors and 217 dwellings
Separate lift and service tower
Every flat has a balcony and large windows
Grade II* listed since 1998
funFacts: It was based on the architect's earlier Balfron Tower in Poplar.
It appears in the film Withnail & I and is believed to have inspired J. G. Ballard's High-Rise.

architects.name: Giuseppe Piermarini
architects.bio: Neoclassical architect who designed La Scala, opened in 1778.

photos.alt: Cream neoclassical façade with a central pediment, a balcony above three arched ground-floor openings and a street lamp in front.
photos.credit: Photo: Reem Al-Kashif · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Sober cream-coloured neoclassical façade with a pediment and arched ground-floor porte-cochère on a paved square
photos.credit: Photo: Jakub Hałun · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This opera house was built on the site of a church, after its predecessor theatre burned down in 1776.
Its season opens every 7 December, the feast day of the city's patron saint.
It opened in 1778 and has premiered Verdi's Otello and Puccini's Turandot.

summary.description: An opera house in Milan designed by Giuseppe Piermarini and opened on 3 August 1778 on the site of the church of Santa Maria della Scala. It has six tiers of boxes below a gallery called the loggione and seats about 2,000.
keyFeatures: Horseshoe auditorium with six tiers of boxes
Loggione gallery above the boxes
Neoclassical façade
Stage about 20 m wide and 26 m high
funFacts: Bombing damaged it severely in 1943; it reopened in 1946 with a concert conducted by Arturo Toscanini.
It premiered Verdi's Nabucco, Otello and Falstaff, and Puccini's Madama Butterfly and Turandot.

architects.name: Francesco Tamburini
architects.bio: Architect who began the Teatro Colón in 1889 and died in 1891.

architects.name: Vittorio Meano
architects.bio: Architect who continued the Teatro Colón after Tamburini's death and was murdered in 1904.

architects.name: Julio Dormal
architects.bio: Belgian architect who completed the Teatro Colón.

photos.alt: Symmetrical cream-coloured opera house front with a central pediment, paired pilasters, arched windows and a flag above the entrance canopy.
photos.credit: Photo: EEJCC · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Large cream-coloured opera house with arched windows, pilasters, sculpted friezes and a corner portico
photos.credit: Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Black-and-white view up to the pediment and attic of a grand building, with sculpted reliefs, small round windows and a semicircular window.
photos.credit: Photo: Andrzej Otrębski · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Gilded horseshoe auditorium with tiers of balconies facing a lit stage and a draped velvet proscenium
photos.credit: Photo: Leandro Kibisz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Horseshoe auditorium with many tiers of lit balconies rising to a painted domed ceiling and a central chandelier above the stalls.
photos.credit: Photo: Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires · CC BY 2.5 ar · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This opera house took nineteen years to build, delayed by financial trouble and the deaths of its architects, one of whom was murdered.
Its acoustics have been ranked the best in the world for opera, and its decor is scarlet and gold.
It opened in 1908 with Verdi's Aida, and a 1910 anarchist bomb landed in the middle of its orchestra.

summary.description: An opera house in Buenos Aires, begun in 1889 by Francesco Tamburini, continued by Vittorio Meano and completed in 1908 by Julio Dormal. It opened on 25 May 1908 with Verdi's Aida and holds about 2,480 seats.
keyFeatures: Eclectic architecture
Scarlet and gold auditorium
Central chandelier of about 700 bulbs
Cupola painted by Raúl Soldi in 1966
Acoustics ranked best for opera in a Leo Beranek survey
funFacts: Anarchists bombed the theatre in 1910.
It reopened on 24 May 2010 after a refurbishment that began in 2006.

architects.name: Le Corbusier
architects.bio: Born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in Switzerland, Le Corbusier became one of the most influential architects of the 20th century. He set out his 'five points of a new architecture', devised the Modulor proportion system and planned the Indian city of Chandigarh. His late work in raw concrete helped shape Brutalism. Seventeen of his works are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

photos.credit: Photo: Jean-Pierre Dalbéra · CC BY 2.0 · Flickr
photos.alt: White box-shaped house raised on slim round columns, with a long ribbon window, a curved rooftop screen and green garage doors below.
White box raised on slender round columns above a stone retaining wall, with a metal ring sculpture on the grass
photos.credit: Photo: Cbyd · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Tubular steel and black leather chaise longue on a tiled floor in front of a glazed wall
photos.credit: Photo: jeanbaptisteparis from Cambridge, MA, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: White-tiled bathroom with a sunken blue-mosaic bath and a curving tiled couch
photos.credit: Photo: scarletgreen from Japan · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A white country house outside a capital, built for a family who wanted a weekend home, with a ramp rising through its centre.
It embodies the architect's five points: pilotis, a roof garden, a free plan, long horizontal windows and a free façade.
Finished in 1931, it was the first modernist building France listed as a historical monument, in 1965.

summary.description: A modernist villa in Poissy, built in reinforced concrete in 1928-1931 for Pierre and Eugénie Savoye by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret. It embodies Le Corbusier's Five Points of architecture, and a ramp runs through the house.
keyFeatures: Raised on pilotis
Roof garden
Free floor plan
Long horizontal windows
Ramp through the house
funFacts: It was the first modernist building listed as a historical monument in France, in 1965.
It joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2016, with 16 other works by the same architect.

architects.name: Adalberto Libera
architects.bio: Italian rationalist architect credited, alongside the writer Curzio Malaparte, as author of Casa Malaparte.

hints.text: A red masonry box stands on a Mediterranean cliff 32 metres above the sea, reached on foot or by 99 steps from the water.
Reverse-pyramid stairs lead up to a roof patio with a freestanding curved white wall.
Begun in 1937 for a writer, it is a famous setting in Jean-Luc Godard's 1963 film Contempt.

summary.description: A house on Punta Massullo on the eastern side of Capri, begun in 1937 for the writer Curzio Malaparte; Adalberto Libera is credited as architect. It is a red masonry box on a cliff 32 m above the sea, with reverse-pyramid stairs leading to a roof patio.
keyFeatures: Red masonry box on a sea cliff
Reverse-pyramid stairs
Roof patio
Freestanding curved white wall
funFacts: It features prominently in Godard's film Contempt (1963).
It was donated to the Giorgio Ronchi Foundation in 1972.

architects.name: Filippo Juvarra
architects.bio: Italian architect who began the design of the Royal Palace of Madrid.

architects.name: Giovanni Battista Sacchetti
architects.bio: Juvarra's disciple, who continued the work on the Royal Palace of Madrid.

photos.alt: Vast granite-and-limestone palace front with giant pilasters, a central clock pediment and a huge paved square
photos.credit: Photo: Carlos Delgado · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Close view of a grand stone palace front with giant columns, a rooftop balustrade with statues and a central arched doorway.
photos.credit: Photo: kallerna · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A long palace with a domed centre seen across a rectangular reflecting pool, clipped hedges, statues and tall evergreen trees.
photos.credit: Photo: Jan S0L0 · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Grand marble staircase hall with gilded lamps, stucco and a painted vaulted ceiling
photos.credit: Photo: Joseolgon · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the largest royal palace in Europe, with about 135,000 square metres of floor area and 3,418 rooms.
It rose on the site of a medieval fortress that burned down on Christmas Eve 1734, when a famous painting was saved by being thrown out of a window.
Its grand staircase is carved from a single piece of San Agustín marble.

summary.description: The official residence of the Spanish royal family, used mainly for state ceremonies. Built after the old Alcázar burned in 1734, it was designed by Filippo Juvarra and continued by Giambattista Sacchetti, with a Late Baroque and Classical exterior of grey granite and white limestone.
keyFeatures: About 135,000 m² and 3,418 rooms
Granite and limestone façade with giant-order columns
Grand Staircase by Francesco Sabatini
Frescoes by Tiepolo, Giaquinto and Mengs
funFacts: Las Meninas was saved from the 1734 fire by being tossed out of a window.
It holds the world's only complete Stradivarius string quintet.

architects.name: John Nash
architects.bio: British architect who expanded Buckingham House for George IV from 1826 and was removed from the project in 1829.

architects.name: Edward Blore
architects.bio: British architect who finished the palace for William IV from 1830 and designed its east wing in 1847-1849.

architects.name: Aston Webb
architects.bio: British architect who redesigned the East Front in Portland stone in 1913.

photos.alt: Wide pale stone palace front with a central pediment and portico, gilded gates, bronze statues and an empty forecourt at dawn.
photos.credit: Photo: Julian Herzog (Website) · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long pale stone palace front with a central pediment, seen across a roundabout, flower beds and a gilded memorial statue
photos.credit: Photo: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: The garden side of a large stone palace with a central bow window and green dome, seen across a wide lawn with white marquees.
photos.credit: Photo: Tony kang peppy · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Wide pale stone palace front with a central portico, gilded gates and railings, and people on the pavement
photos.credit: Photo: Suicasmo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It began as a modest 1703 mansion for a duke and became a royal home after a king bought it in 1761 for his queen.
It has 775 rooms, including 19 state rooms and a ballroom 120 feet long, and the royal family greets crowds from its balcony.
Its Portland-stone East Front dates from 1913, and Queen Victoria was the first monarch to live there, from 1837.

summary.description: The London residence of the British monarch, which grew from Buckingham House (1703) after George III bought it in 1761. John Nash expanded it from 1826, Edward Blore finished the work and added the east wing, and Aston Webb gave the East Front its present Portland-stone face in 1913.
keyFeatures: 775 rooms, including 19 state rooms
East Front balcony
Ballroom 120 ft long
39-acre private garden
funFacts: Queen Victoria was the first monarch to reside there, from 1837.
The palace was bombed nine times in the Second World War.

architects.name: Horace Jones
architects.bio: City Architect of London who designed Tower Bridge but died in 1887, before it was finished.

architects.name: John Wolfe Barry
architects.bio: Engineer of Tower Bridge who took over as its architect after Horace Jones died.

photos.alt: Two Gothic-style stone towers joined by a high blue-and-white walkway, with suspension chains, rising from stone piers on a wide river.
photos.credit: Photo: Acabashi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Two Gothic-style stone towers joined by high walkways, seen over an old fortress wall
photos.credit: Photo: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A road passing through the tall arched base of a Gothic stone tower, framed by pale blue girders under a bright sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Doyle of London · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Aerial view of a twin-towered bridge with blue suspension chains crossing a wide brown river
photos.credit: Photo: Colin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is often mistaken for a different bridge, yet it is a bascule bridge whose roadway can split and lift for ships.
Its steel frame is clad in granite and stone to look like a medieval fortress, and its towers are about 65 metres high.
Its architect died in 1887, seven years before it opened to the public in 1894.

summary.description: Tower Bridge crosses the Thames beside a medieval fortress, so its steel skeleton was dressed in Victorian Gothic stone to match. The central span splits into two bascules that lift in about five minutes to let ships through. It opened in 1894.
keyFeatures: Bascule span in two leaves of about 1,070 tons each
Steel frame clad in Cornish granite and Portland stone
Towers about 65 m high
High-level walkways linking the towers
funFacts: In 1952 a double-decker bus driver accelerated across the gap as the bridge began to rise.
It was painted red, white and blue for the 1977 Silver Jubilee.

architects.name: John A. Roebling
architects.bio: Engineer who designed the Brooklyn Bridge; he died in 1869 before construction began in earnest.

architects.name: Washington Roebling
architects.bio: Son of John A. Roebling and chief engineer of the Brooklyn Bridge; his wife Emily Warren Roebling helped supervise the work.

photos.alt: Suspension bridge with a granite tower, fans of steel cables and a long approach span crossing a river toward a distant shore on a clear day.
photos.credit: Photo: Kidfly182 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Granite tower with two pointed arches and a flag on top, criss-crossed by a web of steel suspension cables against a blue sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Ingfbruno · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Taken by Jeffrey Bary, uploaded by CPacker · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Steel cables fanning out over a roadway toward a city skyline at sunset
photos.credit: Photo: Arild Vågen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: When it opened it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, with a main span of about 486 metres.
Its stone towers have pointed Gothic arches, and its four main cables hold 5,282 steel wires each.
Its designer died before work really began, so his son took over, and later his daughter-in-law supervised; it opened in 1883.

summary.description: The Brooklyn Bridge links two boroughs across the East River with a hybrid of suspension cables and diagonal stays. Its granite-and-limestone towers carry Gothic pointed arches. It was designed by John A. Roebling and finished under his son Washington, with Emily Warren Roebling helping to supervise the work.
keyFeatures: Main span of 1,595.5 ft (486.3 m)
Neo-Gothic towers about 85 m tall
Early use of steel-wire cables
Hybrid of suspension cables and diagonal stays
funFacts: About 150,300 people crossed it on opening day.
It cost about $15.5 million in 1883 dollars.

architects.name: Joseph Strauss
architects.bio: Chief engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge.

architects.name: Irving Morrow
architects.bio: Architect who designed the bridge's towers and Art Deco details.

architects.name: Charles Ellis
architects.bio: Principal engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge, who received little credit until later.

architects.name: Leon Moisseiff
architects.bio: Engineer who conceived the final suspension design of the bridge.

photos.credit: Photo: Goldrock95 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A tall red-orange tower rising out of fog above a roadway full of cars

hints.text: Its colour, a vermilion called International Orange, was chosen partly to stay visible in fog.
Its 1,280-metre main span was the longest in the world until 1964, and its towers rise 227 metres.
It opened in May 1937, after 200,000 people walked and roller-skated across it the day before cars were allowed.

summary.description: This suspension bridge crosses the strait at the mouth of San Francisco Bay. The main span of 4,200 ft held the world record until 1964, and its towers and railings carry Art Deco details. Its International Orange paint was chosen to stand out in the fog.
keyFeatures: Main span of 4,200 ft (1,280 m)
Towers 746 ft (227 m) high
Art Deco tower decoration, streetlights and railings
International Orange colour
funFacts: It was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world when it opened.
Construction began on 5 January 1933 and cost more than $35 million.

architects.name: Théophile Seyrig
architects.bio: Engineer who designed the Dom Luís I Bridge; he was a former partner of Gustave Eiffel and designed the similar Maria Pia Bridge.

photos.alt: Large iron arch bridge with a lattice deck high above, a stone abutment with steps on the left and a lower deck beneath.

photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Close view up at a curving iron lattice arch supporting an upper deck, braced by slender vertical trusses against a pale sky.

photos.alt: A river at dusk with moored boats and lit old quays, and a bridge in the distance
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It has two decks: one high on the cliff tops and another low beside the river.
Its designer was a former partner of the engineer of a famous Paris tower, and his earlier bridge nearby looks similar.
When it opened in 1886, its 172-metre iron arch was the longest of its type in the world.

summary.description: This double-deck iron arch bridge crosses the Douro between Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia. It was designed by Théophile Seyrig, who earlier designed the nearby Maria Pia Bridge. When it opened in 1886 its 172 m span was the longest of its type.
keyFeatures: Two-hinged iron arch with a 172 m span
Two decks at different heights
Upper deck now carries the Porto Metro
Built by the Belgian Société de Willebroek
funFacts: Tolls began in 1886 at 4 reis per person and ended in 1944.
The upper deck closed to motor traffic in 2003 to carry the metro.

architects.name: Antonio da Ponte
architects.bio: Venetian architect who designed the single-span stone Rialto Bridge.

hints.text: It replaced wooden bridges that collapsed twice, in 1444 and 1524.
It is a single stone arch with two ramps of shops leading to a central portico; its span is about 32 metres.
Its design was chosen over rivals, and one famous architect predicted it would fall; it was finished in 1591.

summary.description: The Rialto Bridge crosses the Grand Canal in a single stone arch, with two covered ramps of shops rising to a central portico. It replaced a timber bridge that had collapsed in 1444 and 1524. Antonio da Ponte completed it in 1591.
keyFeatures: Single stone arch of 31.8 m
Two ramps lined with shops
Central portico
Replaced a wooden bridge with a lifting section
funFacts: A timber bridge of 1255 had a movable central section for tall ships.
Vincenzo Scamozzi predicted it would fall, yet it became one of Venice's top attractions.

architects.name: Taddeo Gaddi
architects.bio: Florentine painter and architect to whom Giorgio Vasari attributed the design of the Ponte Vecchio; modern historians suggest Neri di Fioravanti as its possible builder.

photos.alt: Three-arched stone bridge lined with colourful houses and a long covered gallery above, crossing a calm river under a clear sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Ingo Mehling · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A stone bridge lined with houses and shops crossing a river, seen from the grassy bank
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Oblique view along a bridge of stacked yellow and orange houses with shutters and balconies overhanging a green river.

photos.alt: Close view of the stone arches of a bridge, with a row of shuttered houses and a long arcaded corridor on top.
photos.credit: Photo: Julian Lupyan · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A bridge with houses along its edge and a long arcaded building beside it, reflected in a river at dusk
photos.credit: Photo: Martin Falbisoner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its shops first held butchers and tanners until a 1565 decree left only goldsmiths and jewellers.
A private corridor was built above it in 1565 so a ruling family could walk between two palaces.
It was the only bridge in its city not destroyed in the German retreat of August 1944, and it was rebuilt in stone in 1345.

summary.description: The Ponte Vecchio is a medieval stone bridge of three segmental arches, lined with shops on both sides. It was rebuilt in 1345 after earlier bridges were destroyed by floods. Since 1565 its shops have been occupied by goldsmiths and jewellers.
keyFeatures: Three segmental stone arches
Main span of 30 m, side spans of 27 m
Shops built along both sides
Corridor above, added in 1565
funFacts: It was the only Florentine bridge not destroyed in August 1944.
In 2005-2006 the city removed 5,500 love padlocks from its railings.

architects.name: Michel Virlogeux
architects.bio: French structural engineer who led the design team of the Millau Viaduct.

architects.name: Norman Foster
architects.bio: British architect who redesigned the ruined building from 1995 to 1999 for the reunified German parliament, adding a glass dome that opens the roof to the public.

photos.alt: A very long cable-stayed bridge on tall slender piers with white pylons spans a wide valley above fields and a small town.

photos.alt: Tall slender concrete piers rising over farmland

photos.credit: Photo: Richard Leeming from London, UK · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Aerial view of a long white bridge crossing a deep valley, with winding roads, patchwork fields and a town on the far side.
photos.credit: Photo: kallerna · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It carries a motorway across a river gorge on seven slender piers, and its deck is about 2.5 kilometres long.
Seven masts, each 87 metres high, hold the deck, and its tallest pier is 343 metres tall.
It was inaugurated in December 2004 and was the world's tallest bridge for over two decades.

summary.description: This multispan cable-stayed viaduct crosses the gorge of the River Tarn. Michel Virlogeux led the structural design and Norman Foster provided the architecture. It opened in December 2004.
keyFeatures: Deck 2,460 m long
Seven masts of 87 m
Tallest pier 343 m
Six central spans of 342 m
funFacts: Construction cost about 394 million euros.
It has a design life of 120 years.

architects.name: John Fowler
architects.bio: British engineer who designed the Forth Bridge with Benjamin Baker.

architects.name: Benjamin Baker
architects.bio: British engineer who designed the Forth Bridge with John Fowler.

photos.alt: Large red steel cantilever arms rising from stone piers over tidal water, with a small boat
photos.credit: Photo: Graeme Yuill · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A long red steel cantilever bridge on the horizon across a blue estuary
photos.credit: Photo: MrMasterKeyboard · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Red steel cantilever bridge crossing a blue estuary beyond rooftops and trees, with a small rocky island with a fort beside it.
photos.credit: Photo: Holger Uwe Schmitt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Close view of thick red tubular steel struts and lattice girders rising from a stone pier of a large cantilever bridge.
photos.credit: Photo: Myself (Adrian Pingstone). · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A rail bridge so associated with endless upkeep that its name became a phrase for a never-ending task.
Its two main spans are each 520 metres, built from pairs of cantilever arms, and about 6.5 million rivets hold it together.
Opened in March 1890, it was the first major steel structure in Britain, and it is now a World Heritage Site.

summary.description: This railway bridge carries the Edinburgh-Aberdeen line across the Firth of Forth on three huge steel cantilever towers. John Fowler and Benjamin Baker designed it. It was completed in December 1889 and opened in March 1890.
keyFeatures: Two main spans of 1,700 ft (520 m)
Total length 8,094 ft (2,467 m)
About 6.5 million rivets
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015
funFacts: In 1887 a human demonstration of a cantilever used Kaichi Watanabe seated between Fowler and Baker.
It had the longest single cantilever span in the world when it opened.

architects.name: Unknown Roman architects
architects.bio: The builders of this imperial bath complex, erected under Septimius Severus and Caracalla, are not recorded.

photos.credit: Photo: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a bridge that was really a channel: it carried water to a city about 50 kilometres away.
Three tiers of 6, 11 and 35 arches rise 48.8 metres, with stone blocks fitted without mortar.
Newer excavations date it to about 40-60 AD, though it was long credited to Agrippa around 19 BC.

summary.description: This three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge carried water from near Uzes to Nimes. Its stone blocks, some up to 6 tons, were cut to fit together without mortar. It is dated to roughly 40-60 AD.
keyFeatures: Height of 48.8 m
Three tiers with 6, 11 and 35 arches
Dry-stone construction without mortar
Part of a 50 km aqueduct
funFacts: The aqueduct carried an estimated 40,000 cubic metres of water per day.
It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.

architects.name: Edward E. Carlson
architects.bio: Hotel executive who proposed the balloon-like base idea that started the Space Needle.

architects.name: John Graham Jr.
architects.bio: Seattle architect who designed the flying-saucer top of the Space Needle.

architects.name: Victor Steinbrueck
architects.bio: Seattle architect who introduced the hourglass profile and tripod design of the Space Needle.

photos.alt: Slender white tower on splayed legs with a flying-saucer-shaped deck on top, rising above a lawn and a colourful wall under a blue sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Pamjunipero · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A slender tower with a flying-saucer-shaped top rising above trees into a cloudy blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Close view of a saucer-shaped observation deck with a glazed ring, radiating roof ribs, a central spire and white legs below.
photos.credit: Photo: MyName (Cacophony) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A slim tower with a saucer-shaped top stands among a cluster of high-rise towers and low buildings under a hazy sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Candace56 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Tall cream-coloured legs and the underside of a saucer-shaped deck, with a lift shaft between them
photos.credit: Photo: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a world's fair whose theme was the future, and it opened in April 1962.
Its hourglass-shaped legs support a saucer-like top with a revolving restaurant, about 520 feet up.
It was built to withstand winds of up to 200 mph, twice the building code requirement of its day.

summary.description: Built for the 1962 Century 21 Exposition, this tower combines a tripod hourglass profile with a flying-saucer top. Edward Carlson proposed the idea, John Graham designed the top and Victor Steinbrueck the hourglass shape. It is 605 ft (184 m) tall including its antenna.
keyFeatures: Hourglass tripod profile
Flying-saucer top with revolving restaurant
Height of 605 ft (184 m)
Observation deck about 520 ft up
funFacts: Elevators reach the observation deck in about 41 seconds.
The 1962 World's Fair drew more than 2.3 million visitors.

architects.name: Alexandre Chan
architects.bio: Architect of the Juscelino Kubitschek Bridge, who received the 2003 Gustav Lindenthal Medal for it.

architects.name: Mário Vila Verde
architects.bio: Structural engineer of the Juscelino Kubitschek Bridge.

photos.alt: Aerial view of a long road bridge carried by three white steel arches that cross wide calm water toward a green shore.
photos.credit: Photo: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Three white steel arches crossing a wide lake in the distance
photos.credit: Photo: Eliene Vieira de Araújo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Three white arches rising from a road bridge over a wide lake, seen from a grassy shore under a cloudy sky.
photos.credit: Photo: Agência Brasília from Brasília, Brasil · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Black-and-white view along a roadway between rows of cables, with an arch ahead
photos.credit: Photo: hiabba from Brazil · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its steel arches cross the roadway from one side to the other, with cables interlacing in a twisted plane.
It has three spans of 240 metres, and the arches stand about 61 metres tall.
It opened to traffic on 15 December 2002 and later won an international medal for its architect.

summary.description: This bridge crosses Lake Paranoa with three asymmetrical steel arches that alternate from side to side of the deck. It was designed by architect Alexandre Chan and engineer Mario Vila Verde. It opened on 15 December 2002.
keyFeatures: Three steel arches about 61 m tall
Three spans of 240 m
Total length 1,200 m
Cables alternating on each side of the deck
funFacts: Alexandre Chan received the 2003 Gustav Lindenthal Medal.
It cost US$56.8 million.

architects.name: Unknown Inca builders
architects.bio: Inca builders who raised the site as a royal estate, most likely for the emperor Pachacuti, working in fine dry-stone ashlar masonry.

photos.alt: Stone ruins and green terraces on a mountain ridge below a steep peak, under heavy cloud
photos.credit: Photo: Martin St-Amant (S23678) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Rows of roofless stone houses with tall gables on green grass terraces below a steep, forested mountain peak under cloud.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stepped grass terraces and dry-stone walls with a steep green peak behind
photos.caption: Terraces and walls built without mortar.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A roofless room of large, precisely fitted stone blocks with three trapezoidal window openings in one wall, beside smaller boulders.
photos.credit: Photo: WMrapids · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a royal estate built on a mountain ridge high in the Andes, far above a river valley.
Its walls are made of finely cut stones fitted together without mortar, and its terraces cover about 4.9 hectares.
It was brought to international attention in 1911 by an American explorer, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

summary.description: This Inca estate sits at about 2,430 m on a ridge above the Urubamba valley. Most archaeologists believe it was ordered by the emperor Pachacuti around the mid-15th century. Its dry-stone ashlar walls, terraces and solar-aligned buildings made it one of the best-known sites of the Americas.
keyFeatures: Dry-stone ashlar masonry
Agricultural terraces (andenes)
Temple of the Sun (Torreón), a semicircular tower
Intihuatana ritual stone
Mountain ridge setting
funFacts: Hiram Bingham's expeditions recovered 15th-century knives of bismuth bronze, the earliest known objects made of that alloy.
It draws over 1.5 million visitors a year, making it Peru's most visited international destination.

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: The palace grew in campaigns sponsored by King John I from around 1415 and by King Manuel I between 1497 and 1530; its master builders are not recorded.

photos.alt: Rock-cut temple front with four colossal seated pharaoh statues flanking a small doorway
photos.credit: Photo: Abumalek ahmed mohamed · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A rock-cut temple front with four colossal seated figures cut into a sandstone cliff above a wide sandy forecourt with visitors.
photos.credit: Photo: Olaf Tausch · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A smaller rock-cut temple front with six tall standing figures separated by sloping buttresses, carved into a sandstone cliff.
photos.credit: Photo: Olaf Tausch · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Hall with giant standing royal figures against the wall and a painted ceiling with winged vultures
photos.caption: The Osiride pillars of the hypostyle hall.
photos.credit: Photo: MatthiasKabel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Four seated figures carved in the rear wall of a small dim chamber, lit from the front, with hieroglyphs on the walls around them.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Two temples were carved straight into a sandstone cliff by a pharaoh, one for himself and one for his favourite wife.
In the 1960s the whole complex was cut into 1,036 blocks and rebuilt on higher ground to escape a rising reservoir.
Twice a year, around 22 October and 22 February, sunlight reaches the inner sanctuary and lights the statues there, except one that stays in shadow.

summary.description: Ramesses II had two rock temples carved into a cliff in Nubia, beginning around 1264 BC and taking about twenty years. The Great Temple is fronted by four seated colossi about 20 m high, and the smaller temple honours Hathor in the person of Queen Nefertari. Between 1964 and 1968 the temples were moved piece by piece to avoid flooding by Lake Nasser.
keyFeatures: Four seated colossi about 20 m high
Façade about 33 m high and 38 m wide
Hypostyle hall with eight Osiride pillars
Reliefs of the Battle of Kadesh
Solar alignment of the sanctuary
funFacts: The relocation cost about 41.7 million US dollars, shared between Egypt and contributions from 48 countries.
The temples were reassembled about 208 m inland and about 65 m higher.

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: The palace grew in campaigns sponsored by King John I from around 1415 and by King Manuel I between 1497 and 1530; its master builders are not recorded.

photos.alt: A row of ram-headed sphinx statues lines a processional path leading to a massive sandstone gateway with tall window slots.
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Two massive sandstone gateway towers with window slots, seen across a wide paved court
photos.credit: Photo: Marc Ryckaert · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Ancient sandstone temple ruins with an obelisk and palm trees beside a still rectangular lake that mirrors them in warm evening light.
photos.credit: Photo: Taranis-iuppiter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Aerial view of a vast ruined temple precinct with a rectangular lake, walls and gateways, beside a river and a town.
photos.credit: Photo: Ahmed Bahloul Khier Galal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Avenue between enormous carved columns, with a tiny visitor standing at the far end
photos.caption: Columns of the great hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a vast religious precinct that grew for some two thousand years, with about thirty rulers adding to it.
One hall holds 134 giant columns in 16 rows, the tallest about 21 m high.
Its name for the chief god's precinct was Ipet-isut, often translated as the Most Select of Places.

summary.description: This sprawling complex of temples, chapels and pylons near Thebes was begun under Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom and extended into Ptolemaic times. Most of what survives dates from the New Kingdom, and the largest precinct honours the god Amun-Re. It is believed to be Egypt's second most visited ancient site after the Giza pyramids.
keyFeatures: Great Hypostyle Hall with 134 columns
First Pylon about 113 m long and 43 m high
Precinct of Amun-Re
Obelisks of Hatshepsut and others
Sacred lake and processional ways
funFacts: The hall's architraves are estimated to weigh about 70 tons each.
Six hundred black granite statues were found in the courtyard of the Mut temple.

architects.name: Unknown Achaemenid builders
architects.bio: Builders and craftsmen working for the Achaemenid kings, beginning under Darius I and continued by Xerxes I and Artaxerxes I.

photos.alt: Stone gateway with a huge lintel, bearded winged bull guardians and tall slender columns with animal capitals
photos.credit: Photo: User:Ggia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Elevated view over a vast platform of ancient stone ruins with foundations, doorways and rows of columns under a hazy sky.
photos.credit: Photo: F Couin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Massive stone terrace walls of an ancient citadel rising above bright green grass with distant mountains behind.
photos.credit: Photo: Masoudkhalife · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: A wide stone staircase with many shallow steps climbing along a wall of large cut stone blocks to a raised terrace.
photos.credit: Photo: Carole Raddato from Frankfurt, Germany · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stone stairway wall carved with rows of figures and a lion attacking a bull, under a modern roof
photos.caption: Reliefs of a ceremonial staircase.
photos.credit: Photo: A.Davey from Portland, Oregon, EE UU · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was a ceremonial capital on a raised stone terrace, used seasonally rather than as an everyday city.
A king founded it around 515 BC, and its columns once stood about 16.5 m tall and were topped with double-bull capitals.
It was burned in 330 BC after being taken by Alexander the Great, and ancient writers disagree on whether the fire was deliberate or an accident.

summary.description: Darius I made this the ceremonial seat of the Achaemenid Empire, and Xerxes I and Artaxerxes I extended it over the following generations. Built mainly of grey limestone on a partly artificial terrace, it held audience halls, gateways and treasuries. It was destroyed by fire in 330 BC and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979.
keyFeatures: Raised stone terrace
Apadana audience hall
Gate of All Nations with bull guardians
Hall of a Hundred Columns
Processional relief carvings
funFacts: Gold and silver foundation tablets were buried beneath the Apadana.
It is linked with the Nowruz festivities.

architects.name: Unknown Roman architects
architects.bio: The builders of this imperial bath complex, erected under Septimius Severus and Caracalla, are not recorded.

photos.alt: Valley of ruined temple columns, a triumphal arch and low foundations, with a Baroque church dome at the edge
photos.credit: Photo: Nicholas Hartmann · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Ancient temple portico with a Latin inscription on its architrave, beside ruined walls and a distant amphitheatre
photos.credit: Photo: Jon Gudorf Photography · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Jebulon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Weathered triumphal arch with three openings and relief panels beside a lone tall column, with a baroque church front at right.

photos.credit: Photo: Miguel Hermoso Cuesta · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Small round ancient temple on a tall podium with fluted Corinthian columns and a fragment of entablature against a blue sky.

hints.text: It began as a drained marsh in a valley between two hills and grew into the civic heart of a great city.
It hosted triumphal processions, elections, trials and speeches, and a famous dictator was cremated here in 44 BC.
In the 1540s stone was quarried from it for a new basilica, and by then cattle grazed there and it was called the 'cattle field'.

summary.description: This open space between the Palatine and Capitoline hills began as a marketplace and became the civic centre of ancient Rome. Temples, basilicas, arches and speakers' platforms were added over about a thousand years, the last major monument in 608 AD. After the empire fell it decayed, was quarried for building stone, and has been excavated since the 19th century.
keyFeatures: Temple of Saturn, eight columns surviving
Arch of Septimius Severus, 203 AD
Curia Julia, the Senate house
Rostra, the speakers' platform
Basilica of Maxentius, 312 AD
funFacts: Julius Caesar was cremated here, and Mark Antony gave his funeral speech here.
The medieval name of the area was Campo Vaccino, the cattle field.

architects.name: Polykleitos the Younger
architects.bio: Greek architect credited with designing the theatre in the 4th century BC.

photos.alt: Huge semicircular stone auditorium rising up a wooded hillside around a circular flat floor
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Curved rows of weathered limestone seats seen from above, with one person sitting among them
photos.caption: The limestone seat rows.
photos.credit: Photo: Orlovic · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Zde · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tiered stone seating rising behind a stone entrance gateway at the edge of a flat gravel floor, with dense pines above.

photos.credit: Photo: George E. Koronaios · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: View down steep stone seating to a perfectly circular flat floor, with ruins, forest and distant mountains beyond.

hints.text: It is a hillside auditorium built in the 4th century BC as part of a healing sanctuary.
Its 34 original rows were extended by 21 more in Roman times, and it could hold up to 14,000 people.
It is famous for acoustics that carry stage speech to the top row, and it still hosts drama performances today.

summary.description: This theatre belongs to the Sanctuary of Asclepius and is credited to Polykleitos the Younger in the 4th century BC. Its tiered limestone seating wraps around a circular orchestra, and the landscape behind the stage is part of the view. Its sanctuary was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.
keyFeatures: Capacity of up to 14,000
34 original rows plus 21 added by the Romans
Circular orchestra
Limestone seating that filters low-frequency noise
Open view of the landscape
funFacts: Measurements show the seat rows filter out low-frequency crowd murmur and boost high-frequency stage sound.
It is still used for dramatic performances today.

architects.name: Raymond Hood
architects.bio: American architect who was the lead architect of Rockefeller Center.

photos.alt: Tall slender setback skyscraper seen between two lower stone buildings flying flags
photos.credit: Photo: D. Benjamin Miller · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Acediscovery · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall slender stepped-back tower rising between two lower dark buildings under a blue sky, seen from street level.

photos.credit: Photo: King of Hearts · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking straight up the limestone face of a skyscraper, vertical bands of windows and dark spandrels narrowing toward the stepped top.
Lobby wall and ceiling painted in brown tones with muscular workers raising a building and a man in a top hat
photos.caption: A lobby mural of workers building a nation.
photos.credit: Photo: PortableNYCTours · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a tall office tower with a flat roof and stepped setbacks, the centrepiece of a large city complex.
It was completed in 1933, and a restaurant on its 65th floor opened in 1934.
A broadcaster has its headquarters here, and its studio 8H is home to a long-running late-night comedy show.

summary.description: This 66-storey tower is the centrepiece of Rockefeller Center in Midtown Manhattan, completed in 1933. Raymond Hood was the complex's lead architect, working within a group of associated firms. Its stepped Art Deco massing, lobby murals and a sculpture over the entrance made it an icon of New York.
keyFeatures: 66 stories with a flat roof and setbacks
Art Deco styling
Lee Lawrie's sculpture Wisdom over the entrance
Josep Maria Sert's lobby murals
Rainbow Room restaurant on the 65th floor
funFacts: Diego Rivera's mural Man at the Crossroads was destroyed in 1934 because of its communist imagery.
It has had three names: RCA Building, GE Building and, since 2015, Comcast Building.

architects.name: Claud Beelman
architects.bio: American architect who designed this 13-storey building for a department-store company.

photos.alt: Turquoise terracotta tower with vertical fluting and gold trim rising above lower buildings
photos.credit: Photo: Photo: Andreas Praefcke · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Entrance detail with fluted turquoise terracotta piers, a gold sunburst relief and blue zigzag tiles
photos.credit: Photo: Binksternet · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Caterpillar84 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Visitor7 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of blue and turquoise fluted terracotta bays with stepped ochre ornament under the windows.

hints.text: It is a 13-storey department-store headquarters clad in glossy terracotta tiles.
It was built in about nine months and opened in 1930; a clock tower was exempted from the city's 150-foot height limit.
Its turquoise and gold clock tower carries a company name in white neon on all four sides.

summary.description: This building opened on 12 September 1930 as the headquarters of a department-store company that merged a furniture store and a clothing store. It is clad in turquoise terracotta with deep blue and gold trim, and its clock tower is topped by four stylised flying buttresses. It is often called the greatest surviving Art Deco building in Los Angeles.
keyFeatures: Turquoise glazed terracotta
Blue and gold trim
Four-sided clock tower, 264 ft in total
Neon lettering on the tower
Gold sunburst reliefs at the entrance
funFacts: It was built for about 1.25 million dollars in roughly nine months.
It was converted into 147 condominiums in a 2006 renovation.

architects.name: Wallis, Gilbert and Partners
architects.bio: British architectural firm that also designed the Firestone Tyre Factory in Brentford and Victoria Coach Station.

photos.alt: White stair tower with red and black stripes, green glazed bars and arched windows under a deep blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Ethan Doyle White · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: White façade with tall green-glazed windows between pale piers and a colourful geometric entrance
photos.credit: Photo: Ethan Doyle White · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Steve Cadman · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Pale entrance hall with fluted pilasters, a geometric glazed door and a green-ribbed skylight above, over a patterned tile floor.

hints.text: It is a former factory beside a major arterial road in outer West London.
It opened in 1933, with a geometric sunburst pattern above its entrance, and was listed Grade II* in 1980.
A supermarket chain bought it in 1989, and Elvis Costello recorded a song about it in 1980.

summary.description: This former vacuum-cleaner factory on Western Avenue in Perivale, in the London Borough of Ealing, opened on 2 May 1933. It was designed by Wallis, Gilbert and Partners, with large columns, recessed glass bay windows and a sunburst pattern above the entrance. It later became offices and, in 2017-2018, apartments.
keyFeatures: Large columns and recessed glass bays
Geometric sunburst above the entrance
White rendered walls with green and red detail
Grade II* listed since 1980
Converted to apartments in 2017-2018
funFacts: Elvis Costello recorded the song Hoover Factory in 1980 as the B-side of Clubland.
Its architects also designed Victoria Coach Station.

architects.name: Hijman Louis de Jong
architects.bio: Dutch architect who designed this cinema with Willem Kromhout.

architects.name: Willem Kromhout
architects.bio: Dutch architect who, with Hijman Louis de Jong, designed this cinema.

photos.alt: Tall tiled façade with two towers, leadlight windows, ceramic sculptures and a lit entrance canopy
photos.credit: Photo: User:DirkvdM · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Txllxt TxllxT · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of a stained-glass window framed by carved stone brackets with grotesque faces and wrought-iron ornaments on a tiled wall.
Auditorium balcony with glowing amber lamps and walls painted in geometric patterns of red and gold
photos.caption: The main auditorium.
photos.credit: Photo: Jvhertum · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: A. J. van der Wal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Painted figures in angular decorative frames above polished wooden balcony rails, with a scalloped plaster ceiling and a lamp above.

hints.text: It is a cinema that opened in 1921, designed to make visitors feel they are entering an illusion.
Its façade mixes Art Deco, Art Nouveau and Amsterdam School details, with ceramic sculptures and leadlight windows, and its interior has Asian influences.
Its founder was murdered in 1942 after the occupiers seized the company, and it has been owned by a film company since 1995.

summary.description: This cinema opened on 28 October 1921, founded by Abraham Tuschinski and designed by Hijman Louis de Jong and Willem Kromhout. Its façade has two towers, ceramic sculptures and leadlight windows, and its lavish interior has Asian influences. It has been a national monument since 1967 and was restored from 1998 to 2002.
keyFeatures: Façade with two towers and ceramic sculptures
Leadlight windows
Main hall with screen, stage and organ, 1,431 seats
Interior with Asian influences
Rijksmonument since 1967
funFacts: Time Out named it the most beautiful cinema in the world in 2021.
Its founder bought a theatre organ from Brussels when the maker could not deliver in time.

name: Capela das Almas
aliases: Capela das Almas de Santa Catarina

architects.name: Unknown Portuguese builders
architects.bio: Anonymous builders of the late 18th-century chapel, which was enlarged and restored in 1801.

architects.name: Eduardo Leite
architects.bio: Painter who designed the 1929 azulejo panels, made at the Viúva Lamego factory in Lisbon.

photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Small chapel on a street corner with a bell gable and long walls entirely covered in blue and white painted tiles, under a pale sky.
Small stone church with a bell gable whose walls are covered in blue and white tile panels
photos.credit: Photo: John Samuel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Blue and white tile panel of a crucifixion scene framed by angels and scrolls
photos.caption: One of the scenes on the outer walls.
photos.credit: Photo: Krzysztof Golik · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its plain stone walls are wrapped from top to bottom in a skin of blue and white glazed tiles.
The tiles show scenes from the lives of saints and were painted in the twentieth century, long after the chapel itself was built.
About 16,000 tiles, covering some 360 square metres, were fired for it in a Lisbon factory in 1929.

summary.description: A late 18th-century chapel in Porto, enlarged and restored in 1801, whose outer walls are covered with 15,947 azulejos. Eduardo Leite designed the panels in 1929, and the Viúva Lamego factory in Lisbon made them.
keyFeatures: Façades clad in blue and white azulejos
About 360 square metres of tile
Scenes from the lives of saints
Two bodies, the second one lower
funFacts: Its tiles number 15,947.
The Brotherhood of Souls moved here in the late 18th century from the Santa Clara monastery.

architects.name: José Figueiredo Seixas
architects.bio: Architect of the Carmo church, built for the Third Order of Carmel between 1756 and 1768.

photos.alt: Tall church side wall covered by one huge blue and white tile mural between barred windows
photos.credit: Photo: Henrique Matos · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: T meltzer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Granite wall with arched and rectangular windows set in a blue and white tile panel of scrolls, with a wooden door below.

photos.credit: Photo: Jsamwrites · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Upward view of a carved granite church front with a curved gable, statues, a cross, and a niche holding a figure of the Virgin.

photos.credit: Photo: Xcia0069 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Church nave with a coffered barrel vault, pale stone walls and a gilded altarpiece glowing at the far end beneath a chandelier.
Close view of a blue and white tile mural of robed figures gathered on a hillside
photos.caption: Detail of the mural on the side wall.
photos.credit: Photo: Yellow.Cat from Roma, Italy · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A tall Baroque church whose bare side wall was covered with a single enormous painted picture in the early twentieth century.
The mural tells the legend of the order that owns the church, and it sits beside another church with only a sliver of a house between them.
It was built between 1756 and 1768, and the tile mural dates from 1912.

summary.description: A Baroque church with Rococo touches, built between 1756 and 1768 by the Third Order of Carmel and designed by José Figueiredo Seixas. Its side wall carries a large azulejo composition designed by Silvestre Silvestri and painted by Carlos Branco in 1912.
keyFeatures: Baroque design with Rococo elements
Giant azulejo mural on the side wall
Mural dated 1912
A very narrow hidden house separates it from the neighbouring church
funFacts: The Casa Escondida, just over 1.5 metres wide, stands between this church and the Carmelitas church.
The hospital of the order was finished later, in 1801.

architects.name: Unknown Portuguese builders
architects.bio: Builders of the hunting pavilion raised in 1671-72 for João de Mascarenhas, 1st Marquis of Fronteira.

photos.credit: Photo: MFREYNAUD51 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Red and white mansion with arched upper loggia beyond a clipped box-hedge garden, a long balustraded pool and a blue tiled wall.

photos.credit: Photo: GualdimG · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
