photos.alt: Closer view of the red garden front with arched openings and pilasters above formal hedges, statues and a tiled wall.

photos.credit: Photo: Kent Wang · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Symmetrical red courtyard front with a central loggia of arches over an open ground-floor arcade and a paved forecourt.
Garden gallery with niches holding busts, blue tiled walls, a long green pool and clipped box hedges
photos.credit: Photo: GualdimG · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Arched tile panels of horsemen above a green pool, with busts and a pebble-and-tile wall above
photos.caption: Tiled riders reflected in the garden tank.
photos.credit: Photo: GualdimG · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It began as a hunting pavilion in the countryside, and its family still lives in part of it.
Its garden walls are lined with tile panels of mounted knights that mirror in a long pool, and with scenes of monkeys.
It was built in 1671-72 for a nobleman who earned his title from his loyalty during the Restoration War.

summary.description: Built in 1671-72 as a hunting pavilion for João de Mascarenhas, 1st Marquis of Fronteira, this Lisbon palace is still inhabited. It is famed for its tiles, from battle scenes in the Sala das Batalhas to garden panels of horsemen and monkeys.
keyFeatures: Garden gallery with niches and busts of Portuguese kings
Tiled panels of horsemen reflected in a tank
Sala das Batalhas, about the Restoration War
Chapel façade decorated with stones, shells and porcelain fragments
funFacts: The palace complex has been a National Monument since 1982.
The garden busts show Portuguese kings, except the three Philips.

architects.name: Unknown Portuguese builders
architects.bio: Builders of the Madre de Deus convent, founded by Queen Leonor in 1509.

photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira from Torres Vedras, PORTUGAL · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long whitewashed church and convent front with a square stone bell tower, pinnacles along the roofline and a small Gothic-style doorway.
Black and white view along a row of slender stone columns with carved, perforated arches around a cloister court
photos.credit: Photo: Pedro Ribeiro Simões from Lisboa, Portugal · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Cloister corridor with blue tile dado under a white wall and stone arches beside the court
photos.credit: Photo: Jules Verne Times Two · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A queen founded this convent in 1509, and part of its grounds is now a museum devoted to a single craft.
Its collection of glazed tiles runs from the late 15th century to the present, including a c. 1700 panel showing a vast view of a capital.
Its church has a gilded carved wood choir and Baroque chapel, and its cloister is Mannerist.

summary.description: Queen Leonor founded this Lisbon convent in 1509. Since 1965 it has housed the Museu Nacional do Azulejo, which became a national museum in 1980 and traces tile making from the late 15th century to today.
keyFeatures: Sixteenth-century Mannerist cloister
Church with gilded carved wood choir
Baroque Chapel of Saint Anthony with canvases by André Gonçalves
Tile collection from the late 15th century to the present
funFacts: The permanent show includes a c. 1700 panel, the Great View of Lisbon.
It holds one of the largest ceramics collections in the world, according to its Wikipedia article.

name: Igreja de São Lourenço de Almancil
aliases: Igreja de São Lourenço dos Matos

architects.name: Unknown Portuguese builders
architects.bio: Builders of the late 17th-century church; its interior was tiled in 1730 with panels by Policarpo de Oliveira Bernardes.

photos.alt: Whitewashed church with a clock tower, an outer stair and a blue tile plaque on its curved gable
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira from Torres Vedras, PORTUGAL · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Kolforn · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Straight-on view of a whitewashed church front with stone pilasters, a curved gable, a blue tile plaque and a cross, with two potted palms.
Nave and chancel with walls of blue and white tiles around a gilded carved altarpiece
photos.caption: Tiles cover the walls and the dome.
photos.credit: Photo: Marc Ryckaert (MJJR) · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: From outside it is a modest whitewashed church in a southern coastal region.
Inside, blue and white tile panels cover every wall and even the dome, telling the story of a martyred deacon.
Its tiles are dated 1730 and came by ship from Lisbon, the work of a leading master.

summary.description: A late 17th-century Baroque church near Almancil in the Algarve, classified as a Property of Public Interest since 1946. Its interior walls and dome are covered with azulejos dated 1730 by Policarpo de Oliveira Bernardes, illustrating the life of Saint Lawrence of Huesca.
keyFeatures: Whitewashed Baroque exterior
Azulejos over the whole interior and dome
Scenes from the life of Saint Lawrence
Gilded wooden altarpiece attributed to Manuel Martins
funFacts: The tiles were brought from Lisbon in 1730.
The sacristy contains a finely carved piece of furniture.

architects.name: Unknown Portuguese builders
architects.bio: Anonymous builders of the Douro Line station, which opened in 1880; its tile panels were installed in 1937.

photos.alt: Two-storey whitewashed station building with green doors and small blue tile panels beneath the ground-floor windows, with terraced hills behind
photos.credit: Photo: Sanjorgepinho · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Rafael Jiménez · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Low railway station seen from the tracks, with a long covered platform canopy, a red-tiled upper block and blue tile panels between green doors.

photos.credit: Photo: Cornelius from Berlin, Germany · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Platform under an ironwork-trimmed canopy beside the tracks, with tile panels on the wall and terraced vineyard hills beyond.
Tile panel of rabelo boats loaded with barrels on a river below vine-covered hills
photos.caption: Wine barrels being carried downriver.
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira from Torres Vedras, PORTUGAL · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a small riverside station on a line that was built to follow a valley of terraced vineyards.
Its walls carry 24 painted tile panels with more than 3,000 tiles, showing the grape harvest and boats carrying barrels.
The station opened in 1880 and its tiles were added in 1937, donated by a wine institute.

summary.description: This station on the Douro Line opened on 1 June 1880 and was a major depot for the wine trade. In 1937 it received 24 azulejo panels, made by the Aleluia factory in Aveiro, showing vineyards, grape treading and boats carrying wine barrels.
keyFeatures: Douro Line station opened in 1880
24 tile panels with over 3,000 tiles
Scenes of vines, treading and river transport of wine
Panels painted by João Marques Oliveira and Lourenço Rodrigues Limas
funFacts: The tiles were based on photographs by the Casa Alvão studio.
In 2013 the station won the SOS Azulejo conservation and restoration award.

architects.name: António Rodrigues da Silva Júnior
architects.bio: Architect who directed the 1919 renovation that turned the old palace into a casino with a revivalist interior.

photos.alt: Courtyard with horseshoe arches, slender columns, a small fountain and a red-and-white tiled floor
photos.credit: Photo: Concierge.2C · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Maragato1976 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Two marbled columns with carved capitals flank a stained-glass window and round skylight above a band of geometric tile.

photos.credit: Photo: Maragato1976 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall arched stained-glass windows with colourful geometric patterns beside a gilded column, with a small winged bronze figure in front.
Dining room with diners at tables and walls of blue and white tile panels around tall windows
photos.credit: Photo: Heather Cowper from Bristol, UK · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It began as a late 17th-century palace, and was later a school and a furniture warehouse.
In 1919 it was rebuilt as one of the city's first casinos, with an interior mixing neo-Arabic, neo-Gothic and other revival styles.
Since 1932 it has been the seat of a regional association, and its courtyards and tiled dining rooms are open to visitors.

summary.description: This Lisbon building began as a late 17th-century palace of the Paes de Amaral family. In 1919 it was converted into the Magestic Club casino under architect António Rodrigues da Silva Júnior, with a revivalist interior. The regional association Grémio Alentejano moved in in 1932.
keyFeatures: Three courtyards around a quadrangular plan
Neo-Arabic, neo-Gothic, neo-Renaissance and Art Nouveau elements
Azulejos in the restaurant rooms
Decorative work by Jorge Colaço and other artists
funFacts: It once housed a secondary school and a furniture warehouse.
It is classified as a Monument of Public Interest.

architects.name: Waldir Ramos
architects.bio: Brazilian architect credited as one of the designers of the Maracanã Stadium, built for the 1950 FIFA World Cup.

architects.name: Raphael Galvão
architects.bio: Brazilian architect credited as one of the designers of the Maracanã Stadium, built for the 1950 FIFA World Cup.

architects.name: Miguel Feldman
architects.bio: Brazilian architect credited as one of the designers of the Maracanã Stadium, built for the 1950 FIFA World Cup.

architects.name: Oscar Valdetaro
architects.bio: Brazilian architect credited as one of the designers of the Maracanã Stadium, built for the 1950 FIFA World Cup.

photos.credit: Photo: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a huge oval stadium with a pale membrane roof ring around the green pitch, surrounded by city blocks.
Curving grey concrete stadium with a white membrane roof seen from a street lined with young trees
photos.credit: Photo: Валерий Дед · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Diego Baravelli · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close aerial view of the stadium's tensioned white roof ring around a bare pitch and tiers of blue and yellow seats.

hints.text: It was built in the late 1940s for a World Cup that its host country was sure to win.
Its record crowd is officially close to 200,000 people, and its fans' defeat in the final became a national trauma.
In the 2010s its old concrete roof and two-tier bowl were replaced by a one-tier bowl under a tensioned fabric roof.

summary.description: Opened in 1950 for the FIFA World Cup, this stadium was designed by a team of Brazilian architects and was long the largest in the world. It hosted the 1950 final, in which Uruguay beat Brazil 2-1 in the match known as the Maracanazo. Rebuilt for the 2014 World Cup, it also staged the 2016 Olympic ceremonies.
keyFeatures: Vast bowl originally built with open terraces
Terraces gradually replaced by seats
Concrete roof replaced by a PTFE-coated fiberglass membrane
Grey façade with yellow, blue and white seats
funFacts: Its official record attendance is 173,850, though the 1950 final crowd was officially counted at 199,854.
It hosted the 2014 World Cup final and the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2016 Olympics.
It was designated a national landmark in 1998.

architects.name: Herzog & de Meuron
architects.bio: Swiss architecture firm of Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron.

photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Curving stadium wall clad in white inflated diamond-shaped cushions, seen from a snowy walkway under a clear blue sky.
Close view of a glossy white façade made of hundreds of inflated diamond-shaped cushions
photos.credit: Photo: Martin Falbisoner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Oval stadium glowing red and blue at night, reflected in still water
photos.credit: Photo: Unknown author · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced an older stadium whose two football clubs both moved here in 2005.
Its skin is made of thousands of inflated foil panels that can each be lit in different colours.
Its outer shell, about 0.2 mm thick in foil, was the first of its kind in the world to change colour completely.

summary.description: This football stadium on the northern edge of its city opened in 2005 and was designed by a Swiss practice with Arup as structural engineer. Its façade is made of 2,760 air-filled ETFE foil panels that can glow white, red or blue. It hosted the opening match of the 2006 World Cup and several European finals.
keyFeatures: 2,760 inflated ETFE-foil diamond panels
Façade that can be lit in white, red or blue
Roof with built-in roller blinds
Seating for about 70,000 to 75,000
funFacts: It was described as the first stadium in the world with a fully colour-changing exterior.
It hosted the 2012 and 2025 UEFA Champions League finals.
In 2022 it staged the first regular-season NFL game played in Germany.

architects.name: Francesc Mitjans
architects.bio: Catalan architect who, with Josep Soteras, designed the Camp Nou, which opened in 1957.

architects.name: Josep Soteras
architects.bio: Catalan architect who, with Francesc Mitjans, designed the Camp Nou, which opened in 1957.

architects.name: Lorenzo García-Barbón
architects.bio: Architect who collaborated with Mitjans and Soteras on the design of the Camp Nou.

photos.alt: Curving concrete stadium wall with louvred panels and a crowd gathering on the street below
photos.credit: Photo: Little Savage · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: JoJan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long low stadium front with a glazed blue-tinted facade under a flat projecting roof, seen across an empty paved plaza.
Packed three-tier stands curving around a green football pitch
photos.credit: Photo: Mutari 09:33, 21 September 2007 (UTC) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It opened in 1957 and its name means simply 'new field', because it replaced an older ground.
Its rings of seating are oval and continuous with no open corners, a layout borrowed from a Dutch stadium.
A third tier was added for the 1982 World Cup, and its owner club is now rebuilding it for a capacity above 100,000.

summary.description: Opened in 1957 to replace the club's older ground, it was designed by Francesc Mitjans and Josep Soteras, with Lorenzo García-Barbón collaborating. Its continuous oval rings were inspired by a stadium in Rotterdam. It opened with over 106,000 seats and has since been expanded and, from 2023, deeply redeveloped.
keyFeatures: Oval rings of seating with no open corners
Third tier added for the 1982 World Cup
Pitch lowered by 2.5 m in 1993-94
Large redevelopment started in 2023
funFacts: Its record attendance is 120,000, for a match in 1986.
It hosted the 1982 World Cup opening match and the 1992 Olympic football final.
It has hosted two European Cup or Champions League finals, in 1989 and 1999.

architects.name: Manuel Salgado
architects.bio: Lisbon architect who later led urban planning on Lisbon's city council from 2007 to 2019.

photos.alt: Aerial view of an oval stadium with a pale roof and two steel arches, beside a motorway
photos.credit: Photo: CaGeRaGe · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Wide-angle view of blue seats, a green pitch and a translucent roof held by concrete pillars
photos.credit: Photo: Валерий Дед · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Edgar Jiménez from Porto, Portugal · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Floodlit stadium bowl at night with a steel arch truss over the roof edge, a green pitch and stands full of spectators.

hints.text: It was built to host matches of a European football championship, and replaced an older home ground in the same city.
A frame of around 21,000 square metres of decorative glazed tiles surrounds it.
Its first match, a 2-0 win over a Spanish giant in 2003, featured a 16-year-old Lionel Messi.

summary.description: Opened in 2003 and designed by Manuel Salgado, this football stadium was built for Euro 2004 at a cost of about €125 million. It has four stands and about 50,000 seats, and is framed by some 21,000 square metres of azulejos. It hosted the 2021 UEFA Champions League final.
keyFeatures: Four stands, all-seater
About 21,000 m² of azulejo tiles in its frame
96 executive suites
Own Porto Metro station
funFacts: Its inaugural match, a 2-0 win for the home club over Barcelona, featured a 16-year-old Lionel Messi.
Turf problems forced the club to play its first matches back at its old ground.
It hosted the Euro 2004 opening match and the 2021 Champions League final.

name: Estádio da Luz
aliases: Estádio do Sport Lisboa e Benfica

architects.name: Damon Lavelle
architects.bio: Architect at HOK Sport Venue Event (now Populous) who designed the Estádio da Luz, opened in 2003.

photos.alt: Stadium with big red steel arches over a dark roof, seen under a clear blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Red steel arches rising behind palm trees and a fountain
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira from Torres Vedras, PORTUGAL · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Peter Reed · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of an oval stadium with red steel arches and a roof, surrounded by roads, apartment blocks and a shopping centre.

hints.text: It replaced an older stadium on the very same site, once able to hold 120,000 people.
Its roof seems to float over the stands, hung from four steel arches 43 metres high.
It opened in October 2003 and hosted the final of Euro 2004.

summary.description: Opened on 25 October 2003, it replaced the club's original stadium on the same site. It was designed by Damon Lavelle of HOK Sport (now Populous) for Euro 2004 and cost about €160 million. Four steel arches support a polycarbonate roof that seems to float over the stands.
keyFeatures: Four steel arches 43 m high
Polycarbonate roof that lets light through
Wavy arch profile echoing three tiers of seating
Capacity of about 68,000 after 2025 works
funFacts: It hosted the Euro 2004 final and the Champions League finals of 2014 and 2020.
A 2014 online poll by L'Équipe named it the most beautiful stadium in Europe.
The first stadium on the site opened in 1954.

architects.name: Miguel Jacobetty Rosa
architects.bio: Portuguese architect credited in the design of the Estádio Nacional, inaugurated in 1944.

architects.name: Francisco Caldeira Cabral
architects.bio: Portuguese designer who took part in the original design of the Estádio Nacional.

architects.name: Konrad Wiesner
architects.bio: Named among the authors of the original design of the Estádio Nacional.

photos.alt: Pale stepped stands with a small central tribune seen across an open paved area, with pine woods behind
photos.credit: Photo: Tagido · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Packed event in an open-sided bowl stadium among trees, with a tall floodlight mast
photos.credit: Photo: Vitor Oliveira from Torres Vedras, PORTUGAL · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It sits in a wooded valley just outside a capital, inside a large park of sports grounds.
One side of its oval bowl is left open, unusual for a stadium of this kind.
It hosted the 1967 European Cup final, won by a team that became known as the 'Lisbon Lions'.

summary.description: Inaugurated in 1944 after construction began in 1939, this stadium stands in the Jamor sports park near Lisbon. It was designed by Miguel Jacobetty Rosa with Francisco Caldeira Cabral and Konrad Wiesner. Its oval bowl is open on the east side, and it has hosted the Portuguese Cup final almost every year since 1946.
keyFeatures: Oval bowl open on its east side
Set in a forested sports park
Capacity of about 37,600
Grass pitch of 105 x 68 m
funFacts: It hosted the first UEFA club match ever played, in 1955.
Celtic won the 1967 European Cup final here, earning the nickname 'Lisbon Lions'.
It has hosted concerts by The Police, Black Eyed Peas and Iron Maiden.

architects.name: Lykourgos
architects.bio: Athenian statesman who built the first stadium on the site around 330/329 BC.

architects.name: Herodes Atticus
architects.bio: Athenian Roman senator who rebuilt the stadium in Pentelic marble, completed around 144 AD.

architects.name: Anastasios Metaxas
architects.bio: Architect who prepared the plan for the 1896 reconstruction of the stadium for the first modern Olympic Games.

photos.credit: Photo: George E. Koronaios · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long U-shaped marble stadium with stepped seating and a dark running track around a sandy field, with wooded hills behind.

photos.credit: Photo: George E. Koronaios · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: View down a central stair between steep marble tiers toward a dark track and a sandy field, under a bright blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Badseed · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Curved marble stands around a dark running track with a distant rocky hill and city rooftops on the horizon.
Long pale marble horseshoe of stands set into a wooded hill among dense apartment blocks
photos.credit: Photo: Jebulon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Panorama of a U-shaped marble stadium with rows of flagpoles and a paved track
photos.credit: Photo: Bgabel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A racecourse stood on this site in the 6th century BC, set in a natural ravine between two hills.
It is the only stadium in the world built entirely of marble.
It was rebuilt in the 19th century to host the opening and closing ceremonies of the first modern Olympic Games, in 1896.

summary.description: A statesman built a stadium of poros stone here around 330 BC, and a Roman senator rebuilt it in Pentelic marble in the 2nd century AD. After excavations in 1869-70 it was reconstructed to a plan by Anastasios Metaxas for the first modern Olympics in 1896. It is a U-shaped track set in a ravine and is the only stadium in the world built entirely of marble.
keyFeatures: Entirely of Pentelic marble
U-shaped track set in a natural ravine
Original 4th-century BC stadium of poros stone
Rebuilt for the 1896 Olympic Games
funFacts: Harvard Stadium and Albert Speer's unbuilt Deutsches Stadion were modelled on it.
It was the finish line of the marathon at the 2004 Olympics and is still the finish of the Athens Classic Marathon.
A marble chair from the stadium, the 'Biel Throne', is in the British Museum.

architects.name: Werner March
architects.bio: Architect who designed the 1936 Olympic Stadium in Berlin, with his brother Walter assisting.

photos.alt: Two tall stone towers framing a set of five interlocked rings above a low colonnaded oval stadium
photos.credit: Photo: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Rebecca Leisten www.rebecca-leisten.de · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a huge oval stone stadium with a white roof ring open over the pitch, ringed by lawns, trees and a distant skyline.

photos.credit: Photo: Martijn Mureau · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking up from the seats to a glazed oval roof opening above a blue running track and a green pitch.
Bronze bowl on stone pillars in front of a pitch ringed by a roof with translucent panels
photos.credit: Photo: Jan Künzel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built between 1934 and 1936 as the centrepiece of a sports complex for the Summer Games of a dictatorship.
Its pitch lies about 12 metres below ground, and a bell tower and parade lawn stand at its western end.
It was renovated in 2000-2004, lowering the pitch by 2.65 m and adding a roof with transparent panels.

summary.description: Designed by Werner March and built in 1934-36, this stadium opened the 1936 Summer Olympics, where Jesse Owens won four gold medals. Its lower tier is sunk about 12 m below ground. A 2000-2004 renovation lowered the field and added a roof of about 37,000 m² with transparent panels, keeping the original stonework.
keyFeatures: Lower tier sunk about 12 m into the ground
Stone-clad colonnaded exterior
Marathon Gate and 77 m Bell Tower
2004 roof carried by twenty columns
funFacts: Usain Bolt set his 100 m and 200 m world records here in 2009.
It hosted the 1974 and 2006 World Cups, the latter's final included, and the Euro 2024 final.
It has been home to Hertha BSC since 1963.

architects.name: Günter Behnisch
architects.bio: Architect whose firm Behnisch & Partner won the 1967 competition for the Munich Olympic Park and its stadium.

architects.name: Frei Otto
architects.bio: Engineer of the lightweight tent roof of the Munich Olympic Stadium, a revolutionary construction of acrylic glass on steel cables.

photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Stadium roof of pale cable-hung canopies and tall masts beyond a park lake with pedalos and spring trees.

photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of tent-like transparent canopies spreading over a park, with a stadium bowl at the top and a lake at left.

photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Underside of a large curved roof made of square transparent panels in a dark grid, over a wide paved walkway.
Evening aerial view of a stadium bowl and a landscape of cable-hung canopies in a park
photos.credit: Photo: Martin Falbisoner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Panorama of green seating around a running track, with a translucent cable-hung canopy on the far side
photos.credit: Photo: airbus777 from Washington, DC, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for the Summer Games of 1972 and meant to show a new, open and democratic image of its country.
Its roof is a tent of acrylic glass panels hung from steel cables on tall masts, used at this scale for the first time.
The canopy was meant to echo the silhouette of the Alps.

summary.description: Won in competition in 1967 by Behnisch & Partner, with Frei Otto as engineer of the roof, this stadium opened on 26 May 1972 for the Summer Olympics. Its lightweight tent of acrylic glass panels on steel cables was revolutionary at this scale. It later hosted the 1974 World Cup final.
keyFeatures: Tent roof of acrylic glass on steel cables
Roof meant to evoke the Alps
Bowl set into the landscape of the Olympic Park
Seating for about 63,000
funFacts: It hosted the 1974 World Cup final and the Euro 1988 final.
Bayern Munich and TSV 1860 played here until both moved to the Allianz Arena in 2005.
Its roof once covered almost 45,000 seats, and now covers fewer than 40,000.

name: Estádio do Pacaembu
aliases: Estádio Municipal Paulo Machado de Carvalho

architects.name: Escritório Técnico Ramos de Azevedo
architects.bio: São Paulo architectural office of Ramos de Azevedo, credited with the design of the Pacaembu Stadium.

architects.name: Severo e Villares
architects.bio: São Paulo firm credited, with the Ramos de Azevedo office, with the design of the Pacaembu Stadium.

photos.credit: Photo: Janazamb · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Horseshoe stadium with orange and cream terraces around a striped pitch, with a high-rise skyline and radio towers behind.
Tall cream-coloured floodlight tower with rows of lamps and a slit pattern, against a cloudy sky
photos.credit: Photo: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Guilherme B Alves · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tiered orange and blue terraces under a long shallow roof, with pale floodlight towers rising behind and flagpoles on the grass.
Steep concrete stand of orange and cream seats beside the pitch, below a scoreboard
photos.credit: Photo: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was inaugurated in April 1940 in the presence of the country's president.
It is listed as heritage by its state council, partly for its Art Deco style.
A football museum was opened beneath its stands in 2008.

summary.description: Inaugurated on 27 April 1940 with President Getúlio Vargas present, it was designed by the Ramos de Azevedo office with Severo e Villares. Its Art Deco style helped win it heritage listing by the state council in 1998. It hosted six matches of the 1950 World Cup and reopened in 2025 after a long renovation.
keyFeatures: Art Deco architecture
Heritage listing in 1998
Football museum under the stands
South stand rebuilt in a five-storey building
funFacts: Its attendance record is 71,281, set in 1942.
It hosted six matches of the 1950 FIFA World Cup.
It reopened on 27 January 2025 after a 40-month renovation.

architects.name: Unknown Shona builders
architects.bio: Ancestors of the Shona people, most likely the Karanga, who raised the stone walls of the city from the 11th century onward, working in dry stone without mortar.

photos.alt: Aerial view of a huge curved granite wall enclosing trees, beside scattered stone ruins on a dry hillside
photos.credit: Photo: Janice Bell · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Jens Klinzing · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall curving dry-stone wall with a patterned band along its top rising from long green grass, with trees beyond.

photos.credit: Photo: Andrew Moore from Johannesburg, South Africa · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Solid conical stone tower behind curved dry-stone walls, with a large tree overhead and tumbled stones in the foreground.

photos.credit: Photo: Mike from Vancouver, Canada · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Narrow earth path between high dry-stone walls leading to a curved wall and a small round stone platform among trees.

hints.text: This stone city in southern Africa was a capital and trading centre for several centuries before it was abandoned.
Its walls were laid in dry granite blocks with no mortar, and the largest rises up to about 11 metres.
Early European writers refused to believe Africans built it, and its name, from Shona words for houses of stone, was later given to a whole country.

summary.description: Settled around 1000 AD, this city grew in stone from the 11th century and became the capital of its kingdom from the 13th century. Its granite walls are laid without mortar, and the Great Enclosure has an outer wall up to 11 m high and about 250 m long. It was abandoned in the 16th or 17th century and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
keyFeatures: Dry granite walls with no mortar
Great Enclosure with an outer wall up to 11 m high
Conical tower about 9 m tall
Soapstone Zimbabwe Birds carved for monoliths
Ruins covering about 730 hectares
funFacts: Colonial-era writers credited Phoenicians, Arabs or the Queen of Sheba, and an African origin was accepted by scholars only from the 1950s.
The soapstone bird carvings, probably bateleur eagles, appear on the national flag and coat of arms.

architects.name: Unknown Zagwe builders
architects.bio: Builders working for King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty, who carved the church downward out of volcanic tuff in the late 12th or early 13th century.

photos.credit: Photo: Sailko · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Square red stone church carved down from solid rock, standing in a deep pit with a stepped base and a doorway, a person seated below.
Cross-shaped red-brown stone church seen from above, sunk in a square pit cut into the rock, with stepped plinths and small arched windows
photos.credit: Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Katie Hunt from St Albans, UK · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close oblique view of the rock-cut church's pink walls banded in yellow lichen, with pointed windows and a stepped base.
Narrow trench cut in solid rock beside the stepped base of a carved stone building
photos.credit: Photo: Ji-Elle · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This church was not built up from the ground: it was carved down into a hillside of volcanic rock, and its roof lies level with the surrounding ground.
Its plan and its roof are shaped like a cross, and it stands in a deep square pit reached by a trench.
A king of the Zagwe dynasty who is venerated as a saint said a vision told him to make it, and it is the most famous of eleven rock-hewn churches in his holy town.

summary.description: Carved downward from a single block of volcanic tuff in the late 12th or early 13th century, this cross-shaped church sits in a pit open to the sky. Tradition says King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty had a vision telling him to build it. It belongs to the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, inscribed by UNESCO in 1978.
keyFeatures: Carved from one block of volcanic tuff
Cross-shaped plan and roof
Sunk in a square pit reached by a trench
Stepped plinth and arched windows cut in relief
Part of a UNESCO-listed group of churches
funFacts: The church was cut from the top down, so the roof was finished before the walls.
The trench between two church groups is said to represent the River Jordan.

architects.name: Unknown Teotihuacan builders
architects.bio: The people of Teotihuacan, who raised the pyramid in two phases from about 200 AD and whose own name for it is unknown.

photos.credit: Photo: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Massive stepped stone pyramid with a long central staircase rising above a low stone platform and an open paved plaza under blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Burkhard Mücke · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Large stepped pyramid rising behind terraced platforms with staircases and many visitors, with mountains on the horizon.

photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Steep pyramid face of rough stone rubble sloping down to a grass strip and a plaza under scattered clouds.
Rubble-paved terrace along a steep stone pyramid with a smaller pyramid and green plain far below
photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the largest structure in a vast ancient city of Mesoamerica whose own name for it is lost.
Its main stair faces a long processional avenue that the city's grid follows, and it stands between two other great monuments.
Its name comes from the Aztecs, who found the city already abandoned centuries earlier, and the pyramid is over 200 metres wide at the base.

summary.description: Built in two phases from about 200 AD, this is among the largest pyramids of the pre-Columbian Americas. It rises beside the Avenue of the Dead, and the city's central grid follows its orientation. The name Pyramid of the Sun was given by the Aztecs long after the city was abandoned, and what the Teotihuacanos called it is unknown.
keyFeatures: Two construction phases from about 200 AD
Base roughly 220 to 230 m per side
Beside the Avenue of the Dead
Once plastered and painted with murals, now lost
A cave about 6 m under its centre
funFacts: A pit found in 1971 leads to a cave under the pyramid that may be man-made and may have been a royal tomb.
Sources disagree on its height, giving figures from about 65 m to 75 m.

name: Palacio de Bellas Artes

architects.name: Adamo Boari
architects.bio: Italian architect who drew up the original design in 1904, in Art Nouveau and Neoclassical forms, and began construction.

architects.name: Federico Mariscal
architects.bio: Mexican architect who resumed construction in 1932 and completed the interior in Art Deco style.

style: Art Nouveau and Neoclassical exterior, Art Deco interior

photos.credit: Photo: Xavier Quetzalcoatl Contreras Castillo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Symmetrical white marble palace with a central arched entrance, sculpted pediment and a golden-orange striped dome under a blue sky.
White marble opera house with a large central dome and ornate sculpted facade beside a park
photos.credit: Photo: Jeses · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ludan68 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Circular stained-glass ceiling with a winged figure at the centre inside a ring of ornaments and radiating coloured panes.
Marble hall with tall columns, geometric Art Deco details and balconies on several levels
photos.credit: Photo: José Luiz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This marble opera house and arts centre in a Latin American capital took three decades to finish because a revolution stopped the work.
It has sunk about four metres into soft ground, and its stage curtain is made of nearly a million pieces of glass.
Its outside is Art Nouveau and Neoclassical while its inside is Art Deco, and its halls hold murals by Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros.

summary.description: Begun on 1 October 1904 to a design by Adamo Boari, construction stalled around 1913 during the Mexican Revolution and resumed in 1932. Federico Mariscal finished it, giving the interior an Art Deco character, and it opened on 29 November 1934. It holds a 1,590-seat theatre and murals by leading Mexican painters.
keyFeatures: Exterior in Art Nouveau and Neoclassical styles
Marble from Mexico and Carrara
Art Deco interior
Glass stage curtain made by Tiffany's
Murals by Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros
funFacts: The Tiffany glass curtain weighs about 24 tons.
The building has sunk about four metres into the soft subsoil of the city.

name: Central Library of UNAM
aliases: Central Library of the National Autonomous University of Mexico

architects.name: Juan O'Gorman
architects.bio: Mexican architect and painter who co-led the design of the library from 1948 and created its exterior mural, Historical Representation of Culture.

architects.name: Gustavo Saavedra
architects.bio: Architect who co-designed the Central Library with Juan O'Gorman and Juan Martínez de Velasco.

architects.name: Juan Martínez de Velasco
architects.bio: Architect who co-designed the Central Library with Juan O'Gorman and Gustavo Saavedra.

style: Mexican Modernism with stone mosaic mural

photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Windowless tower covered in a colourful stone mosaic mural above a low glazed pavilion and a carved stone relief wall, under blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Dead.rabbit · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Corner view of a tall mosaic-covered block with circular motifs, rising above a low glazed base shaded by trees.

photos.credit: Photo: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Dark carved stone relief of a stylised face with water pouring into a turquoise pool beneath the building's base.

photos.credit: Photo: Noahedits · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Full wall of a stone-mosaic mural packed with figures, suns, buildings and scrolls in teal, white, red and brown.
Reading room with a large abstract mural above book shelves and a window of translucent stone panels
photos.credit: Photo: Laboratorio Restauración · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This university library is a tall windowless block, because its upper floors are made to hold books rather than readers.
Its four walls are covered by a huge mural made of natural stone tiles in twelve colours, not paint.
The mural tells the history of a nation from pre-Hispanic times to the modern university, and the campus around it is a World Heritage Site.

summary.description: Designed from 1948 by Juan O'Gorman, Gustavo Saavedra and Juan Martínez de Velasco, the library opened in 1956. The ten upper floors are windowless storage covered by O'Gorman's mural, Historical Representation of Culture. The mural uses natural stone tiles in 12 colours from across Mexico, and the library is part of the UNESCO-listed Central Campus of University City.
keyFeatures: Ten windowless book-storage floors
Mural of natural stone tiles in 12 colours
Four walls: pre-Hispanic, colonial, contemporary and university Mexico
Raised platform with basalt fountains
Reading-room light filtered through thin tecali stone
funFacts: Each of the ten storage floors holds about 120,000 volumes.
The library and the Central Campus were inscribed by UNESCO in July 2007.

architects.name: Augusto Pérez Palacios
architects.bio: Mexican architect who designed the university stadium together with Raúl Salinas and Jorge Bravo.

architects.name: Raúl Salinas
architects.bio: Mexican architect who co-designed the university stadium with Augusto Pérez Palacios and Jorge Bravo.

architects.name: Jorge Bravo
architects.bio: Mexican architect who co-designed the university stadium with Augusto Pérez Palacios and Raúl Salinas.

photos.alt: Curving concrete stands around a running track and green pitch, with floodlight towers and wooded hills behind
photos.credit: Photo: Nortonvonwerl · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stadium entrance front clad in dark stone with a large colourful relief mural of figures and an eagle
photos.credit: Photo: Elisa.rolle · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a university stadium whose stands are asymmetric, with one side built far higher and more developed than the other.
It opened in 1952 and was enlarged to about 80,000 seats for a Summer Olympics in the late 1960s.
A relief mural in natural stone on one side shows a family and athletes lighting the torch, and it is where two sprinters raised fists on a medal podium in 1968.

summary.description: Opened on 20 November 1952, the stadium was designed by Augusto Pérez Palacios, Raúl Salinas and Jorge Bravo. For the 1968 Summer Olympics its capacity was raised from 70,000 to 83,700 without substantially changing the original structure. Its stands are asymmetric, with the west side more developed.
keyFeatures: Asymmetric stands, the west side more developed
Opened 20 November 1952
Stone relief mural on the east side
Capacity raised to 83,700 for 1968
Stands complete the axis of University City
funFacts: The stadium hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of the 1968 Olympics.
Tommie Smith and John Carlos gave their Black power salute here during the 200-metre medal ceremony.

architects.name: Tadao Ando
architects.bio: Self-taught Japanese architect and former boxer, winner of the Pritzker Prize in 1995. Ando is known for poured-in-place concrete, with a smooth finish, that frames light, water and nature in quiet, geometric spaces, from the Church of the Light to the museums of Naoshima.

photos.alt: Plain grey concrete wall with a cross-shaped glazed slit, partly hidden by hedges and a conifer
photos.credit: Photo: Bergmann · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Bare concrete chapel with dark wooden pews and a cross of daylight cut through the wall behind the altar
photos.credit: Photo: The original uploader was Bujatt at English Wikipedia. · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Chun-Hung Eric Cheng · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Black-and-white view into a corner of a bare concrete room where narrow slits of daylight form a cross along two walls.

hints.text: This small church in a residential neighbourhood is built almost entirely of bare, smooth concrete.
A wall set at 15 degrees to the box cuts through its plan, separating the chapel from the entrance.
Its only ornament is a cross cut through the wall behind the altar, so the cross is made of daylight, and a roof was nearly left out for lack of money.

summary.description: Completed in 1989 in a residential district of Ibaraki, Osaka Prefecture, this small chapel is a concrete box of about 113 square metres. A wall angled at 15 degrees cuts through three cubes to separate the chapel from the entrance. The cross is cut into the concrete behind the altar and lit by daylight.
keyFeatures: Bare cast concrete throughout
Wall angled at 15 degrees
Cross cut through the altar wall and lit by daylight
About 113 m² of floor area
Sunday School wing added in 1999
funFacts: Because of funding delays, the architect considered building it without a roof, but a construction firm donated the roof.
A Sunday School extension was added in 1999.

architects.name: Snøhetta
architects.bio: Norwegian architecture firm that won the competition for the opera house from 350 entries.

photos.credit: Photo: kallerna · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: White angular building with a sloping stone roof, a tilted glass front and people walking on the paved apron beside the water.
White angled building with glass walls glowing at dusk, its sloping roof reaching down to the water
photos.credit: Photo: Pierre Blaché · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Guy Delsaut · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Broad white stone slope rising from a paved plaza beside a glass wall, with the harbour and older buildings behind.
Tall foyer with slanting white columns, a glass wall, stone floor and a curved timber-clad wall
photos.credit: Photo: Palickap · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This national opera house sits at the edge of a fjord, and its roof slopes down so visitors can walk up it from the water.
Its outside is clad in white Italian marble and white granite, with angled surfaces that seem to rise out of the sea.
It opened in April 2008, finished under budget, and a glass-and-steel sculpture floats in the water beside it.

summary.description: Chosen from 350 entries in a competition, this opera house opened on 12 April 2008 in Bjørvika at the head of the Oslofjord. Its angled marble and granite surfaces make it seem to rise from the water, and its roof slopes down to ground level as a public plaza. The main auditorium seats 1,364.
keyFeatures: Roof slopes to ground level as a public plaza
Carrara marble and white granite cladding
About 49,000 m² across roughly 1,100 rooms
Main auditorium with 1,364 seats
Sculpture She Lies floating in the fjord
funFacts: It was finished about 300 million NOK under its budget of about 4.4 billion NOK.
It won the World Architecture Festival culture award in 2008 and the 2009 European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture.

name: Harpa
aliases: Harpa Reykjavik Concert Hall and Conference Centre

architects.name: Henning Larsen Architects
architects.bio: Danish architecture firm that designed the concert hall together with the artist Ólafur Eliasson.

architects.name: Ólafur Eliasson
architects.bio: Danish-Icelandic artist who designed the building's glass facade in collaboration with Henning Larsen Architects.

photos.credit: Photo: Holger Uwe Schmitt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Large angular building clad in green and blue glass honeycomb panels, with two people walking on the paved quay in front.
Dark faceted glass building beside a harbour, seen across a snow-covered slope at dusk
photos.credit: Photo: Tristan Ferne from UK · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Two folk musicians in traditional dress playing violins in front of a wall of geometric glass panels
photos.credit: Photo: James Poulson · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This concert hall and conference centre stands on a harbour in a northern capital and was meant to give the city a landmark.
Its steel frame is clad in coloured, geometric glass panels inspired by the basalt landscape of its country.
Work began in 2007 and halted during a national financial crisis, until the government chose in 2008 to fund the rest, and it opened in 2011.

summary.description: Designed by Henning Larsen Architects with the artist Ólafur Eliasson, who made the facade, this concert hall has a steel frame clad in coloured geometric glass panels inspired by Iceland's basalt landscape. Construction began in 2007 and was halted during the 2008 to 2011 financial crisis before the government chose to fund the rest. It opened in 2011 at a cost of about 164 million euros.
keyFeatures: Steel frame with geometric coloured glass panels
Facade by Ólafur Eliasson
Inspired by Icelandic basalt landscape
Main hall Eldborg
Mies van der Rohe Award 2013
funFacts: It won the EU's Mies van der Rohe award for contemporary architecture in 2013.
The government decided in 2008 to pay for the remaining construction after the banking crisis.

architects.name: I. M. Pei
architects.bio: Architect of the glass pyramid added to the Cour Napoléon in 1989 as the main entrance to the museum.

photos.alt: Glass pyramid glowing at dusk in a vast courtyard framed by two wings of an ornate stone palace
photos.credit: Photo: Benh LIEU SONG (Flickr) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Darafsh · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Glass pyramid in a sunlit courtyard seen from a high corner, with small pyramids, a long stone palace wing and a blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: KimonBerlin · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Glass pyramid with fountains and reflecting pools in front of a grand stone palace with a domed pavilion, seen from above.
View upward through the steel-and-glass lattice of a pyramid, with the sun and a stone building reflected
photos.credit: Photo: Erik Drost · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This glass pyramid is the entrance to a former royal palace that is now one of the world's largest museums.
It is about 21.6 metres tall, with a square base about 34 metres wide, and critics at first called it an Egyptian death symbol.
It was completed in 1989 as part of a presidential project, and a popular myth says it has 666 panes, though the real count is 603 rhombi and 70 triangles.

summary.description: Selected in 1983 for the Grand Louvre project announced by President Mitterrand in 1981, this glass pyramid was completed in 1989. It is about 21.6 m tall on a square base about 34 m wide, and its sides meet the base at 51.52 degrees. Many critics objected to a modernist form beside Renaissance architecture.
keyFeatures: About 21.6 m tall, base about 34 m
603 rhombus and 70 triangular glass segments
Sides rise at 51.52 degrees
Entrance to a historic palace-museum
Inverted pyramid skylight in the Carrousel du Louvre
funFacts: A rumour says it has 666 panes, but the museum counts 673 segments.
Critics nicknamed it Pharaoh François' Pyramid.

architects.name: Guðjón Samúelsson
architects.bio: Icelandic state architect whose design for the church was commissioned in 1937; he drew on Iceland's columnar basalt formations.

photos.alt: Tall pale concrete church with a stepped, ribbed front rising to a slender tower, with a statue of an explorer beside it
photos.credit: Photo: Andreas Tille · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ziko van Dijk · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Rounded concrete apse topped by an egg-shaped dome, with tall narrow arched windows and stepped, ribbed walls under a blue sky.
Long pale nave with slender pointed arches, tall narrow windows, wooden pews and a large organ at the far end
photos.credit: Photo: GRANDE PUFFO VCO · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This is the largest church in its country, and its tower is among the tallest structures there.
Its stepped, ribbed front is meant to recall the columnar basalt formations, mountains and glaciers of the landscape.
Work lasted from 1945 to 1986, and it is named after a 17th-century poet and cleric who wrote the Passion Hymns.

summary.description: Commissioned in 1937 and built between 1945 and 1986, this is the largest church in Iceland, at 74.5 m tall. Its design resembles Iceland's trap rocks, mountains and glaciers, especially columnar basalt. It is named after the poet and cleric Hallgrímur Pétursson, author of the Passion Hymns.
keyFeatures: Tower 74.5 m high
Stepped front recalling basalt columns
Crypt consecrated in 1948
Klais organ with 5,275 pipes
Consecrated on 26 October 1986
funFacts: The statue of Leif Erikson in front, by Alexander Stirling Calder, was a US gift in 1930 and predates the church.
Its organ has 102 ranks and 72 stops.

name: Santiago de Compostela Cathedral

architects.name: Master Mateo
architects.bio: Master sculptor and builder who, with his workshop, made the Romanesque Pórtico da Gloria for King Ferdinand II of León.

architects.name: Fernando de Casas Novoa
architects.bio: Architect who designed the Baroque Obradoiro façade, completed about 1740.

style: Romanesque with Gothic and Baroque additions

photos.alt: Twin bell towers and an elaborately carved granite Baroque facade rising above red-tiled roofs
photos.credit: Photo: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez (Lmbuga) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Fernando Pascullo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Twin carved stone towers and a lower dome rising above a cluster of tiled rooftops in warm evening light.

photos.credit: Photo: Fernando Pascullo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Side facade of pale granite with classical pilasters, sculpted niches and arched doorways on a paved square under a stormy sky.
Dark Romanesque nave with round arches, a gallery above and a lantern dome at the crossing
photos.credit: Photo: D.Rovchak · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Fernando Pascullo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Ornate gilded high altar with carved figures and a hanging lamp, framed by stone arches and a raised wooden platform.

hints.text: This cathedral marks the traditional end of a great medieval pilgrimage route that crosses a whole region of Europe.
It is the reputed burial place of an apostle, and a huge silver incense burner, about 80 kg, is swung through its transept on ropes.
Begun in 1075 and consecrated in 1211, its Romanesque body hides a Gloria portico and is fronted by a Baroque facade from the 18th century.

summary.description: Begun in 1075 and consecrated in 1211, this cathedral is mainly Romanesque, with Gothic and Baroque additions. It is the traditional end of the Way of St James and the reputed burial place of the apostle. Its Baroque Obradoiro facade was designed by Fernando de Casas Novoa, and the Romanesque Pórtico da Gloria is by Master Mateo.
keyFeatures: Romanesque plan begun in 1075
Baroque Obradoiro facade, about 1740
Pórtico da Gloria by Master Mateo
Botafumeiro incense burner of 1851
Reputed tomb of Saint James
funFacts: The botafumeiro is described as the largest censer in the world, about 1.6 m tall and about 80 kg.
Building was halted several times over the 12th century and early 13th.

architects.name: Unknown master masons
architects.bio: The architects of the 1194–1220 rebuilding are unknown; Jean Texier later added the Flamboyant north spire in 1507–1513.

photos.alt: Long red sandstone church with a green copper roof, a domed crossing and four slender towers with pointed caps
photos.credit: Photo: Sole Creator and Copyright Holder: Alfred Hutter aka Gentry · Attribution · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Odineva · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Broad red and cream sandstone front with arched galleries, a round window and two towers glowing in low golden sunlight.

photos.credit: Photo: Carsten Steger · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a long stone church with green copper roofs, four towers and a central dome beside a paved square and trees.
Tall nave of banded pink and cream stone with groin vaults, round arches and a ring-shaped hanging lamp
photos.credit: Photo: DerHexer, Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This church was founded by an emperor in the 11th century and became the burial place of many of the medieval emperors and kings of his empire.
Its nave was raised and given groin vaults around 1090, an early bold use of the technique on this scale, and its crypt is Europe's largest Romanesque columned hall.
It is listed by UNESCO and is described as the largest surviving Romanesque church, with a west front that was rebuilt in the 1850s after a fire in 1689.

summary.description: Emperor Conrad II ordered this church in 1025 and construction began in 1030. Around 1090 Henry IV enlarged it, raising the nave and adding groin vaults, and the expanded church was finished in 1106. It is described as the largest surviving Romanesque church and was added to the UNESCO list in 1981.
keyFeatures: Square groin-vaulted nave bays
Nave about 33 m high
Crypt of about 850 m², consecrated 1041
Burials of Salian, Staufer and Habsburg rulers
Neo-Romanesque west front of 1854 to 1858
funFacts: French troops set it on fire in 1689, and the western nave collapsed.
The last ruler buried here was Albert I in 1308.

architects.name: Heinrich Parler
architects.bio: Member of the Parler family of master builders, credited with the original design of the minster, begun in 1377.

architects.name: Matthäus Böblinger
architects.bio: Late Gothic master builder who worked on the minster's tower in the late 15th century.

photos.credit: Photo: Unknown photographer (Neue Photographische Gesellschaft) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Old black-and-white photograph of a huge Gothic church with one very tall openwork spire rising above a square and town houses.
Slender openwork Gothic spire under scaffolding rising behind a medieval tower, half-timbered houses and a glass pyramid
photos.credit: Photo: Flocci Nivis · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Uoaei1 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Gilded carved altarpiece with an open triptych of painted wings beneath three stained-glass windows in a stone chancel.
Tall Gothic nave with a large organ above the entrance arch, wooden pews and a checkered stone floor
photos.credit: Photo: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Although it is called a minster it has never been a bishop's seat, and the citizens of the town paid for it themselves.
Work began in 1377, stopped for centuries from 1543, and was finally completed on 31 May 1890.
Its single steeple, about 161.5 metres high, was the tallest of any church in the world until 2025, and a staircase of 768 steps climbs it.

summary.description: This Gothic Lutheran church was begun in 1377 and completed on 31 May 1890, after a long hiatus starting in 1543. Its steeple is 161.53 m high, and it was the world's tallest church from 1890 until Barcelona's Sagrada Família surpassed it in October 2025. The town's citizens financed it themselves.
keyFeatures: Steeple 161.53 m high
Gothic design begun by Heinrich Parler
Mostly brick with stone towers and ornament
768 steps up the spire
Never a cathedral despite its size
funFacts: Construction paused for centuries after 1543.
It was financed by Ulm's own citizens.

architects.name: Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff
architects.bio: Prussian architect who designed Sanssouci for Frederick the Great; he was dismissed in 1746 and Jan Bouman finished the project.

photos.credit: Photo: Steffen Heilfort · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Low yellow palace with tall arched windows between sculpted figures and a green dome, seen at an angle across an open gravel terrace.
Aerial view of a low yellow palace with a green dome above six broad garden terraces, a round pond and formal lawns
photos.credit: Photo: Carsten Steger · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Yuropoulos · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long flight of vine terraces rising from a still reflecting pool to a small palace at the top of the hill in autumn light.
Rococo room with a green-and-pink ceiling covered in gilded ornament, a tall curtained window and marble busts
photos.credit: Photo: w:fa:User:سندباد · GFDL · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a one-storey summer retreat for a king who wanted to escape court ceremony, with about ten main rooms.
It stands on a terraced vineyard, and its name is French for 'without worries'.
Built from 1745 to 1747, it hosted a famous French philosopher between 1750 and 1753, and its king was reburied here in 1991 in a crypt he had wished for.

summary.description: Built in 1745 to 1747 near Berlin for Frederick the Great, this small summer palace is the finest example of Frederician Rococo. It has a single storey of about ten principal rooms on a terraced vineyard. Its name is French for 'without worries'.
keyFeatures: Single storey with about ten main rooms
Terraced vineyard setting
Rococo interiors
Voltaire Room
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990
funFacts: Voltaire stayed in Potsdam from 1750 to 1753 and often used the Voltaire Room.
Frederick's remains were reinterred in a crypt on the vineyard terrace in 1991, as he had wished.

architects.name: Jean-Baptiste Le Blond
architects.bio: French architect who designed the initial palace and gardens for Peter the Great.

architects.name: Bartolomeo Francesco Rastrelli
architects.bio: Court architect of the Russian empresses Anna and Elizabeth, and the master of the Russian Baroque, who designed the present Winter Palace in the 1750s and its great staircase.

photos.credit: Photo: Florstein (Telegram:WikiPhoto.Space) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long yellow and white palace with a gilded cupola above a stepped cascade of golden statues and fountains under a blue sky.
Long yellow and white palace with a gilded cupola above a cascade of fountains and a straight canal lined with trees
photos.credit: Photo: Perituss · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Godot13 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a long palace at the head of a canal, with symmetrical formal gardens and dense woods around it.

photos.credit: Photo: Florstein (Telegram:WikiPhoto.Space) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Cluster of gilded onion domes and crosses on a yellow and white palace wing against a bright blue sky with clouds.

hints.text: A tsar ordered this seaside complex partly as a rival to a French royal palace, earning it a nickname that compares it to that palace.
Its fountains run on natural springs and gravity, with no pumps, and one jet shoots about 20 metres into the air.
German forces occupied it from 1941 to 1944 and largely destroyed it, and the golden statue of a lion-tearing hero was looted and later replaced by a replica in 1947.

summary.description: Peter the Great commissioned this complex on the Gulf of Finland partly as a response to Louis XIV's Versailles, and work began in 1714. Jean-Baptiste Le Blond designed the initial palace and gardens, and Francesco Bartolomeo Rastrelli expanded it from 1747 to 1756. The Grand Cascade has 64 fountains, and the site was largely destroyed in the Second World War and is still being restored.
keyFeatures: Grand Cascade with 64 fountains
Samson Fountain with a 20 m jet
Fountains run without pumps
Expanded by Rastrelli, 1747 to 1756
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990
funFacts: It is nicknamed the Russian Versailles.
The Samson Fountain was looted in the war and a replica was installed in 1947.

architects.name: Eliel Saarinen
architects.bio: Finnish architect whose competition entry for the Helsinki railway station, substantially redesigned, became the building completed in 1919.

photos.credit: Photo: Aaaatu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Heavy granite station front with a huge rounded arch, stone figures holding globe lamps and a green-roofed clock tower, seen across a street.
Heavy granite station building with a tall green-roofed clock tower and a great arched entrance seen from above
photos.credit: Photo: Anne Pietarinen · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: kallerna · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Passengers walking along a platform between red-and-white double-deck trains under a dark iron-framed train shed with hanging lamps.

hints.text: Its stone walls rise from thousands of wooden piles driven into what was once a shallow bay.
Two pairs of giant stone figures flank its main entrance, each holding a spherical lamp.
The present building was inaugurated in March 1919 after about twelve years of construction, and is clad mostly in local granite.

summary.description: This terminus was designed after an architectural competition and heavily reworked by its architect, moving from fairy-tale National Romanticism toward a more rational, monumental form. Its main facade is clad in red granite, with a big arched entrance, a clock tower and lamp-bearing statues. Inside, reinforced-concrete vaults cover the halls.
keyFeatures: Finnish granite cladding, red granite on the main facade
Giant arched main entrance
Clock tower
Lamp-holding statues by Emil Wikström
Hennebique reinforced-concrete vaults
funFacts: It stands on about 10,000 wooden piles driven into the former Kluuvi bay.
The BBC counted it among the world's most beautiful railway stations.

architects.name: Santiago Calatrava
architects.bio: Architect, structural engineer, sculptor and painter known for bridges with leaning pylons and stations, stadiums and museums whose forms resemble living organisms.

photos.credit: Photo: Bert Kaufmann from Roermond, Netherlands · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Giant white arched steel-and-glass vault seen head-on, spanning a station entrance behind lawns and a wide paved approach under blue sky.
Sweeping white steel-and-glass canopy curving over a wide paved forecourt beside a row of tapering concrete piers
photos.credit: Photo: Ralf Roletschek · GFDL 1.2 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Japplemedia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Side of a white ribbed station canopy with escalators, steel railings and a curved wing sweeping toward a grassy park under a cloudy sky.
View between huge white concrete ribs down onto train platforms under a vaulted glass roof
photos.credit: Photo: Trougnouf · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced a 1958 building that was demolished in 2009 to make way for a far more dramatic structure.
Its glass-and-steel vault is about 160 metres long and 32 metres high, and shelters five platforms with nine tracks.
The white concrete, steel and glass station opened in September 2009 at a cost of about 312 million euros.

summary.description: This station opened in 2009 on the site of a 1958 building. A great white steel, glass and concrete arch about 160 m long and 32 m high shelters the platforms like a wave. It is among the best-known works of its Spanish architect.
keyFeatures: Monumental arch 160 m long and 32 m high
Steel, glass and white concrete
Nine tracks and five platforms
Replaced a 1958 International-style station
funFacts: The building cost 312 million euros.
The original station on the site opened on 1 May 1842.

architects.name: Louis Delacenserie
architects.bio: Belgian architect who designed the station building of Antwerpen-Centraal, built between 1895 and 1905.

architects.name: Clément Van Bogaert
architects.bio: Engineer who designed the iron-and-glass train hall of Antwerpen-Centraal.

photos.credit: Photo: DRG-fan · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Ornate grey and pink stone station front with a glass centre, a round clock, blue-slate domes and arched entrances along the street.
Great arched end of an iron-and-glass train shed painted burgundy, rising above a stone viaduct
photos.credit: Photo: Wikihydro · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: T meltzer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Vast stone hall with a polished patterned marble floor, golden coffered vaults, a large arched window and a grand double staircase.

photos.credit: Photo: T meltzer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking straight up into a stone hall at a square coffered dome ringed by four arches, gilded vaults and tall arched windows.
Escalators climbing through a modern brick-lined void toward a grand stone hall under a ribbed glass roof
photos.credit: Photo: Michielverbeek · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its nickname compares it to a house of worship, because of its huge dome.
The iron-and-glass train hall is about 44 metres high, tall enough to let locomotive steam escape.
Built between 1895 and 1905, it was turned from a terminus into a four-level through station when a rail tunnel opened in 2007.

summary.description: This station was built between 1895 and 1905, with a lavish stone building in front and a huge iron-and-glass shed behind. Its eclectic style and domed hall earned it the nickname 'railway cathedral'. A tunnel opened in 2007 turned it into a four-level station, with new platforms deep below the old ones.
keyFeatures: Domed stone waiting hall
Iron-and-glass train hall 185 m long and about 44 m high
Four platform levels, down to 18 m below ground
Eclectic, hard-to-classify style
funFacts: World War II V-2 hits left visible waves in the roof.
It won a Grand Prix at the 2011 Europa Nostra Awards.

name: Milano Centrale

architects.name: Ulisse Stacchini
architects.bio: Italian architect who won the 1912 competition for the new Milan central station with a project titled 'In Motu Vita'.

style: Eclectic 'Assyrian-Lombard' with Liberty and Art Deco touches

photos.credit: Photo: Ludvig14 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Monumental pale stone station front with a tall central block, columned portals, sculpted horse groups and flags across a wide paved square.

photos.credit: Photo: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long stone concourse with a wide staircase, hanging lamps, travellers and a row of glass-roofed arches receding into the distance.
Passengers and trains under a huge curved steel and glass roof above a polished marble concourse
photos.credit: Photo: Benjamin Smith · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced a smaller station from 1864 that left no trace, after a design competition won in 1912.
Its facade is about 200 metres wide and the steel platform vault, about 72 metres high, was a record when built.
Work began with a cornerstone in 1906 but resumed only in 1925, and it was officially opened on 1 July 1931.

summary.description: This station was chosen through a competition won in 1912, then slowed by war and economic problems and finished under Mussolini's government. It mixes many styles, called 'Assyrian-Lombard', with abundant sculpture. Its 24 platforms sit under huge steel canopies.
keyFeatures: Facade about 200 m wide
Vault about 72 m high
24 platforms under steel canopies about 341 m long
Abundant sculpture on a monumental stone portico
funFacts: The cornerstone was laid in 1906 by King Victor Emmanuel III.
The station was electrified in 1938.

name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus

architects.name: Frederick William Stevens
architects.bio: British architect who built the Victoria Terminus in Bombay, working from an initial design by Axel Haig.

architects.name: Axel Haig
architects.bio: Swedish-born draughtsman and architect whose initial design for the Victoria Terminus was built by F. W. Stevens.

style: Victorian Gothic Revival with Indo-Saracenic elements

photos.alt: Long ornate sandstone building with a central ribbed dome crowned by a statue, corner turrets and pointed arches
photos.credit: Photo: Joe Ravi · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Central clock gable and ribbed dome topped by a statue of a standing figure holding a torch, with carved arches and palm trees below
photos.credit: Photo: Joe Ravi · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Nishnai 1101 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Gothic station front lit in green, pink and orange at night, with a ribbed central dome, a round clock and a statue on top.

hints.text: It replaced a much smaller station of 1853 and was named after a ruling queen before being renamed twice.
A central dome carries a statue symbolising Progress, and carved figures of a lion and a tiger guard its gates.
Construction began in 1878 and it opened to the public in 1888; UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 2004.

summary.description: This station was designed in the British colonial era and built from 1878, blending Victorian Gothic Revival with Indian palace and Indo-Saracenic motifs. A ribbed central dome topped by a statue of Progress rises over a long polychrome stone front with turrets and pointed arches. It is still a working terminus with 18 platforms and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
keyFeatures: Central dome with a statue of Progress
Four corner turrets
Victorian Gothic with Indo-Saracenic influences
Stone lion and tiger at the gates
18 platforms
funFacts: It was renamed in 1996 and again in 2017.
The statue of Queen Victoria that once stood here went missing after the 1950s and has never been found.

architects.name: Meinhard von Gerkan
architects.bio: Architect of Gerkan, Marg and Partners, whose firm won the 1993 design competition for the new Berlin central station.

photos.alt: Glass office blocks and a long curved glass roof over an elevated rail viaduct, reflected in a river
photos.credit: Photo: Ansgar Koreng · CC BY 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ondřej Žváček · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Two tall glass office blocks bridged by a glass arch beside a curved glass train hall, seen across a river embankment.
Wide panorama of glass towers and arched glass train halls beside a river and a road bridge
photos.credit: Photo: Norbert Nagel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on the site of a terminus that opened in 1871 and was demolished in 1957-58.
Eight underground tracks cross at right angles with six elevated tracks, under a curved glass roof about 321 metres long.
It was ceremonially opened on 26 May 2006, and its glass roofs were shortened by about 100 metres to speed construction.

summary.description: This station replaced the old Lehrter Bahnhof and opened in 2006 after a design competition won in 1993. It is a crossing of two lines on two levels, with elevated east-west tracks under a curved glass roof and underground north-south tracks. Its glass-and-steel hall is flanked by two office bridges.
keyFeatures: Elevated hall 321 m long under a curved glass roof
Eight underground mainline tracks
Crossing on two levels, with a U-Bahn station below
About 2,700 m² of photovoltaic panels
funFacts: The glass roofs were shortened by roughly 100 m to speed up construction.
In January 2007 Cyclone Kyrill knocked steel beams from the southwest facade.

architects.name: Alberto de Palacio
architects.bio: Spanish architect who, working with Gustave Eiffel, designed the iron-and-glass station rebuilt in 1892 after a fire.

photos.credit: Photo: Gryffindor · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long red brick and stone station with an ornate cornice, arched doors and a huge curved iron-and-glass gable under a bright blue sky.
Huge arched iron-and-glass gable above a red brick and stone building, with a clock at its base and a griffin on top
photos.credit: Photo: Marc Ryckaert (MJJR) · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Dense tropical garden of palms and bamboo growing inside a big iron-roofed hall, with travellers resting at the edge
photos.credit: Photo: Felipe Gabaldón · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It began in 1851 as its city's first railway station and was rebuilt in 1892 after a fire.
Its old iron-and-glass hall now shelters a tropical garden of about 4,000 square metres.
A modern architect remodelled it from 1985, and a memorial to the victims of a March 2004 attack stands here.

summary.description: This station opened in 1851 as Madrid's first, was largely destroyed by fire, and was rebuilt to reopen in 1892 as an iron-and-glass hall. Since a remodel completed in 1992 the old building has served as a concourse with a tropical garden, while a new terminal handles trains. It is also the site of a memorial to the 11 March 2004 train bombings.
keyFeatures: Iron-and-glass hall of 1892
Brick and stone front with a central clock
Tropical garden of about 4,000 m²
1985-1992 remodel by Rafael Moneo
funFacts: It opened on 9 February 1851 as the Estación de Mediodía.
A memorial to the victims of the 2004 bombings was dedicated on 10 June 2004.

architects.name: Marius Toudoire
architects.bio: Architect from Toulon who designed the thirteen-track Gare de Lyon building for the 1900 World's Fair.

photos.credit: Photo: Marie Thérèse Hébert & Jean Robert Thibault · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long cream stone station front with a dark mansard roof, arched ground-floor openings and a tall clock tower under a pale blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Mbzt · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of a richly carved station wing with sculpted groups on a steep slate roof, arched windows and a blue-faced clock tower.
Pale stone clock tower with a huge ornate blue clock face, carved lions and a grey domed top
photos.credit: Photo: Chabe01 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Wide station concourse under a glass-and-iron roof with timber panels, a clock and departure boards
photos.credit: Photo: Florian Pépellin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its first building opened in 1849, and a fire during the Paris Commune of 1871 partly destroyed it.
The present building was designed for a world's fair held in its city in 1900.
It was inaugurated in April 1901 by the French president, and a lavishly decorated restaurant here has served meals since that year.

summary.description: This terminus was rebuilt by a Toulon architect as a thirteen-track station for the 1900 World's Fair and inaugurated in April 1901 by President Émile Loubet. A large clock tower marks one corner. Inside the building is a famous ornate restaurant that has served meals since 1901.
keyFeatures: Large clock tower on one corner
Thirteen-track building designed for the 1900 World's Fair
Iron-and-glass concourse roof
Ornate Le Train Bleu restaurant
funFacts: The first station here opened on 12 August 1849.
The restaurant's wall paintings include work by Albert Maignan.

architects.name: Michel Pinseau
architects.bio: French architect who had lived in Morocco and designed the Hassan II Mosque; the Bouygues company built it.

photos.credit: Photo: Tinuzzo · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Very tall square minaret with carved and tiled panels beside a long hall with green roofs and rows of horseshoe arches, under misty clouds.
Very tall square minaret with green tilework and carved panels, seen through a horseshoe-shaped arch at dusk
photos.credit: Photo: OussamaHamama · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Signaling dogs · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Prayer hall with stout columns topped by intricately carved capitals and tall carved arches leading to a dim gallery.

hints.text: This huge modern mosque stands on a promontory, partly over the sea, so that worshippers can pray above the water.
Its minaret is among the tallest in the world and carries a laser beam aimed towards Mecca, while the prayer hall has a retractable roof.
It was inaugurated in 1993 and paid for largely by public subscription, but salt water began corroding its structure within about ten years.

summary.description: A vast mosque on the Atlantic shore, started in 1986 and inaugurated in 1993, designed by Michel Pinseau and built by the Bouygues company. Its 210 m minaret is the world's second-tallest, and the hall holds up to 25,000 worshippers with room for 80,000 more on the grounds.
keyFeatures: 210 m minaret topped by a laser aimed at Mecca
Retractable roof of about 1,100 tons
Platform partly over the Atlantic
Cedar, marble and granite with zellij tilework
Museum, madrasa, hammams and 41 fountains
funFacts: About 6,000 artisans worked for roughly five years on the decoration.
Corrosion from salt water was found about ten years after opening; repairs began in 2005 at about 50 million euros.
