architects.name: Ismaila Traoré
architects.bio: Head of the masons' guild of Djenné and the architect of the mosque rebuilt in 1907.

photos.credit: Photo: Ruud Zwart · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Huge earthen building with three tall tapering towers topped by pinnacles and rows of protruding wooden beams along its walls.
Huge sand-coloured earthen building with tall buttress towers bristling with wooden stakes, seen across an open square
photos.credit: Photo: Andy Gilham · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Row of earthen pinnacles, each topped by an ostrich egg, with protruding wooden beams
photos.caption: The roofline of cone-shaped pinnacles.
photos.credit: Photo: Albert Backer · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Devriese · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Earthen building with pointed towers rising behind a busy open-air market of stalls, carts and people on bare sand.

hints.text: This giant of sun-dried earth stands on a floodplain at the edge of the Sahel, and its walls bristle with bundles of palm sticks.
Every year the whole town gathers to re-plaster it after the rains, climbing on the protruding sticks that serve as built-in scaffolding.
The present building dates from 1907, replacing one that had fallen into ruin, and it is often called the largest mud-brick building in the world.

summary.description: The current mosque was completed in 1907 on the site of an older one that was in ruins by the 1830s. It is built of sun-dried earth bricks coated in plaster and is described as the world's largest adobe building. Ismaila Traoré, head of Djenné's masons' guild, was its architect.
keyFeatures: Sun-dried earth bricks coated in plaster
Bundles of palm sticks (toron) projecting about 60 cm from the walls
Three box-like towers on the qibla wall
Cone-shaped pinnacles topped with ostrich eggs
funFacts: The whole community takes part in the yearly replastering: boys stir the mud, women carry water and the masons' guild directs the work.
Together with the Old Towns of Djenné it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.

architects.name: Ali Akbar Isfahani
architects.bio: Architect who most likely completed the Shah Mosque for Shah Abbas the Great.

photos.credit: Photo: Patrickringgenberg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tiled entrance portal with two slim minarets and a turquoise dome rising behind a long arcaded building, seen across a garden square.
Looking up into a deep portal niche covered in blue mosaic tiles, with a honeycomb vault of stalactite-like cells
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Large courtyard framed by tall tiled iwans and two-storey arcades under a deep blue sky, with a few visitors sitting in the shade.
Looking straight up into a round dome covered in deep blue tilework with calligraphic bands and lattice windows
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It closes one side of an immense rectangular royal square and is turned at an angle so that its dome still faces the right direction.
Its portal and domes are covered in 'seven-colour' tile mosaic, mostly in blue, and the dome is double-shelled.
Begun in 1611 under the Safavid king Abbas the Great, it took about two decades and reportedly used some 18 million bricks and 475,000 tiles.

summary.description: A masterpiece of Safavid architecture on the south side of Naqsh-e Jahan Square, begun in 1611 for Shah Abbas the Great and finished around 1630. The entrance vestibule turns about 45 degrees so the prayer hall can face the qibla while the portal faces the square. The outer dome is 52 m high.
keyFeatures: Four-iwan plan around a central courtyard
Haft rangi ('seven-colour') tile mosaics
Outer dome 52 m high, inner dome 38 m
Two entrance minarets of 33.5 m
Vestibule turned about 45 degrees towards the qibla
funFacts: It reportedly contains about 18 million bricks and 475,000 tiles.
Its dome appears on the reverse of the Iranian 20,000-rial banknote.

architects.name: Muhammad Reza Isfahani
architects.bio: Builder from Isfahan, son of Husayn, whose name appears in an inscription around the mihrab of the mosque.

photos.credit: Photo: Nicolas Hadjisavvas · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Large tiled dome in cream and turquoise above a blue-tiled entrance portal, beside a long arcade with awnings and clipped shrubs.

photos.credit: Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Domed building at the centre of a long two-storey arcade across a huge reflecting pool and paved square, with small figures at the edge.
Square prayer chamber with walls of blue and gold tilework, pointed arches and a ring of lattice windows under a gold-toned dome
photos.credit: Photo: Amirpashaei · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Unlike its giant neighbour across the same square, this small mosque has no minarets and no courtyard, because it was a private place of worship.
Visitors enter by a winding L-shaped passage, and under its dome a ceiling of cream and gold tile forms a peacock-like pattern of sunlight at the centre.
It was built between about 1603 and 1619 for Shah Abbas the Great and named after a respected religious scholar who lived nearby.

summary.description: A small royal mosque on the east side of Naqsh-e Jahan Square, built between 1603 and 1619 under Shah Abbas the Great for the court rather than for the public. A winding entrance passage once shielded the women of the court from view. Its single-shell dome is about 13 m across inside.
keyFeatures: No minarets and no courtyard
Winding L-shaped entry passage
Single-shell dome, about 13 m across
Haft rang tile mosaics above marble lower walls
Dome offset from the entrance axis to face the qibla
funFacts: A sunlit 'peacock' shape appears at the centre of the dome through an opening in the ceiling.
A tunnel once ran under the square from the Ali Qapu Palace.

architects.name: Unknown Mughal builders
architects.bio: Mughal craftsmen who built the mosque for the emperor Aurangzeb, with construction overseen by his foster brother Muzaffar Hussein (Fidai Khan Koka), governor of Lahore.

photos.credit: Photo: Romero Maia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Red sandstone mosque with a central arched gateway, three white marble domes and slim corner minarets across an empty paved courtyard.

photos.credit: Photo: M.junaid0906 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Red mosque with white domes and tall minarets glowing at dusk, perfectly mirrored in a still pool in the foreground.

photos.credit: Photo: Mhtoori · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a vast square courtyard with four tall corner minarets, a domed prayer hall at the far end and a gateway near.
Tall red sandstone minaret with a small domed pavilion on top, beside a large pale marble dome and a long red wall
photos.credit: Photo: Muhammad Umair Mirza · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Prayer hall with a cusped marble mihrab arch under a hanging lamp, with men praying on red carpets in front
photos.credit: Photo: Ashhad Ahmed · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This red sandstone mosque was the largest in the world when it was built, and its courtyard can hold a hundred thousand people.
At the corners of a vast square courtyard stand four tall minarets, and above the prayer hall rise three white marble domes.
Commissioned in 1671 by an emperor and finished in 1673, it served as a stable for an army's horses in the early 19th century.

summary.description: The largest mosque of the Mughal era, commissioned in 1671 by the emperor Aurangzeb and completed in 1673. Red sandstone with white marble inlay forms a complex about 170 m by 170 m with a courtyard of some 25,600 square metres. After Ranjit Singh's army took Lahore in 1799, the courtyard served as a stable for army horses.
keyFeatures: Red sandstone with white marble inlay
Four main minarets of 60 m
Three white marble domes
Courtyard of about 25,600 m²
Capacity of about 100,000 with the courtyard in use
funFacts: It remained the world's largest mosque for over 300 years.
In 1974, 39 heads of Muslim states prayed there during the Second Islamic Summit.

architects.name: Al-Nasrani
architects.bio: Architect of the mosque who, according to the 10th-century author al-Balawi, was a non-Muslim, possibly a Christian.

photos.credit: Photo: Holger Uwe Schmitt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Sand-coloured stone courtyard with a domed fountain house on the right, pointed arcades and a spiral-topped minaret rising behind.
Stone minaret with a rectangular base, a round shaft and a small domed lantern, behind a wall crest of cut-out openwork
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Vast empty courtyard ringed by plain pointed arcades, with a domed ablution pavilion in the middle
photos.credit: Photo: User:Berthold Werner · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Holger Uwe Schmitt · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Prayer hall with broad pointed brick arches, carved plaster borders, a small wooden balcony and a green carpet on the floor.

hints.text: Its austere brick arcades and huge open court make it the oldest mosque in its country to survive in nearly its original form.
The stone minaret has an unusual spiral staircase on the outside, and a legend says its design came from a ruler absentmindedly winding a scroll around his finger.
It was begun in 876 by an Abbasid governor and finished in 879, and the architect is said to have been a Christian.

summary.description: Built by Ahmad ibn Tulun, Abbasid governor of Egypt, from 876 to about 879, on a small hill in what is now Islamic Cairo. It is described as the oldest well-preserved mosque in Egypt. Brick walls, pointed arches on brick piers and a palm-wood roof surround a central courtyard.
keyFeatures: Brick piers carrying pointed arches around a huge courtyard
Stone minaret with an external spiral staircase
Carved stucco decoration and a Kufic inscription of nearly 2 km
Octagonal fountain under a dome, added in 1296
Prayer hall five aisles deep
funFacts: A local legend says Noah's Ark came to rest on the hill, not on Mount Ararat.
It appears on the Egyptian five-pound banknote and in the film The Spy Who Loved Me.

architects.name: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu
architects.bio: Shogun who bought the Saionji family's villa in 1397 and turned it into the Kinkaku-ji complex, where the pavilion was built around 1399.

photos.credit: Photo: Basile Morin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Three-storey pavilion with gold-covered upper floors and dark roofs beside a calm pond that mirrors it, ringed by pines and forested hills.
Three-storey pavilion with gold-covered upper floors and dark roofs, reflected in a still pond framed by red maple leaves
photos.credit: Photo: Martin Falbisoner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Close view of a gold-leafed pavilion with two upper floors, a balcony and a bronze phoenix on the roof, among pine trees
photos.credit: Photo: Nacaru · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Hyppolyte de Saint-Rambert · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Golden pavilion with snow-dusted roofs on a pond shore, framed by snowy pines and misty hills in falling snow.

hints.text: This three-storey pavilion by a pond was built as part of a shogun's retirement villa and later became a Zen temple's relic hall.
Each floor has a different style: the first is in the manner of a noble's mansion, the second a warrior's house, the third a Chinese Zen hall, and the top two are covered in gold leaf.
In 1950 a young monk burned it down, an event that inspired a famous novel, and the present building dates from the 1955 reconstruction of the original of about 1399.

summary.description: A shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, bought the villa in 1397 and made it the temple complex whose pavilion was built about 1399. The three floors are in different styles, and the upper two are covered in gold leaf. A novice monk burned it down in 1950, and the present pavilion was rebuilt in 1955.
keyFeatures: Three floors in three styles: shinden, warrior and Chinese Zen
Top two floors covered in gold leaf
Mirror-like pond garden
Serves as a reliquary housing Buddha relics
funFacts: Yukio Mishima's 1956 novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion fictionalises the 1950 arson.
It is part of the UNESCO site Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

architects.name: Guru Arjan
architects.bio: Fifth Sikh Guru, who founded the Harmandir Sahib, began building it in 1581 and installed the Adi Granth there on 16 August 1604.

photos.alt: Two-storey shrine covered in gold panels with small domes and kiosks, standing at the edge of a pool with pilgrims along its rail

photos.alt: Gilded shrine reflected in a large pool, reached by a covered walkway full of visitors, with white buildings behind
photos.credit: Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Daniel Romanson · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a square pool surrounded by white buildings, with a small gold shrine linked to the shore by a straight causeway.

photos.credit: Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Gilded shrine glowing at dusk with its golden domes and kiosks, mirrored in the dark water of the surrounding pool.

photos.credit: Photo: SM14 · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Octagonal ceiling panel with a gilded sun-ray medallion at the centre, surrounded by blue and red floral patterns and a gold border.

hints.text: This shrine stands in the middle of a sacred pool and is reached by a single causeway, yet it has a door on each of its four sides.
Its four entrances stand for welcome to people of every caste and creed, and the building sits lower than its surroundings, so visitors walk down to it.
It was begun in 1581 and in 1604 the community's holy scripture was installed in it, while the gold covering came in the 1830s under a Punjabi maharaja.

summary.description: The holiest shrine of Sikhism, founded by the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, with work starting in 1581 and the brick temple finished in 1589; the Adi Granth was installed on 16 August 1604. Maharaja Ranjit Singh rebuilt it in marble and copper in 1809 and gilded the sanctum in 1830. The architecture blends Indo-Islamic Mughal and Hindu Rajput elements.
keyFeatures: Gilded sanctum on a pool called the Amrit Sarovar
Single causeway to the shrine
Four entrances open to all
Sanctum set lower than its surroundings
Blend of Mughal and Rajput architecture
funFacts: Over 100,000 free vegetarian meals are served daily in its community kitchen.
More than 150,000 people visit each day.

architects.name: Rajaraja I
architects.bio: Chola emperor who built the Brihadisvara Temple, constructed between 1003 and 1010 CE.

photos.alt: Floodlit stepped granite tower with a domed top beside a pillared pavilion, at twilight
photos.credit: Photo: Original: Rainer Halama Derivative work: UnpetitproleX · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Pyramidal tower of many tiers of small shrines and sculpture, topped by a domed cap, rising above low entrance halls
photos.credit: Photo: Matthew T Rader · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Vinayaraj · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall carved gateway tower of reddish stone with tiers of sculpted figures, seen across a paved courtyard with visitors walking and sitting.

photos.credit: Photo: Ilasun · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of a granite tower wall with stacked tiers of pilasters, latticed windows and carved deities in recessed niches.

hints.text: A king built this granite temple to a god of the Hindu faith as a monument to his power, and its tower rises about 63 m, among the tallest of its kind in the south of the subcontinent.
A huge stone bull faces the sanctum, and the tower is crowned by a domed cap carved from a single block that is said to weigh around 80 tons.
Completed in 1010 under the Chola dynasty, it was inscribed by UNESCO in 1987 as part of a group of 'Great Living' temples.

summary.description: A Hindu temple to Shiva built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I between 1003 and 1010 CE. Its granite vimana is about 63 m tall, and the main linga inside is a monolith around 8.7 m high. Chola frescoes found in 1931 cover about 670 m².
keyFeatures: Granite vimana about 63 m tall
Domed capstone carved from a single block
Monolithic Nandi bull facing the sanctum
Monolithic linga about 8.7 m high
81 of the 108 dance karanas carved on an upper wall
funFacts: It is also called Dakshina Meru.
It was inscribed by UNESCO in 1987 and extended in 2004 as the Great Living Chola Temples.

architects.name: Narasimhadeva I
architects.bio: King of the Eastern Ganga dynasty who built the temple around 1250 CE.

photos.alt: Stepped, pyramid-roofed stone hall with a dark doorway, partly under scaffolding and surrounded by visitors
photos.credit: Photo: Subhrajyoti07 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Giant carved stone wheel with eight broad spokes and a richly decorated rim, set into a wall of sculpture
photos.caption: One of the temple's 24 carved wheels.
photos.credit: Photo: Joydeep · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This 13th-century temple is built in the form of a gigantic stone chariot, pulled by seven horses, dedicated to a god of light and the day.
Twenty-four huge carved wheels decorate its base, and it is made mainly of dark khondalite stone.
Built around 1250 by a king of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, it was called the 'Black Pagoda' by European sailors and became a World Heritage Site in 1984.

summary.description: A temple built around 1250 CE by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, shaped as a stone chariot dedicated to Surya, the sun god. It stands as a masterpiece of Kalinga architecture, with 24 carved wheels and seven horses. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.
keyFeatures: Chariot-shaped temple of Surya
24 carved stone wheels
Seven horses pulling the chariot
Mainly khondalite stone
Kalinga (Odisha) architecture
funFacts: The wheels are said to work as sundials that tell time to within a minute.
The temple appears on the reverse of the Indian 10-rupee note.

architects.name: Unknown Thai royal builders
architects.bio: Builders working for the Chakri kings: Rama II restored the temple and planned its great tower, and work on it began under Rama III.

photos.alt: Floodlit tiered gold-toned tower with a trident finial, flanked by four smaller towers, against a night sky
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: White hall with an orange and white tiled roof and a slender spire, guarded by a colourful giant statue in a garden
photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This riverside temple takes its name from the Hindu charioteer of the sun god, and its spire was the first sign of the capital that travellers saw sailing upstream.
Its tall central tower is encrusted with pieces of porcelain, which once served as ballast on boats arriving from China.
The main tower was finished in 1851 and is topped by a seven-pronged trident; it stands on the west bank, across from the Grand Palace.

summary.description: A temple on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River in Thonburi. Rama II restored it and planned a great tower of 70 m, and the main prang was completed in 1851 under Rama III, after about nine years of work. The prang is encrusted with porcelain and shells.
keyFeatures: Central prang between about 67 and 86 m high, depending on the source
Surface encrusted with porcelain and Mauritia mauritiana shells
Four smaller prangs around the main tower
Seven-pronged trident finial
Named after Aruna, the sun god's charioteer
funFacts: King Taksin renamed it Wat Chaeng in the 1700s and is believed to have vowed to restore it after passing it at sunrise.
The 2013-2017 restoration's lime-plaster finish looked whitewashed to some, which drew criticism.

architects.name: Unknown Mon and Burmese builders
architects.bio: Generations of Mon and Burmese builders and donors; after the 1768 earthquake King Hsinbyushin raised the stupa to its present height in 1775.

photos.alt: Enormous bell-shaped gilded stupa tapering to a slender spire, ringed by small golden shrines on a wet marble terrace with people under umbrellas
photos.credit: Photo: Jakub Hałun · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Golden multi-roofed pavilion with green roof tiles beside gilded spires on a marble platform under a blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Golden bell-shaped stupa and ring of small gilded shrines glowing in warm low sun against a blue and amber sky

hints.text: Tradition says this gold-plated stupa was built more than 2,500 years ago to enshrine hairs of the Buddha and relics of three earlier Buddhas.
It crowns a hill above a city, rising about 99 m, and its umbrella-like crown is tipped with thousands of diamonds and rubies and a 76-carat diamond.
An earthquake in 1768 brought down its top, and a king raised it to its present height in 1775; visitors must go barefoot.

summary.description: A great gilded stupa on Singuttara Hill, rising to 99 m (112 m with its spire), with a brick body covered in gold plates attached by rivets. Tradition says it is over 2,500 years old and holds eight strands of the Buddha's hair. After the 1768 earthquake brought down the top, King Hsinbyushin rebuilt it to its present height in 1775.
keyFeatures: Brick stupa covered in gold plates
Crown tipped with 5,448 diamonds and 2,317 rubies and a 76-carat diamond
Four entrances each guarded by a pair of giant leogryphs
Terrace ringed by smaller shrines and pavilions
Height capped by city zoning to keep it prominent
funFacts: The Great Bell of Dhammazedi, donated in 1485, fell into a river while being moved and has never been recovered.
King Mindon donated a new hti (umbrella crown) in 1871.

architects.name: Unknown Japanese temple carpenters
architects.bio: Temple carpenters of the Asuka period; Prince Shōtoku commissioned the temple, believed complete by 607, and after a fire in 670 it was rebuilt, by about 711.

photos.credit: Photo: ONO Masanobu · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Two-storey wooden hall with tiled hip-and-gable roofs beside a tall five-storey pagoda, on a gravel courtyard under clear blue sky
Eight-sided wooden hall with a tiled roof topped by a bronze finial, standing on a low stone platform
photos.credit: Photo: 663highland · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: 663highland · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Oblique view of a two-storey wooden hall with deep overhanging tiled roofs and bracketed eaves, a pagoda rising behind it

hints.text: This Buddhist temple near an ancient capital in Japan was founded by a regent prince, and its main hall is widely recognised as the oldest wooden building in the world.
Its five-storey pagoda, about 32 m tall, has a central pillar whose wood has been dated by tree rings to the year 594.
A fire in 670 destroyed the first buildings and a 1949 fire damaged the main hall's murals; in 1993 it became one of Japan's first World Heritage Sites.

summary.description: A Buddhist temple commissioned by Prince Shōtoku and believed complete by 607. The Nihon Shoki records a fire in 670, after which it was rebuilt by about 711. Its main hall, the Kondō, is widely recognised as the world's oldest wooden building, and the five-storey pagoda is 32.45 m tall.
keyFeatures: Kondō, widely recognised as the world's oldest wooden building
Five-storey pagoda, 32.45 m tall
Central pillar dated by dendrochronology to 594
Eight-sided Yumedono hall
Home of the Kudara Kannon statue
funFacts: Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site, registered in 1993.
Fire-prevention day for cultural properties is 26 January, the day of the 1949 fire in the main hall.

name: Lotus Temple
aliases: Bahá'í House of Worship, New Delhi

architects.name: Fariborz Sahba
architects.bio: Architect of the Bahá'í House of Worship in New Delhi, who drew his lotus inspiration partly from carvings at the Ajanta and Ellora caves.

photos.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: White marble building of huge curved petal-shaped shells rising above a low platform, seen from a garden path under a clear blue sky

photos.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close oblique view of the white petal-shaped shells with a curved entrance canopy and a reflecting pool in front
Inside a shell-like concrete vault with a web of ribs lit warmly, above rows of wooden benches and arched windows
photos.credit: Photo: Dinudey Baidya from Bangalore, India · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: This house of worship is open to people of any religion and has no sermons, rituals or musical instruments, only scripture read or chanted.
Its form is a flower: 27 free-standing marble-clad petals in three rings of nine, surrounded by nine pools, with nine doors.
It was completed in 1986, clad in marble from a mountain in Greece, and has been compared to the Sydney Opera House.

summary.description: A Bahá'í House of Worship completed on 30 September 1986 and opened to the public in January 1987. Fariborz Sahba designed it as a lotus of 27 marble-clad concrete petals in three rings of nine, rising 40.8 m, with nine pools and nine doors. It welcomes people of any religion, and over 5 million people visit each year.
keyFeatures: 27 free-standing marble-clad petals in three rings of nine
Nine surrounding pools and nine doors
About 10,000 m² of white marble from Mount Pentelicus in Greece
Seats about 1,300
Height of 40.8 m
funFacts: Fritz Leonhardt called it the Taj Mahal of the 20th century.
In 2015 it installed over 400 solar panels producing about 120 kW.

architects.name: João Carvalho Ferreira
architects.bio: Architect credited with the design of the Joanina Library, built for King John V at the University of Coimbra between 1717 and 1728.

photos.credit: Photo: Chris · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Whole front of a low white and ochre stone building with a columned doorway under a carved crest, seen across a sunlit paved square
Tall white and ochre stone building with arched windows, urn finials and a statue on a stair
photos.credit: Photo: GFreihalter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Hall of gilded and painted two-storey bookcases with a royal portrait framed by carved ornament
photos.caption: One of the three halls, divided by decorated arches.
photos.credit: Photo: Jl FilpoC · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Trishhhh · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Corner of a hall lined with tall dark wood bookcases with gilded columns and a gallery, and a polished table in the foreground

hints.text: It was founded by a king of Portugal to serve one of Europe's oldest universities.
Its gilded, chinoiserie-painted shelves are made largely of exotic wood from Brazil, and its thick walls and teak door keep the air at a steady temperature.
A colony of bats lives inside and eats the insects that would otherwise damage the books.

summary.description: This Baroque library was built between 1717 and 1728 for King John V on a university hill in Coimbra. Three halls, divided by ornate arches, hold shelves of gilded and painted wood, with ceilings by Lisbon artists. Its oak construction and thick walls help protect the books from insects and heat.
keyFeatures: Three halls divided by decorated arches
Two-storey gilded and painted shelves
Painted ceilings by Simões Ribeiro and Vicente Nunes
Chinoiserie motifs
Walls about 2.11 m thick
funFacts: A colony of bats lives in the library and eats insects that threaten the books.
A 1725 portrait of King John V by Domenico Duprà hangs at the end of the main hall.

architects.name: James Gibbs
architects.bio: Architect appointed in 1736 to design the Radcliffe Camera after the death of Nicholas Hawksmoor; he published its design in Bibliotheca Radcliviana (1747).

photos.alt: Round stone building with paired columns, a balustrade and a lead-covered dome with a small lantern
photos.credit: Photo: Diliff · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Circular honey-coloured stone building with a rusticated base and a domed roof across a lawn

Photo: Julian Herzog (Website) · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: High view of a round domed stone building standing in a square surrounded by pinnacled collegiate buildings and a street

hints.text: It was paid for by the bequest of a royal physician who died in 1714.
It is the earliest circular library in England, with a heavily rusticated ground stage and a lanterned dome on an octagonal drum.
Construction began in May 1737 and it opened in April 1749; since 1861 it has served as a reading room for a university library.

summary.description: This domed rotunda stands in the heart of a university city, built with money left by the physician John Radcliffe. Its architect won the commission after another famous architect died. It is the earliest circular library in England and became a reading room after the books moved out in 1861.
keyFeatures: Circular plan
Rusticated ground stage with pedimented projections
Coupled Corinthian columns
Lanterned dome on an octagonal drum
Local Headington and Burford stone
funFacts: The design was recorded in the architect's 1747 book Bibliotheca Radcliviana.
It was fully completed in 1748 and opened on 13 April 1749.

architects.name: Thomas Burgh
architects.bio: Engineer and architect whose major work is the Old Library at Trinity College Dublin, built between 1712 and 1732.

photos.alt: Long grey stone building of three storeys with rows of windows and arches beside a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: Patrick Theiner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Very long hall with a wooden barrel vault, two levels of dark bookcases and marble busts down the aisle
photos.caption: The hall is about 65 metres long.
photos.credit: Photo: Diliff · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Rafesmar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Dark wooden bookcases with marble busts on pedestals receding down a long hall, visitors walking between them

photos.credit: Photo: Rob Hurson · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking up at a curved wooden barrel-vaulted ceiling above two tiers of galleries packed with old books

hints.text: Its main hall is one of the longest single-room libraries in the world, lined with marble busts of writers and thinkers.
It was built between 1712 and 1732, and in 1860 its flat ceiling was raised to make room for an upper gallery of books.
It houses a medieval illuminated manuscript presented to the college in 1661, an ancient Irish harp and a surviving copy of the 1916 Proclamation.

summary.description: The Old Library was designed by Thomas Burgh and built between 1712 and 1732 at a college in Dublin. Its main hall is 65 metres long and holds about 200,000 of the library's oldest books. The room's roof was raised in 1860 to add an upper gallery.
keyFeatures: 65 m long main hall
About 200,000 of the oldest books
Upper gallery added in 1860
Marble busts along the aisle
Home of the Book of Kells
funFacts: One of the four volumes of the Book of Kells, given to the college in 1661, is on display at any time.
The hall holds one of the last copies of the 1916 Proclamation of the Irish Republic.

name: Library of Congress Thomas Jefferson Building

architects.name: John L. Smithmeyer
architects.bio: Co-winner with Paul Pelz of the 1873 design competition for the Library of Congress building; dismissed in 1888.

architects.name: Paul J. Pelz
architects.bio: Co-winner of the 1873 competition and the lead designer of most of the exterior; dismissed in 1892.

architects.name: Edward Pearce Casey
architects.bio: Architect who replaced Pelz in 1892 and worked through the final years of construction.

photos.alt: Grand white stone entrance with three arches, tall columns, carved busts and a wide flight of steps
photos.credit: Photo: Carol M. Highsmith · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Carol M. Highsmith · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a large grey stone building with a central copper dome and wings around courtyards, amid lawns and streets
Great marble hall with stained-glass ceiling panels, painted vaults, staircases and a mosaic floor
photos.credit: Photo: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Carol M. Highsmith · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Octagonal reading room seen from above, with curved wooden desks around a central desk beneath tall arches and a high dome

photos.credit: Photo: Daderot · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Bronze sea-god and sea-horse sculptures in a stone fountain basin set in an arched granite wall below classical facade

hints.text: It is the oldest of three buildings that house the largest library in the world, and it has been a National Historic Landmark since 1965.
Its Great Hall has a stained-glass ceiling and mosaic floor, and a gilded dome crowns the Main Reading Room.
It opened to the public on 1 November 1897 and was once linked to the Capitol by a book tunnel with a conveyor.

summary.description: Opened in 1897, this Beaux-Arts palace was designed to house a national library on Capitol Hill. Its richly decorated interior has murals, mosaics and marble, and a copper dome gilded with 23-karat gold leaf. It was renamed for the president whose books founded the collection in 1980.
keyFeatures: Classical Beaux-Arts façade
Great Hall with stained glass and mosaics
Main Reading Room under a gilded dome
Court of Neptune Fountain
Murals by Edwin Blashfield
funFacts: A book tunnel once linked the building to the Capitol; part of it was removed for the Capitol Visitor Center.
It was named for Thomas Jefferson in 1980.

architects.name: Gunnar Asplund
architects.bio: Swedish architect who moved from classicism toward functionalism; the Stockholm Public Library is one of his most important works.

photos.credit: Photo: En Dum En · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Orange stucco block topped by a large plain cylindrical drum, seen across a pond and trees under a partly cloudy blue sky

photos.credit: Photo: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Orange building with a tall cylinder on a wide wing of regular small windows, framed by trees under a bright cloudy sky
Ochre-coloured building with a tall cylinder rising from a block, lit at dusk beside a pool
photos.credit: Photo: Holger.Ellgaard · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of the curved orange drum and the block below it, with evenly spaced rectangular windows and dark trees in front

hints.text: Its tall cylindrical drum, rising from a square block, is the form people remember from the outside.
It was the first public library in its country to use open shelves, a system its architect studied in the United States.
It opened on 31 March 1928, and a west wing was added in 1932.

summary.description: This library opened in 1928 and combines a plain, tall rotunda with a block of reading rooms. Its architect reduced classical elements to abstract geometric forms and removed most decoration. It was the first public library in Sweden with open shelves.
keyFeatures: Tall cylindrical rotunda
Classical elements reduced to simple geometry
Open shelves, a first in Sweden
Furnishings designed room by room
West wing added in 1932
funFacts: The rotunda was partly inspired by Ledoux's Barrière Saint-Martin in Paris.
Arnos Grove tube station in London is said to be based on this library.

architects.name: Rem Koolhaas
architects.bio: Dutch architect, theorist and urbanist, founder of OMA, often cited as a representative of deconstructivism and author of 'Delirious New York'.

Angular glass and steel building with a diamond lattice skin and projecting floating platforms

Photo: Ɱ · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

Narrow escalator rising between walls of vivid acid-green colour
photos.credit: Photo: Another Believer · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A steel net wraps around its glass skin, and several platforms seem to float inside the shell.
A continuous ramped display holds the nonfiction collection in unbroken numerical order across four floors, sloping at most 2 degrees.
Opened in May 2004, it was part-funded by a $20 million gift from a software billionaire.

summary.description: Opened in 2004, this eleven-storey glass and steel library was designed by OMA with LMN Architects. A diamond-patterned steel net wraps its glass skin, and its platforms appear to float. Its Book Spiral keeps the nonfiction collection in one continuous run.
keyFeatures: Steel net over a glass skin
Book Spiral across floors 6 to 9
Floating platforms
Red Floor in 13 shades of red
Nearly 10,000 custom windows
funFacts: Critic Paul Goldberger called it the most important new library built in a generation.
About 2.3 million people visited in its first year.

architects.name: Alvar Aalto
architects.bio: Finnish modernist architect who worked in partnership with his wife Aino; their studio designed buildings, furniture and lighting as integrated wholes.

architects.name: Aino Aalto
architects.bio: Finnish architect and designer, partner in the Aalto studio, who led much of its interior and furniture design.

photos.alt: White modernist building with long ribbon windows, a glazed stair tower and a grey stone entrance in a park

Aerial view of white flat-roofed blocks, one roof pierced by rows of round skylights, among trees

Photo: Ninaras · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Ninaraas · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long hall with a rippling wooden ceiling, rows of stools facing a stage and tall windows opening onto a park

hints.text: It was designed by a couple for a town that has since changed country, and it sits in a park near a harbour.
Its sunken reading hall is lit by dozens of deep round skylights, and the lecture hall once had a famous undulating timber ceiling.
Neglected for decades after the Second World War, it was restored by 2013 and won a European heritage prize in 2015.

summary.description: Designed between 1927 and 1935, this library began as a Nordic Classical scheme and became a pioneering work of functionalism. Its stepped, sunken reading hall is lit by cylindrical skylights, and it had Finland's first dedicated children's wing. After wartime damage and abandonment, it was restored and reopened in 2013.
keyFeatures: Stepped, sunken reading and lending hall
Deep cylindrical skylights
Undulating timber ceiling in the auditorium
Open-shelf lending and a children's wing
Concrete, glass, steel and timber
funFacts: After the Second World War it was renamed after Nadezhda Krupskaya; it is now the Central City Alvar Aalto Library.
It won the 2014 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize and the 2015 Europa Nostra Award.

architects.name: Snøhetta
architects.bio: Norwegian architecture firm that won the 1988 UNESCO competition for the Bibliotheca Alexandrina against 524 other entries.

photos.alt: Curved grey granite wall carved with signs and letters from many writing systems, beneath a glass facade

Black and white view of a cascading reading hall under a sloping glazed roof with tall concrete columns

Photo: Azniv Stepanian · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Terraced reading levels with wooden desks stepping down beneath tall columns and a glazed roof, seen from a high gallery

hints.text: It commemorates one of the most famous libraries of the ancient world, on the Mediterranean coast.
A tilted disc roof about 160 metres across slopes toward the sea like a sundial, and its granite wall is carved with characters from 120 writing systems.
It was inaugurated in October 2002, after a 1988 competition won by a Norwegian firm.

summary.description: Inaugurated in 2002, this library commemorates the ancient Library of Alexandria. Its reading room, about 20,000 square metres on eleven cascading levels, sits under a tilted, glass-panelled roof. A granite wall carved with characters from 120 writing systems encloses the complex.
keyFeatures: Tilted disc roof about 160 m in diameter
Reading room on eleven cascading levels
Granite wall with 120 writing systems
Shelf space for about eight million books
Conference centre, museums and planetarium
funFacts: When built, its reading room was the largest in the world.
Critics have called it a white elephant, arguing construction spending exceeded spending on the collection.

architects.name: Henri Labrouste
architects.bio: French architect who won the Prix de Rome in 1824 and designed the Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève, completed in 1850.

photos.alt: Long pale stone building with a row of tall arched windows above a solid base and carved garlands
photos.credit: Photo: Priscille Leroy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long reading room with slender cast-iron arches, barrel vaults and rows of wooden tables with green lamps
photos.caption: Slender iron columns carry openwork arches.

Photo: Marie-Lan Nguyen · CC BY 2.0 fr · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Gallery of wooden bookcases with a balcony railing and stairs, with green glass desk lamps on long reading tables in front

hints.text: Its façade carries a list of the names of famous scholars instead of conventional sculpture.
The whole upper floor is one reading room, whose barrel vaults rest on slender, exposed cast-iron columns and lace-like iron arches.
It was completed in December 1850 and opened to the public in February 1851.

summary.description: This Paris library combines a calm, Italian-inspired stone façade with a bold iron interior. Its reading room fills the whole upper floor, with sixteen slender cast-iron columns supporting openwork arches and plaster vaults. Modernists value it for bringing high technology into a monumental building.
keyFeatures: Arched windows over a solid base
Façade inscribed with scholars' names
Reading room filling the upper storey
Sixteen cast-iron Ionic columns
Openwork iron arches under plaster vaults
funFacts: The reading room held about 60,000 books, with 40,000 more in reserve.
The architect studied Italian classical and Renaissance buildings for six years after winning the Prix de Rome.

architects.name: Cass Gilbert
architects.bio: American architect who designed the Woolworth Building in the Neo-Gothic style.

Photo: Spinklink · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was the tallest building in the world until 1929, and its style was likened to a European cathedral.
A nickname coined in a 1916 booklet calls it a cathedral of commerce, and its lobby has a cruciform arcade of marble and glass mosaic.
It was completed in 1912 and rises 792 feet in Lower Manhattan for a chain of five-and-dime stores.

summary.description: This Neo-Gothic skyscraper in Lower Manhattan was completed in 1912 and stands 792 feet tall. Its terracotta-clad tower, pinnacles and copper roof evoke a medieval cathedral. It remained the world's tallest building until 1929.
keyFeatures: Neo-Gothic terracotta facade
792 ft (241 m) tower
Green copper pyramid roof
Cruciform lobby arcade of Skyros marble
Glass mosaic ceilings
funFacts: The 'Cathedral of Commerce' nickname was coined by Rev. S. Parkes Cadman in a 1916 booklet.
It stayed the tallest building until 40 Wall Street and the Chrysler Building surpassed it in 1929.

architects.name: Daniel Burnham
architects.bio: American architect and urban planner of the Chicago school who designed the Flatiron Building, working with Frederick P. Dinkelberg.

photos.alt: Very narrow wedge-shaped stone tower with a rounded prow and ornate cornice seen from a street junction

photos.alt: Triangular limestone skyscraper rising above a busy junction against a blue sky

hints.text: Its triangular plot gives it a prow only a few metres wide, like the bow of a ship.
It was originally named after the contractor whose company built it, but people kept using the nickname inspired by a household appliance.
Early critics called it 'Burnham's Folly', doubting its stability, but it opened on 1 October 1902.

summary.description: This triangular tower, completed in 1902, fills a wedge-shaped block where a famous avenue crosses a broadway. It was officially the Fuller Building, but its shape, like a cast-iron clothes iron, gave it its lasting name. Early critics doubted its stability, yet it has stood for over a century.
keyFeatures: Triangular, wedge-shaped plan
Vertical Renaissance palazzo styling
Beaux-Arts ornament
22 storeys, 307 ft (93.6 m)
Retail 'cowcatcher' annex at the tip
funFacts: It was first 20 storeys and 285 ft tall; a 1905 expansion made it 22.
It was originally called the Fuller Building after contractor George A. Fuller.

architects.name: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
architects.bio: A former assistant of Peter Behrens, Mies reduced architecture to steel, glass and fine materials ('less is more'). Last director of the Bauhaus, he emigrated to Chicago, where he built the Illinois Institute of Technology campus and later the Seagram Building in New York.

architects.name: Philip Johnson
architects.bio: American architect who, with John Burgee, designed the tower in the postmodern style.

Lower floors of a dark bronze-and-amber glass tower raised on columns above a granite plaza with pools

hints.text: It is a rectangular slab that sits about 90 feet back from the avenue, leaving a granite plaza with two pools.
Its facade was the first on an office building to use extruded bronze, about 1,600 tons of it, for the vertical mullions.
It was finished in 1958 and the 38-storey tower, 516 feet tall, once housed a famous restaurant on its lower floors.

summary.description: Completed in 1958, this 38-storey tower is a landmark of the International Style. Its bronze and tinted-glass curtain wall sits behind a pink granite plaza set back from the avenue. The pools and open space gave the city a new kind of public room.
keyFeatures: Bronze and tinted-glass curtain wall
About 1,600 short tons of bronze
Pink granite plaza with two pools
No setbacks, the slab stands back from the street
516 ft (157 m) roof height
funFacts: It was the first office building to use extruded bronze on its facade.
Critics called it 'a no-setback building but a building all set back'.

architects.name: Norman Foster
architects.bio: British architect who redesigned the ruined building from 1995 to 1999 for the reunified German parliament, adding a glass dome that opens the roof to the public.

photos.credit: Photo: Carlos Delgado · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

Aerial view of a bullet-shaped glass tower with a diamond lattice and dark spiral bands above city rooftops

Illuminated egg-shaped glass tower at night behind a small medieval church tower

hints.text: It stands on a site cleared after a 1992 bomb badly damaged a historic trading hall.
A triangulated perimeter structure keeps its rounded, 41-storey shape rigid, and a glass 'lens' tops it, echoing a dome that once stood on the old building.
It won the Stirling Prize in 2004 and is better known by a nickname inspired by its pickle-like shape.

summary.description: Completed in 2003, this 180-metre, 41-floor tower was designed by Foster + Partners with Arup as structural engineers. A triangulated perimeter structure holds its curved form. It replaced the Baltic Exchange, which was badly damaged by a 1992 bomb.
keyFeatures: Rounded, aerodynamic profile
Triangulated perimeter structure
Glass 'lens' at the top
180 m (591 ft) tall, 41 floors
Opened April 2004
funFacts: It won the 2004 Stirling Prize and the 2003 Emporis Skyscraper Award.
Its top dome recalls the glass dome of the Baltic Exchange that stood on the site.

architects.name: Bruce Graham
architects.bio: Architect at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill who designed the Sears (now Willis) Tower.

architects.name: Fazlur Rahman Khan
architects.bio: Structural engineer at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill whose bundled tube design for this tower was the first of its kind.

hints.text: For nearly 25 years from 1973 it was the tallest building in the world.
It is built as nine square tubes, each 75 feet across, bundled in a 3 by 3 grid, with setbacks at the 50th, 66th and 90th floors.
A glass-floored observation deck on the 103rd floor, about 1,353 feet up, draws around 1.7 million visitors a year.

summary.description: Completed in the early 1970s for a retailer, this 110-storey tower rises 1,451 ft to its architectural top. Its structural system bundles nine square tubes, a design later used in most supertall buildings. Its facade is anodized aluminium and black glass.
keyFeatures: Nine bundled square tubes in a 3x3 grid
Setbacks at floors 50, 66 and 90
1,451 ft (442 m) architectural height
Black anodized aluminium and glass facade
Observation deck on the 103rd floor
funFacts: It was renamed in 2009 after its original corporate tenant had left in 1994.
Its bundled-tube system has been used in most supertall buildings since, including the Burj Khalifa.

architects.name: Jean Nouvel
architects.bio: French architect and Pritzker Prize laureate of 2008, known for buildings that play with light, transparency and layered screens, from the Institut du Monde Arabe in Paris to the Louvre Abu Dhabi. In 2009 he was named lead coordinating architect of the Île Seguin project in the Paris suburbs.

photos.alt: Tall rounded tower with a pixel-like pattern of blue and red facade panels against a clear sky
photos.credit: Photo: Diliff · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Distant view of a bullet-shaped tower rising above a flat city with a wide road and railway tracks, seen from a high point on a hazy day

hints.text: Its designer drew on the rock formations of a nearby mountain and a rising geyser.
Its concrete structure is covered with about 59,000 painted metal strips and over 4,500 window openings, with sensors that adjust blinds to cut air conditioning.
Finished in 2004 for a water company, it has more than 4,500 LED devices that can light it in about 16 million colours.

summary.description: Finished in 2004 and opened in 2005, this 144-metre tower was designed by Jean Nouvel with b720 Fermín Vázquez Arquitectos. Its concrete core is clad in glass and painted aluminium strips. Local nicknames refer to its bullet-like shape.
keyFeatures: Rounded, bullet-like profile
About 59,619 painted metal strips
Over 4,500 LED devices designed by Yann Kersalé
Temperature-controlled blinds
funFacts: It is nicknamed 'el supositori' and 'l'obús' because of its shape.
It won the International Highrise Award in 2006.

architects.name: Rakai Pikatan
architects.bio: Javanese king of the Mataram kingdom who is believed to have begun the temple compound; a script bearing his name was found on a finial of the Shiva temple. Its builders are not recorded by name, so the king who started it is credited.

photos.credit: Photo: Gunawan Kartapranata · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Arabsalam · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built by a Hindu dynasty in the 9th century, said to answer the Buddhist monument that stands only a few kilometres away.
Its tallest tower is 47 metres high and honours Shiva, while two neighbouring towers are for Brahma and Vishnu.
A Javanese legend about a cursed princess turned to stone gives the compound its popular name, and a major earthquake in 2006 damaged it.

summary.description: Prambanan is a 9th-century Hindu temple compound in central Java, dedicated to the Trimurti of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. Its tall, pointed towers, the central one 47 metres high, rise within a complex that originally held 240 temple structures. It is the largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
keyFeatures: Steep, tapering temple towers with stacked tiers
A 47 m central Shiva temple flanked by Brahma and Vishnu temples
Originally 240 temple structures in concentric courts
Reliefs and carvings from the classical period of Java
funFacts: The Shiva temple is linked to an inscription of 856 CE, which describes its inauguration on 12 November that year.
The ruins inspired the folktale of Rara Jonggrang, which gave the compound its popular name.
The 2006 Yogyakarta earthquake scattered carvings and debris over the ground.

architects.name: Unknown Pandya and Nayak builders
architects.bio: No single architect is recorded. The oldest surviving masonry dates to the Pandya king Sadayavarman Kulasekaran I (r. 1190–1216), and the Madurai Nayaks rebuilt and extended the temple on a vast scale in the 16th and 17th centuries.

photos.credit: Photo: Bernard Gagnon · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

A tall pyramidal gateway tower covered from base to top in thousands of brightly painted figures, seen from below against a blue sky
photos.caption: The southern gateway tower, the tallest of the complex
photos.credit: Photo: Madhuranthakan Jagadeesan · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: The Thousand-Pillared Hall

hints.text: It sits on the southern bank of a river in a Tamil city and is dedicated to a goddess whose name means "fish-eyed" and to her consort.
Four huge gateway towers, the tallest about 52 metres, mark the entrances to a set of concentric walled enclosures, with a hall of a thousand pillars inside.
Its west tower is the model for the emblem of the state of Tamil Nadu, and a golden lotus pond lies inside.

summary.description: Meenakshi Temple is a historic Hindu temple in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, dedicated to Meenakshi, a form of Parvati, and her consort Sundareswarar (Shiva). The earliest surviving masonry dates to the Pandya period, and the Madurai Nayaks extended it extensively in the 16th and 17th centuries. Its complex of concentric enclosures has four great gopurams and ten smaller ones.
keyFeatures: Concentric walled enclosures spread over 5.7 hectares
Four large gopurams and ten smaller ones covered in painted stucco figures
The southern tower rises to about 52 m (170 ft)
The Thousand-Pillared Hall and the Golden Lotus Pond
funFacts: The state emblem of Tamil Nadu is based on the temple's west gopuram.
Meenakshi means "fish-eyed" in Tamil.
In October 2017 it was judged the best "Swachh Iconic Place" in India.

architects.name: Vidyadhara
architects.bio: Chandela king who is believed to have built the temple to celebrate his success against Mahmud of Ghazni. An inscription names the builder as Virimda, read as a pseudonym of Vidyadhara; the architects themselves are not recorded.

hints.text: It was built in the 11th century by a dynasty that made its small town a capital, as a monument to a victory over an invading ruler.
It rises from a high platform in a steep mountain shape, standing for the mythical Mount Meru, and its main tower is surrounded by 84 miniature spires.
It is the largest of a famous group of temples in central India whose walls carry bands of sculpture, including musicians, nymphs and celebrated erotic scenes.

summary.description: Built in the 11th century under the Chandela king Vidyadhara, the temple is dedicated to Shiva and is the largest and most ornate of the medieval temples at Khajuraho. A series of porches and towers rises to a 31 m spire ringed by smaller spires, evoking a mountain range. The exterior is covered with bands of sculpture.
keyFeatures: A 31 m shikhara with 84 miniature spires
A 4 m plinth reached by steep steps
Five-part plan with three successive halls, rising in height
Exterior walls carved in three layers of sculpture
A garland-like entrance arch cut from a single stone
funFacts: Its construction is dated to between 1025 and 1050 CE.
The temple's name means "the Great God of the Cave", after its dim, cave-like sanctum.
Khajuraho's temples were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

architects.name: Tokugawa Iemitsu
architects.bio: Third Tokugawa shogun, whose donation paid for the rebuilding of the main hall in 1633 after a fire in 1629. The carpenters are not named, so the patron is credited.

photos.alt: A huge hipped roof of dark thatch over a wooden hall whose wide veranda juts out on a scaffold of tall timbers above green treetops

A gilded seated Buddha on a lotus throne in front of a halo, under a black coffered ceiling and red and orange painted beams

photos.credit: Photo: Basile Morin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: The temple was founded in the late 8th century, before the city around it became the capital, and its name means "pure water".
Its main hall has a large veranda held out over a hillside by tall pillars in the kakezukuri method, and not a single nail is used in the whole structure.
The expression "to jump off the stage" at this temple became the Japanese way of saying "take the plunge".

summary.description: Kiyomizu-dera, "Pure Water Monastery", is a Buddhist temple in eastern Kyoto, founded in 778 according to legend and part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site. The present main hall was rebuilt in 1633 with a donation from the shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu. A large wooden stage projects from the hall over the hillside.
keyFeatures: A large hipped roof over the main hall
A wooden stage supported on a scaffold of tall timbers over the slope
Honours a statue of the eleven-faced Kannon
Otowa Falls, the spring that gives the temple its name
funFacts: The complex burned down nine times, from 1063 until its destruction in 1629.
In the Edo period a leap of about 13 m from the stage was believed to grant a wish if one survived.
Since 1995 the temple holds the Kanji of the Year ceremony each 12 December.

architects.name: Kim Daeseong
architects.bio: Chief minister of the Silla kingdom who began the present temple in 751, according to the Samguk Yusa, to pacify the spirits of his parents. He died before it was finished and the royal court completed it in 774.

photos.caption: The main hall flanked by its two pagodas

hints.text: It sits on a mountain slope in the old capital of a kingdom that unified much of its peninsula, and its name means "Temple of the Buddha Land".
In front of its main hall stand two pagodas of different character: one plain and austere, the other highly ornate.
The pagoda with the intricate design appears on a country's 10 won coin, and the temple shares a World Heritage listing with a nearby grotto.

summary.description: Bulguksa is a Buddhist temple on Mount Toham in Gyeongju, South Korea, begun in 751 under the Silla chief minister Kim Daeseong and completed in 774. It is regarded as a masterpiece of the golden age of Silla Buddhist art and contains six National Treasures. Its wooden halls were burned in the Imjin wars and rebuilt, but the famous stone structures are original.
keyFeatures: Two stone pagodas before the main hall: the plain Seokgatap and the ornate Dabotap
A double staircase and bridge, the Cheongungyo and Baegungyo, with 34 steps
Stone terraces below painted timber halls
Six National Treasures
funFacts: The 34 steps of the entrance stairway correspond to the 34 steps to enlightenment.
Dabotap is 10.4 m tall and appears on the South Korean 10 won coin.
A Dharani sutra found here in 1966, dated between 704 and 751, is among the earliest woodblock prints in the world.

architects.name: Taira no Kiyomori
architects.bio: Powerful Heian-period noble and later chancellor who, as governor of Aki Province, lavished wealth on the shrine and ordered the construction of its main hall in 1168. The builders are not recorded by name, so the patron is credited.

A long vermilion-pillared corridor with a thatch-like roof raised on posts over a tidal flat, with mountains behind

photos.credit: Photo: JohnnyOneSpeed · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Shrine pavilions and a distant gate seen across calm water at high tide, framed by dark timber beams in the foreground

hints.text: This Shinto shrine is built on an island held so sacred that for much of its history ordinary people were not allowed to set foot on it.
To keep the island pure, the buildings were raised on piers over a bay so they seem to float at high tide, and no births or deaths are permitted nearby.
Its giant vermilion gate, about 15 metres tall, stands in the sea off the shore and is the best-known sight of the site.

summary.description: Itsukushima Shrine is a Shinto shrine on the island of Miyajima in Hiroshima Prefecture, dedicated to the three daughters of the god Susano-o. Patronised by Taira no Kiyomori from 1168, it is laid out in the shinden-zukuri style on piers over the bay so that it appears to float. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and best known for its "floating" torii.
keyFeatures: Buildings and corridors raised on piers over the bay
Shinden-zukuri layout of the Heian period
A vermilion torii about 15 m tall standing in the sea
Honsha shrine and the Marodo shrine among 17 other structures
funFacts: The current torii dates to 1875, although a gate has stood on the site since 1168.
Commoners once had to steer their boats through the torii before approaching the shrine.
Since 1878 no births or deaths have been permitted near the shrine.

architects.name: Heitor da Silva Costa
architects.bio: Brazilian civil engineer who won the 1924 competition to build a monument to Christ on Corcovado. He designed the statue with the artist Carlos Oswald and directed its construction.

architects.name: Paul Landowski
architects.bio: French monument sculptor of Polish descent whose best-known work is the Christ in Rio de Janeiro. He created the statue, commissioning the Romanian sculptor Gheorghe Leonida to model the face.

architects.name: Albert Caquot
architects.bio: French engineer who designed the reinforced-concrete structure of the statue, which the engineers judged better suited to the cross-shaped figure than steel.

architects.name: Carlos Oswald
architects.bio: Brazilian artist who worked with Heitor da Silva Costa on the design of the statue.

photos.alt: Giant stone figure with arms stretched wide on a dark granite pedestal, against a forested mountainside
photos.credit: Photo: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 DE · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Close view of a robed stone figure with outstretched arms against a blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Arturdiasr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Built between 1922 and 1931, it stands on a 700-metre peak inside a national park, above a great port city.
It is 30 metres tall on an 8-metre pedestal, its outstretched arms span 28 metres, and it weighs about 635 tonnes.
Voted one of the New 7 Wonders of the World, it is the most famous symbol of Rio de Janeiro and of Brazil.

summary.description: Completed in 1931 on the peak of Corcovado, this 30-metre statue of Jesus with outstretched arms was designed by the engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and sculpted by Paul Landowski, with a reinforced-concrete structure by Albert Caquot and an outer layer of soapstone. It is the largest Art Deco-style sculpture in the world.
keyFeatures: 30 m statue on an 8 m pedestal, arms spread 28 m wide
Reinforced concrete faced in soapstone
About 635 tonnes, on the 700 m peak of Corcovado
Chapel under the statue, consecrated in 2006
funFacts: The first plan showed a Christ holding a globe in one hand and a cross in the other; the open-armed design replaced it.
Lightning struck the statue in 2008 and again in 2014, damaging fingers and, the first time, the head and eyebrows.
Landowski commissioned the Romanian sculptor Gheorghe Leonida to model the face.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

photos.alt: Low white building with a glass box under a deep roof slab, held by slender curved columns, beside a reflecting pool
photos.credit: Photo: Senado Federal · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Floodlit glass box under a wide white roof slab with a row of tall, curved columns, at night
photos.credit: Photo: Leandro Neumann Ciuffo · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was inaugurated on 21 April 1960, one of the first buildings opened in a capital built from scratch.
Its name is Portuguese for the central highland plateau on which the capital stands.
It is the official workplace of the president of Brazil, facing the Supreme Court across the Three Powers Plaza.

summary.description: Designed by Oscar Niemeyer in 1958 and inaugurated on 21 April 1960, the building is the official workplace of the president of Brazil, on the Three Powers Plaza in Brasília. It is a modernist work inside the Brasília World Heritage Site.
keyFeatures: Workplace of every Brazilian president since Juscelino Kubitschek
Stands on the Three Powers Plaza, across from the Supreme Federal Court
Part of the Brasília World Heritage Site (UNESCO, 1987)
Restored in 2009-2010 at a cost of R$ 111 million
funFacts: The name means 'highland', after the Brazilian Central Plateau where Brasília stands.
Planalto is often used as a metonym for the executive branch of the federal government.
Construction began on 10 July 1958 and was led by Construtora Rabello S.A.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

photos.alt: Glass-walled box under a broad white roof slab with curved columns at the ends, and a seated blindfolded statue in front
photos.credit: Photo: Leandro Neumann Ciuffo · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Row of tall white columns curving out from a glass box under a flat roof, beneath a stormy sky
photos.credit: Photo: Ricαrdo · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on a plaza named for the three branches of government, facing the presidential workplace.
Its structural calculations were made by the engineer Joaquim Cardozo, and it was first used on 21 April 1960.
It houses the court of last resort for constitutional questions in Brazil.

summary.description: Designed by Oscar Niemeyer, with structural calculations by the engineer Joaquim Cardozo, this building on the Three Powers Plaza held the court's first session on 21 April 1960, when the capital moved to Brasília. It houses Brazil's supreme court, the final authority on constitutional questions.
keyFeatures: Designed by Oscar Niemeyer, structure by Joaquim Cardozo
Stands on the Three Powers Plaza, across from the president's workplace
Annex buildings I and II complete the complex
First session held on 21 April 1960
funFacts: From 1909 to 1960 the court sat in a building on Avenida Rio Branco in Rio de Janeiro.
The court has had 11 members since 1969.
Since 2002 all its judicial and administrative sessions have been broadcast live on television.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

photos.alt: Tall concrete arches framing a glass-walled building, with islands of green plants in a pool in front
photos.credit: Photo: Lou Fernando · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Colonnade of concrete arches over glass walls, rising from a large pool dotted with plant beds
photos.credit: Photo: Boaventuravinicius · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its cornerstone was laid in 1960, but technical difficulties delayed its inauguration until 1970.
All its gardens were designed by Brazil's best-known landscape architect, and inside it has a gravity-defying spiral staircase.
It is the seat of Brazil's foreign ministry, and its name is used as shorthand for the ministry itself.

summary.description: Designed by Oscar Niemeyer, with gardens by Roberto Burle Marx, the palace is the headquarters of Brazil's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The arches of its facade first gave it the name Palácio dos Arcos. Niemeyer again used the theme of a glass box held between two concrete slabs with a colonnade, but changed the character of the building.
keyFeatures: Facade of concrete arches
Gardens and landscaping by Roberto Burle Marx
Gravity-defying spiral staircase inside
Sculpture Meteoro by Bruno Giorgi above the reflecting pool
Listed as national heritage in 2007
funFacts: The name comes from the ministry's former palace in Rio de Janeiro, and Itamaraty is used to mean the ministry itself.
Its cornerstone was laid by President Juscelino Kubitschek on 12 September 1960; it opened in April 1970.
Its interior holds works by Portinari, Volpi, Athos Bulcão and many other Brazilian artists.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

photos.credit: Photo: Gabriel de Andrade Fernandes · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long curved residential slab with a wavy façade of horizontal concrete fins, seen over lower buildings under a clear sky

photos.credit: Photo: Pablo Trincado · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Street-level view of the sweeping curved façade of fins rising above trees and a ground-floor arcade
Curving wall of closely spaced horizontal concrete fins sweeping up against a blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Victorgrigas · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Seen from below, a very tall wavy residential tower with horizontal fins, partly covered by a blue net
photos.credit: Photo: Paul R. Burley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its name is an acronym of the hotel and tourism company that first developed it.
It was meant to celebrate its city's fourth centenary, but was only completed in 1966 after several interruptions.
This S-shaped tower holds 1,160 apartments and even has its own postal code.

summary.description: Completed in 1966, the Copan is one of the symbols of modern Brazilian architecture, built to celebrate the fourth centenary of São Paulo. Oscar Niemeyer's office designed it, with Niemeyer himself responsible for the sinuous facade, and Joaquim Cardozo designed the structure. It has the largest reinforced-concrete structure in the country.
keyFeatures: 115 m tall, 32 floors, six blocks
1,160 apartments and more than seventy shops
Largest reinforced-concrete structure in Brazil
Sinuous facade designed by Niemeyer himself
funFacts: The name is an acronym of the Companhia Pan-Americana de Hotéis e Turismo, the original developer.
The building has its own postal code, 01046-925.
Since 2014 a transparent blue-black drape has covered it to protect pedestrians from loose mosaic tiles.

name: Museu de Arte Moderna do Rio de Janeiro
aliases: Museum of Modern Art of Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Affonso Eduardo Reidy
architects.bio: Brazilian architect, son of an English father and a Brazilian mother, who graduated in Rio de Janeiro in 1930 and became a leading figure of Brazilian modernism. He worked on the Ministry of Education and Health team and designed the museum, with Carmen Portinho as chief engineer.

photos.alt: Long concrete building on a row of slanting external pillars, with glass walls, beside a pond of water plants
photos.credit: Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Dornicke · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Slanting concrete pillars rise beside a glazed wall, with a tree at the left and a walkway running to a low building.

photos.credit: Photo: Andrevruas · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Wide covered open ground floor beneath a heavy concrete slab, with people walking and a glazed volume at the back.
Dark curving staircase with thin railings in a large hall with a brick wall and polished floor
photos.credit: Photo: Boaventuravinicius · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands in a park built on landfill in a bay, so the footings of its pillars reach 20 metres down.
The landscape of its gardens and the park around it was the work of the great Brazilian landscape designer Roberto Burle Marx.
A fire in 1978 destroyed about 90% of its collection, including works by Picasso, Miró and Dalí.

summary.description: Designed by Affonso Eduardo Reidy with Carmen Portinho as chief engineer and completed in 1955, the museum stands in Flamengo Park beside Guanabara Bay. A cadence of external pillars joined by longitudinal beams leaves the gallery level free of internal columns and structural walls.
keyFeatures: External pillars linked by longitudinal beams
Gallery level free of internal columns or structural walls
Gardens by Roberto Burle Marx
Pillar footings reaching 20 m down through landfill
Aluminium shutters on the north facade to control light
funFacts: On 8 July 1978 a fire destroyed 90% of the museum's collection.
The building and its theatre wing frame a large outdoor terrace.
The museum hosted the 2024 G20 Summit.

name: Catedral Metropolitana de São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro
aliases: Catedral Metropolitana do Rio de Janeiro
Catedral de São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Edgar de Oliveira da Fonseca
architects.bio: Brazilian architect who designed the Rio de Janeiro cathedral in a modern style based on the pyramids of Mayan architecture.

photos.alt: Huge cone-shaped concrete building with a grid of deep recessed panels, rising to a flat top
photos.credit: Photo: Rjcastillo · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Haakon S. Krohn · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall truncated cone of gridded concrete seen across a plaza, with a slender lattice bell tower beside it under a blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Acediscovery · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Dark conical concrete tower with a gridded surface rising above green treetops against a blue sky with thin clouds.
Looking up inside a vast conical hall at a glowing cross-shaped skylight and tall stained-glass strips
photos.credit: Photo: Aline L. Rosa · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built between 1964 and 1979 to replace a series of churches that had served as the city's cathedral since 1676.
Its design is a modern work based on the pyramids of Mayan architecture.
Four tall stained-glass windows rise 64 metres inside this cone, which seats 5,000 and holds 20,000 standing.

summary.description: Built between 1964 and 1979 to a design by Edgar de Oliveira da Fonseca, the cathedral is a cone 75 metres high and 106 metres across, in a modern style based on Mayan pyramids. Inside, four rectilinear stained-glass windows soar 64 metres from floor to ceiling.
keyFeatures: Conical form 75 m high, 96 m inside diameter
Four stained-glass windows 64 m tall
Seats 5,000, with standing room for 20,000
Seat of the Archdiocese of Rio de Janeiro
funFacts: It replaced a series of cathedrals dating from 1676, the last being the Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, now called the Old Cathedral.
It is dedicated to Saint Sebastian, patron saint of Rio de Janeiro.
Its interior covers 8,000 square metres.

name: FAU-USP Building
aliases: Faculdade de Arquitetura e Urbanismo da USP
Faculty of Architecture and Urbanism, University of São Paulo

architects.name: João Batista Vilanova Artigas
architects.bio: Born in Curitiba, Artigas is considered one of the most important names in the architectural history of São Paulo and the founding figure of the Paulista School, known for expressed reinforced concrete. He taught at the school whose building he designed, and lost his post in 1969 because of his Communist Party membership.

architects.name: Carlos Cascaldi
architects.bio: A São Paulo architect and a student of Artigas at the Polytechnic School, he later became a partner in his office through the 1950s. Together they designed the Londrina bus station, the Morumbi stadium and this university building.

photos.credit: Photo: Arte Fora do Museu · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Large raw-concrete box on a few thick pillars, with a deep overhang above a glazed ground floor and a lawn in front.

photos.credit: Photo: Lombana · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Corner of a heavy concrete block floating over slender supports, with grass in the foreground and trees behind at dusk light.
Vast open hall under a concrete ceiling of pyramid-shaped skylights, with a polished floor, ramps and balconies on every side
photos.caption: A single open space shared by every floor, lit from above.
photos.credit: Photo: Mike Peel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Gabriel Fernandes from São Paulo, Brasil · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long open ground-floor hall with round concrete columns, a low concrete ceiling, glazed walls and people working at tables.

hints.text: A university building designed by one of its own professors, who lost his teaching post a year after it opened.
Inside there is no corridor maze: a huge central atrium with skylights and long ramps connects every floor, with the classrooms around the edge.
Raw concrete on columns, built in the late 1960s by a leading figure of the Paulista School, it houses a school of architecture in the largest city of South America.

summary.description: Designed by Vilanova Artigas with Carlos Cascaldi, built in 1968 and inaugurated in 1969 on the university campus in São Paulo. A central atrium with a main ramp and skylights hosts political and cultural events and fosters conversation, with classrooms around the outside edge. It is considered one of the main representatives of architectural modernism in Brazil.
keyFeatures: Exposed reinforced concrete
Central atrium with a main ramp and skylights
Classrooms around the outer edge
Built to reflect austerity rather than consumerism
funFacts: The school was founded in 1948 by a group of teachers from the university's Polytechnic School.
Artigas helped create its Bauhaus-style curriculum, giving equal weight to technical skills, history and design.
Artigas and Paulo Mendes da Rocha were removed from teaching in 1969 for Communist Party membership; both were reinstated in the 1980s.

architects.name: Santiago Calatrava
architects.bio: Born near Valencia, Calatrava trained as an architect and a structural engineer, and is particularly known for bridges supported by single leaning pylons, railway stations, stadiums and museums whose sculptural forms often resemble living organisms.

photos.alt: White skeletal roof sweeping out over a shallow reflecting pool, with a silver star sculpture in the water and city buildings behind
photos.credit: Photo: Wilfredor · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
