photos.alt: Aerial view of a long white building on a pier jutting into a bay, with a city skyline and a rocky peak behind.
Long white cantilevered roof ribbed with slats, with a tall fin of louvres rising at its far end, above the water of a bay
photos.credit: Photo: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands at the end of a pier in a harbour district that was renewed for the Olympic Games held in the year after it opened.
Its exhibitions run from the cosmos and the Anthropocene to questions about the future of sustainable cities.
A long white roof reaches out over the water like a skeleton, with movable fins on top that follow the sun.

summary.description: Opened in December 2015 on Pier Mauá, this science museum was designed by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava as an icon of the reurbanization of Rio's port area. Its main exhibition leads visitors through five areas: Cosmos, Earth, Anthropocene, Tomorrow and Us.
keyFeatures: Cantilevered white roof over the waterfront
Neofuturist, organic structure
Exhibitions on sustainable cities and an ecological world
Part of the 2016 Olympic port renewal
funFacts: It cost approximately 230 million reais and was supported by the Roberto Marinho Foundation.
It opened on 17 December 2015 with President Dilma Rousseff in attendance.
One of its goals was to strengthen the cultural and international identity of Rio de Janeiro.

architects.name: Catão Francisco Ribeiro
architects.bio: Credited as the author of the bridge's design for the São Paulo city government. His scheme crossed two opposite curved roadways under a single pylon, a layout found in no other bridge.

architects.name: João Valente Filho
architects.bio: A São Paulo architect whose office, Valente e Valente Arquitetos, softened the contours of the engineered design and gave the bridge its finishing touches.

photos.alt: Tall X-shaped concrete pylon with hundreds of stay cables fanning out to two curved roadways, above a river and city towers
photos.credit: Photo: ikedaleo · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Side view of a single concrete pylon holding two crossing curved decks with a fan of cables, beside a river and glass office towers
photos.credit: Photo: Wilfredor · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking up from the roadway at an X-shaped concrete pylon with yellow-tinted stay cables fanning out against a deep blue sky.

hints.text: It crosses a polluted river in South America's largest city, and only motor vehicles are allowed on it.
Two curved roadways that cross over each other hang from one single tower, which is unique in the world.
Locals simply call it the "cable-stayed bridge"; its X-shaped tower is 138 metres tall and is lit up with colours at Christmas.

summary.description: Opened in May 2008 over the Pinheiros River, this cable-stayed bridge has two oppositely curved roadways suspended from a single X-shaped concrete tower. It is the only bridge in the world with two curved roadways supported by one pylon, and one of São Paulo's best-known postcards.
keyFeatures: X-shaped concrete pylon 138 m tall
Two curved roadways with a constant radius of 275.1 m
144 stay cables, interlaced over the river
Roadways cross at 12 m and 24 m above the ground
funFacts: The cable stays are interlaced, a crisscrossing arrangement not found in any other cable-stayed bridge.
At the end of December lights on the cables create colour effects like those on a Christmas tree.
Construction began in 2005 and the total cost came to R$233 million.

architects.name: Christiano Stockler das Neves
architects.bio: Architect of the Júlio Prestes Station, which he based on an eclectic, neoclassical Louis XVI style and which was clearly influenced by the old Pennsylvania Station in New York.

photos.alt: Cream-coloured stone station with a tall clock tower topped by a small dome and a curved wing of columns
photos.credit: Photo: Wilfredor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Wide concert hall with giant fluted columns, wooden balconies, and an orchestra platform below a coffered wooden ceiling
photos.caption: The old station concourse turned into a shoebox concert hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Webysther Nunes · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ed1983 at English Wikipedia · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Empty concert hall seen from the stage end, with rows of columns, gilded balconies and a grand piano under a coffered wooden ceiling.

photos.credit: Photo: Luiz coelho · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long bright foyer with a polished wooden floor, benches, potted palms and tall pale walls leading to an arched doorway.

hints.text: Its main hall was once full of trains, with a small railway running through it during construction.
The city's state symphony orchestra now plays in the former station concourse, under an adjustable ceiling.
An old railway terminus of the coffee era in São Paulo, reopened in 1999 as one of Latin America's main concert halls.

summary.description: Built between 1926 and 1938 as the Júlio Prestes Station, headquarters of the Sorocabana Railway, the building was restored and converted into a concert hall inaugurated on 9 July 1999. Its grand hall, shaped like a 19th-century shoebox hall, seats 1,498 people and is home to the São Paulo State Symphonic Orchestra.
keyFeatures: Eclectic neoclassical Louis XVI style station
Shoebox concert hall in the former grand hall
Adjustable ceiling designed by the American firm Artec
22 balconies between large columns
funFacts: During construction in the 1920s, a small railway ran through the Grand Hall to bring in material from Europe.
A 150-ton crane replaced an old train to lift the massive girders about 25 metres during the conversion.
The station is named after Júlio Prestes, a railwayman who became governor of São Paulo.

architects.name: Vilmos Fillinger
architects.bio: A Hungarian architect trained at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, who designed the Martinelli Building in São Paulo.

architects.name: Giuseppe Martinelli
architects.bio: The Italian-born entrepreneur who conceived the building in 1922 and drove its construction, raising its height again and again to beat a rival tower in Rio.

photos.alt: Stepped pink-granite skyscraper with four towers of classical windows, seen from the street below a cloudy sky
photos.credit: Photo: Mauro Cateb · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Wilson da Silva Vitorino · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking up the pink stone front of a tall stepped skyscraper to its row of crowning towers, with palm fronds and a lamp post in front.
Pink stone facade with pairs of pilasters topped by scroll capitals and rows of windows with pediments and balconies
photos.credit: Photo: Wilfredor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its owner, an immigrant entrepreneur, kept raising its height to outdo a rival tower in another city.
The owner had a villa-style house built on its roof to prove to a nervous public that the building would not fall.
The first skyscraper in Brazil, in the heart of São Paulo's historic centre, once the tallest in Latin America.

summary.description: Planned in 1922 by the Italian-born Giuseppe Martinelli and designed by the Hungarian architect Vilmos (William) Fillinger, this is the first skyscraper built in Brazil. Construction began in 1924; it opened unfinished in 1929 with 12 floors and was completed in 1934 at 30 floors and 105 metres.
keyFeatures: 105 m tall, 30 floors
Brick masonry with a reinforced-concrete frame
Main floor clad in pinkish-red granite
Classical, eclectic facades
funFacts: It was the tallest building in Latin America for a time, until the Kavanagh Building in Buenos Aires overtook it in 1935.
Martinelli had a replica Italian villa built on the roof as his family home, to show the public the building was safe.
It was completely remodelled by Mayor Olavo Setúbal from 1975 to 1979.

name: Catedral de São Pedro de Alcântara
aliases: Cathedral of Saint Peter of Alcantara

architects.name: Francisco Caminhoá
architects.bio: A Bahian engineer and architect commissioned in 1884 to design the cathedral. He conceived a Neo-Gothic building, very fashionable at the time, inspired by the old cathedrals of northern France.

architects.name: Heitor da Silva Costa
architects.bio: A Rio de Janeiro engineer who took command of the works in 1918, starting their second, intense phase. He is also the author of Christ the Redeemer.

photos.alt: Grey and sand-coloured Gothic church up a flight of steps, with a rose window over a pointed portal and a tall slender spire
photos.credit: Photo: Boaventuravinicius · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Shadowdancer · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Side wall of a Gothic stone church with a large traceried window, buttresses and pinnacles, and a tall spire rising behind.

photos.credit: Photo: Filipo tardim · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a town in forested green mountains, with a tall slender spire rising from a church beside a tree-lined canal.
Long nave with slender clustered columns, ribbed vaults and stained-glass windows around the altar
photos.credit: Photo: Wilfredor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It took 37 years to build, and its tower was added only in the 1960s.
It is the burial place of the last emperor of Brazil and his family.
A Gothic Revival church inspired by northern French cathedrals, in a mountain city that was the imperial family's summer retreat.

summary.description: The Neo-Gothic cathedral of Petrópolis was begun in 1884 and inaugurated on 29 November 1925, though the main facade and the 70-metre tower came only in the 1930s and 1960s. Inspired by the old cathedrals of northern France, it is a Latin-cross church with three naves and an ambulatory. It is the final resting place of Emperor Dom Pedro II.
keyFeatures: Neo-Gothic Latin-cross plan with three naves
Portal with multiple pointed archivolts and a rose window
Sculptures by Adam Bordignon on the facade
Tower 70 m tall with a chime of five bronze bells
funFacts: The Imperial Mausoleum, inaugurated in 1939, holds Emperor Pedro II and Empress Teresa Cristina; Princess Isabel and her husband were buried there in 1971.
The tower was built between 1960 and 1969.
The five bells were cast in Passau, Germany, and weigh nine tons.

name: Palácio Quitandinha

architects.name: Luis Fossati
architects.bio: Italian architect who designed the Quitandinha casino hotel for the entrepreneur Joaquim Rolla, giving it a Norman-French exterior over interiors mixing Brazilian Baroque and Art Deco.

style: Norman-French revival with Art Deco interiors

photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Sant'Anna Lisbôa · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Huge white half-timbered hotel with steep dark roofs across a still lake, with a small white lighthouse and a pergola at the shore.

photos.credit: Photo: Rogerio Santana · CC BY 2.0 br · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close corner of a white half-timbered building with dark gabled roofs, wooden balconies and arched openings below.
Huge white half-timbered hotel with steep dark roofs and gables, across a lawn and a lake, in front of a forested hill
photos.credit: Photo: Wilfredor · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Long hall with a chequered marble floor, a plaster shell above a curved doorway and a star-shaped chandelier in the distance
photos.credit: Photo: Cecioka · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as the largest casino hotel in Latin America, but gambling was outlawed in Brazil only two years after it opened.
In front of it lies an artificial lake shaped roughly like the country, built as a water source in case of fire.
A huge half-timbered palace in a mountain city, once the stay of film stars and the site of a 1947 inter-American treaty signed in the presence of Harry Truman.

summary.description: Built from 1941 for the entrepreneur Joaquim Rolla by the Italian architect Luis Fossati, the Palácio Quitandinha was the largest hotel casino in Latin America. Its exterior is in the Norman-French style, while the interior mixes Brazilian Baroque and Art Deco. Gambling was banned in 1946, the hotel closed in 1962 and its rooms were sold as private residences.
keyFeatures: Norman-French half-timbered exterior
Interiors mixing Brazilian Baroque and Art Deco
About 50,000 square metres, six floors, 440 rooms
Artificial lake loosely shaped like Brazil
funFacts: In 1947 it hosted the Rio Treaty, attended by US President Harry Truman.
Guests included Errol Flynn, Orson Welles, Greta Garbo, Carmen Miranda, Walt Disney and Eva Perón.
Since 2007 the public areas have been restored by SESC; a town in Paraná was named Quitandinha after it in 1961.

architects.name: Imhotep
architects.bio: Vizier to Pharaoh Djoser, Imhotep is credited by most Egyptologists with designing the pyramid complex, and a statue of him was found in it. He was later deified, and the Greeks identified him with Asclepios.

photos.alt: Six-tiered stepped pyramid of rough stone rising from a flat desert plain under a clear sky
photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Richard Mortel · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Closer view of a stepped stone pyramid of rough tiers, with two low arched doorways at its base under a blue sky with clouds.

photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall ancient stone wall with a recessed panelled facade and a narrow doorway, with a small group of visitors at its foot.
Narrow passage between ribbed stone columns attached to the wall, leading towards the light
photos.caption: A colonnaded entrance corridor.
photos.credit: Photo: Panegyrics of Granovetter · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built in the 27th century BC and is regarded as the first pyramid in Egypt, and the earliest colossal stone building there.
Its design is credited to a royal vizier who was later worshipped as a god of medicine and healing.
Instead of smooth sloping sides, it rises in six great tiers like a stack of ever smaller flat-topped tombs, in a necropolis near ancient Memphis.

summary.description: Built in the 27th century BC for the Third Dynasty pharaoh Djoser, this six-tier pyramid at Saqqara was the first pyramid in Egypt and the earliest colossal stone building there. It originally stood 62.5 metres tall and was clad in polished white limestone. It is the centrepiece of a vast mortuary complex with a colonnaded entrance, courts and ceremonial pavilions.
keyFeatures: Six tiers, originally 62.5 m high
Base of about 109 m by 121 m
Polished white limestone casing
Underground galleries totalling nearly 6 km
Colonnaded entrance and Sed festival courts
funFacts: Beneath it a labyrinth of tunnels and galleries reaches a central shaft 28 m deep, and some walls are inlaid with blue faience tiles that imitate reed matting.
After a 14-year restoration, it reopened to visitors in March 2020.

architects.name: Senenmut
architects.bio: Overseer of Works under Queen Hatshepsut and one of her most trusted officials. He is traditionally thought to have been responsible for the design of her terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari.

photos.credit: Photo: MusikAnimal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long terraced temple with pillared porticoes and a central ramp, backed by a tall pink desert cliff, with visitors walking toward it.
Long terraced temple of pillared porticoes with a central ramp, set against a high desert cliff
photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Row of tall mummiform statues standing before square pillars at the top of a short stair on a pillared terrace.
Pale terraced temple seen from the cliffs above, tucked into a curved wall of rock
photos.caption: The temple tucked into the cliffs.
photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a woman who ruled as pharaoh, and after her death her images and name were hacked away from its walls.
Its three broad terraces, linked by long ramps and fronted by pillared porticoes, rise straight from the desert floor into a limestone cliff opposite Luxor.
Reliefs on its walls record a famous trading expedition to the Land of Punt and the divine birth of its builder.

summary.description: Built for the Eighteenth Dynasty pharaoh Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, opposite Luxor, this mortuary temple is considered a masterpiece of ancient architecture. Three massive terraces rise from the desert floor into the cliffs, and its design owes much to the nearby temple of Mentuhotep II, built six centuries earlier. It was constructed between Hatshepsut's seventh and twentieth regnal years.
keyFeatures: Three colonnaded terraces joined by ramps
Reliefs of the expedition to the Land of Punt
Reliefs of the divine birth of Hatshepsut
Shrines to Hathor and Anubis on the middle terrace
Sanctuary of Amun-Re on the central axis
funFacts: Two decades after her death, under Thutmose III, references to her rule were erased, usurped or obliterated.
Its ancient name was Djeser-Djeseru, meaning Holy of Holies.
A Coptic monastery of Saint Phoibammon was built there between the 6th and 8th centuries AD.

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: Luxor Temple grew over centuries under Amenhotep III, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II and later rulers including Alexander. The names of its master builders are not recorded.

photos.credit: Photo: Ad Meskens · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Massive sandstone gateway towers with sloping walls flank an entrance, with a tall obelisk and colossal seated statues before it.
Huge sandstone gateway wall beside a single tall obelisk and seated colossal statues at its foot
photos.credit: Photo: Gary Todd · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Row of huge papyrus-bundle columns holding a stone beam, on a ruined stone platform in warm late light.
Floodlit court ringed by tall columns with flaring papyrus-bud capitals against a night sky
photos.caption: A colonnaded court lit at night.
photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built around 1400 BC on the east bank of the Nile and, unlike its neighbours, is not dedicated to a god or a dead king but to the renewal of kingship.
It was linked to a great sister temple about three kilometres away by an avenue of sphinxes, and a festival each year carried a god's statue between them.
A mosque still stands on top of its ancient columns, and its twin obelisk now stands in the Place de la Concorde in Paris.

summary.description: Constructed around 1400 BC on the east bank of the Nile at ancient Thebes, Luxor Temple is dedicated to the rejuvenation of kingship, and may have been where pharaohs were crowned. Chapels at the rear were built by Amenhotep III and Alexander, and other parts by Tutankhamun and Ramesses II. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979.
keyFeatures: Entrance pylon with colossal statues of Ramesses II
Obelisk (its twin is in Paris)
Colonnade and court of Amenhotep III
Avenue linking it to Karnak
Active mosque built among the ancient columns
funFacts: The two obelisks at the entrance were not the same height, but were set so as to create the illusion that they were.
In Roman times the temple and its surroundings were a legionary fortress and the seat of the local government.
The annual Opet Festival carried the cult statue of Amun from Karnak to stay at the temple with his consort Mut.

name: Philae Temple Complex

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: The island sanctuary of Isis grew from the 4th century BC under Nectanebo I and the Ptolemies, with Roman additions. Its builders are not recorded.

style: Late Period and Ptolemaic temple complex

photos.credit: Photo: Warren LeMay from Cullowhee, NC, United States · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Two sloping gateway towers carved with figures of a king, with a dark doorway between them and visitors at the foot.

photos.credit: Photo: Warren LeMay from Cullowhee, NC, United States · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Open colonnade of slender columns with flower-shaped capitals along a sunlit stone courtyard, beside a tall carved tower wall.
Pair of tall sloping gateway towers carved with figures, with lower temple buildings stepping away behind
photos.credit: Photo: Marc Ryckaert · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Open court lined with columns carved with reliefs and flower-shaped capitals, in strong sunlight
photos.caption: A colonnaded outer court.
photos.credit: Photo: Jorge Láscar · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was once an island sanctuary in the first cataract of the Nile, famed as the Pearl of the Nile.
Flooding after a dam of 1902 left it half underwater for much of the year, and in the 1970s it was taken apart stone by stone.
UNESCO's rescue moved about ninety-five structures to a levelled islet 12.4 metres higher, and it is the main temple of the goddess Isis.

summary.description: This island temple complex near the First Cataract grew around a sanctuary of the goddess Isis, with surviving early elements from Nectanebo I (380 to 362 BC) and most buildings from the Ptolemaic period. After the Aswan dams threatened it with flooding, it was dismantled and rebuilt on nearby Agilkia Island between 1977 and 1980.
keyFeatures: Temple of Isis with a monumental first pylon
Outer court with colonnades
Kiosk of Nectanebo I
Ninety-five structures moved to higher ground
Reliefs studied by the Philae Temple Text Project
funFacts: The rescue raised the monuments 12.40 metres above their original level by levelling the islet of Agilkia.
The French writer Pierre Loti described it in La Mort de Philae in 1909.
The Italian architect Giovanni Joppolo supervised the work for the Italian consortium.

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: The temple was built under the Ptolemies on the site of an older shrine, following the traditional temple plan, which Egyptian tradition credited to the gods Thoth and Seshat. Its builders are not recorded.

photos.credit: Photo: Patrick.reb · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Two huge flat-topped gateway towers with carved giant figures and a central doorway under a clear blue sky, seen across a paved forecourt.

photos.credit: Photo: Rémih · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking out from a columned courtyard through a central doorway in a tall carved gateway wall into the bright light.
Looking up at huge columns covered in hieroglyphs, topped by capitals shaped like palm and papyrus plants
photos.caption: Columns of the hypostyle hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Warren LeMay · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: timsdad · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Dim green-lit sanctuary with a tall stone shrine and a carved falcon figure in front of it.

hints.text: It is among the best preserved shrines in Egypt, partly because it lay buried under about twelve metres of sand and silt for centuries.
It was built under Greek-speaking kings of Egypt between 237 and 57 BC, yet it follows the old pharaonic plan.
It is the largest temple of the falcon-headed god Horus, and each year the goddess Hathor travelled to it from Dendera for a sacred marriage festival.

summary.description: Begun on 23 August 237 BC under Ptolemy III and completed in 57 BC under Ptolemy XII, the Temple of Edfu is one of the best preserved shrines in Egypt. It is the largest temple dedicated to Horus. Its walls carry inscriptions on language, myth and religion, including the building texts and the Sacred Drama of the conflict between Horus and Seth.
keyFeatures: Giant pylon at the entrance
Pillared hypostyle hall
Barque sanctuary surrounded by nine chapels
Naos of Nectanebo II in the inner sanctuary
Building texts and creation myth on the walls
funFacts: It was buried to a depth of 12 metres until Auguste Mariette began freeing it from the sand in 1860.
Only the tops of its pylons were visible when a French expedition identified it in 1798.
It was the model for the Temple Works in Holbeck, Leeds, whose frontage copies the courtyard columns.

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: Built for the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khafre beside his father's Great Pyramid, it was the work of royal architects and large labour gangs whose names are not recorded.

photos.alt: Steep pyramid of rough stone blocks, with a smooth pale cap near the top, rising above scattered stones
photos.credit: Photo: MusikAnimal · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Daaaveee · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of a steep stone pyramid with a smooth pale casing at the top, rising above a low wall of large blocks.

photos.credit: Photo: M1chu · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Pyramid with a pale cap on a rocky plateau, with a reclining human-headed lion statue and quarried ground in front.
Large pyramid with a pale casing at the apex on a rocky rise, with visitors in the foreground and another pyramid behind
photos.caption: The second of the Giza pyramids.
photos.credit: Photo: Jerome Bon · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the second tallest of a famous group of three pyramids on a desert plateau, yet it looks the tallest because it stands on higher ground.
It is the only one of the three that still keeps part of its original smooth casing, at the very top.
It stands beside a monumental sphinx and was built for the son of the builder of the Great Pyramid.

summary.description: The middle of the three pyramids of Giza, this tomb of the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khafre, who ruled c. 2558 to 2532 BC, has a base of 215.5 metres and rises to 136.4 metres. It is the only one of the three that still has cladding at the top. It looks taller than its neighbour because it sits on bedrock 10 metres higher.
keyFeatures: Base length of 215.5 m, height of 136.4 m
Slope of 53°08', steeper than the Great Pyramid
Casing stones of Tura limestone still near the top
Bottom course of pink granite casing
Burial chamber cut into the bedrock
funFacts: Giovanni Belzoni found its original entrance on 2 March 1818, but the burial chamber held only an empty sarcophagus.
In the 1960s Luis Alvarez used cosmic-ray muon scanning to look for hidden chambers and found none.
It was opened in 1372, according to the Arab historian Ibn Abd al-Salam.

name: Ramesseum
aliases: Temple of Ramesses II at Thebes

architects.name: Unknown royal builders
architects.bio: The memorial temple of Ramesses II follows the standard canons of New Kingdom temple architecture. The royal builders are not named here.

photos.credit: Photo: Marc Ryckaert · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Temple portico of square pillars each fronted by a standing mummiform statue, with a ruined stone wall at the left under blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Tim Adams · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Pillars with standing statues beside a huge broken statue lying in pieces on the ground, in bright sunlight.

photos.credit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of two ruined temple colonnades among green fields and palm groves at the edge of a desert, with a road beyond.
Looking up at thick columns with flaring papyrus-bud capitals under a carved stone ceiling
photos.caption: Columns of the hypostyle hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Steve F-E-Cameron · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the second largest temple in Egypt, occupying about ten hectares on the west bank, across the Nile from Luxor.
It was built as a memorial temple, a house of millions of years, for a long-reigning pharaoh, with scenes of his battle against the Hittites on its pylon.
A giant fallen statue here, once about a thousand tonnes of stone, is linked to a famous Romantic sonnet about a ruined king.

summary.description: The memorial temple of Ramesses II lies in the Theban Necropolis on the west bank of the Nile, opposite Luxor. At about ten hectares it is the second largest temple in Egypt. Scenes of the pharaoh's triumph over the Hittites at Kadesh decorate its pylon, and its walls repeat the rout of the Hittites.
keyFeatures: Second largest temple in Egypt, about 10 hectares
Pylon with scenes of the Battle of Kadesh
Hypostyle hall with papyrus-bud columns
Fallen colossus of Ramesses II
Surrounding storerooms, granaries and workshops
funFacts: Its fallen syenite colossus was estimated to weigh 1,000 tonnes and to stand 16 to 19 metres tall.
The poet Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Ozymandias, whose name derives from the pharaoh's throne name, against the excitement of a statue arriving in Britain.
Papyri found here show it was home to an important scribal school in the Third Intermediate Period.

architects.name: Unknown Maya builders
architects.bio: The temple was raised by the Classic Maya of Tikal as a funerary monument for their king. No individual architect is recorded; its construction is credited to the king's son and heir, Yik'in Chan K'awiil, and the city's builders.

photos.credit: Photo: Raymond Ostertag · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Front view of a tall stepped pyramid with a central stair and a small shrine with a roof comb on top, among green trees.
Steep stepped limestone pyramid with a small shrine and tall roof comb on top, rising above a grass plaza
photos.credit: Photo: Kaldari · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo:  · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Steep stepped pyramid seen across a green plaza, with weathered stone terraces and thatched shelters in the foreground.
Steep, narrow stepped pyramid with a tall roof comb seen from below through trees
photos.caption: Seen from the side, the pyramid rises steeply to its shrine.
photos.credit: Photo: Simon Burchell · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

summary.description: Built around AD 732 over the tomb of the king Jasaw Chan K'awiil, this nine-level limestone pyramid rises 55 metres above the Great Plaza of Tikal. A steep stair leads to a three-chamber shrine crowned by a tall roof comb.
keyFeatures: Nine stepped levels, perhaps symbolising the nine levels of the underworld
55 metres high above the Great Plaza
Summit shrine with three corbel-vaulted chambers
Roof comb once carved with a seated king
funFacts: The tomb was built first, and the temple was raised over it.
The shrine's carved sapodilla-wood lintels gave it the name Temple of the Great Jaguar; two were taken to the British Museum in the 19th century.
Putting it on the east side of the Great Plaza broke with the tradition of placing royal funerary temples north of the plaza.

hints.text: A funerary pyramid of nine stepped levels, rising about 55 metres above the main plaza of a great Maya city in a Guatemalan rainforest.
A steep staircase climbs it to a shrine of three narrow chambers under a tall roof comb, carved with a seated king.
Its nickname comes from a carved wooden lintel showing a king on a jaguar throne; the king buried beneath it ruled from AD 682 to 734.

architects.name: Unknown Palenque Maya builders
architects.bio: The pyramid was begun by K'inich Janaab' Pakal, ruler of Palenque, as his funerary monument and finished by his son and successor, K'inich Kan Bahlam II. No individual architect is recorded; the work is credited to the Maya builders and craftsmen of Palenque.

photos.alt: Wide stairway climbing eight stepped terraces to a long temple with five doorways, in front of dense forest
photos.credit: Photo: Bernard DUPONT · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Stepped stone pyramid with a small temple on top, seen across a wide lawn with visitors and a backdrop of forested hills.

photos.credit: Photo: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of the upper temple with five rectangular doorways under a sloping roof topped by a decorated crest, above stone steps.
Dark stone terraces rising to a pale temple with a row of square doorways under a flat roof
photos.credit: Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

summary.description: Begun by the king K'inich Janaab' Pakal and finished shortly after AD 683 by his son, this is the largest stepped pyramid at Palenque. A temple with five doorways sits on eight terraces, and a hidden stair inside leads to the king's tomb.
keyFeatures: Eight stepped terraces under a temple, nine levels in all
Five entrances framed by piers with stucco reliefs
Hieroglyphic tablets that gave it its name
A stairway inside leading to the crypt of Pakal
funFacts: Its Classic Maya name means 'House of the Nine Sharpened Spears'.
Although the site had been studied for over 200 years, Pakal's tomb was not found until 1952, when Alberto Ruz Lhuillier lifted a floor slab.
The stairway to the tomb was filled with rubble and took two years to clear.

hints.text: A pyramid of eight stepped terraces carries a long temple with five doorways, in a Maya city of the Chiapas jungle.
In 1952 an archaeologist lifted a floor slab inside and found a stairway choked with rubble that led down to a royal tomb.
It is named for the long glyph texts on its tablets, and holds the sarcophagus of the king Pakal, who ruled for almost 70 years.

name: Monte Albán

architects.name: Unknown Zapotec builders
architects.bio: The city was built over about a thousand years by the Zapotecs, who levelled a mountain ridge to make its monumental core. No individual architect is recorded; the work is credited to Zapotec rulers and builders.

style: Zapotec ceremonial city on an artificial ridge

photos.alt: Vast open plaza of pale dust with a low stepped platform at its centre and terraced mounds on the far side, under a blue sky
photos.credit: Photo: Nosferattus · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: nsaum75 !Dígame¡‎ · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Stepped stone platform with a flat top rising above a dry golden plain, with scattered trees and a blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Uspn · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Broad ancient stone staircase rising to a flat platform edge, with grassy slopes on both sides.

photos.credit: Photo: Anagoria · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Massive sloping wall of rough-fitted stone blocks of an ancient platform, with carved slabs at its foot under a blue sky.
Row of upright carved stone slabs set against a wall of rubble masonry on a grassy slope
photos.credit: Photo: MAHC-oaxaca · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

summary.description: Founded around 500 BC on a levelled ridge about 400 metres above the Valley of Oaxaca, this was the pre-eminent Zapotec capital for nearly a thousand years. The great plaza is ringed by platforms, temples and ball court, much of it reconstructed in the 1930s and 1940s.
keyFeatures: Monumental core on an artificially levelled ridge at 1,940 m
Several hundred artificial terraces across the ridgeline
Founded c. 500 BC as one of Mesoamerica's earliest cities
Large-scale excavation led by Alfonso Caso from 1931
funFacts: The ancient Zapotec name of the city is not known.
The city lost its political pre-eminence by the end of the Late Classic and was largely abandoned soon after.
Oaxaca City lies about 9 km to the east.

hints.text: A civic-ceremonial centre on an artificially levelled mountain ridge, rising about 400 metres above a valley floor.
Founded around 500 BC, it was the capital of a people who dominated the southern Mexican highlands for almost a thousand years.
Its builders were the Zapotecs, and it overlooks the valley of Oaxaca; its ancient name is unknown.

architects.name: Unknown Tiwanaku builders
architects.bio: The monolith was carved by the Tiwanaku culture, an Andean civilization that thrived around Lake Titicaca. No individual sculptor is recorded; the gate is credited to the Tiwanaku stoneworkers.

photos.alt: Single grey stone doorway with a carved frieze of rows of small figures running toward a central figure above the opening
photos.credit: Photo: Sasha India · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Doorway cut from one block of stone standing on a flat reddish ground with distant hills and low buildings behind
photos.credit: Photo: CivArmy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Rear of a monolithic stone gateway with recessed niches and rectangular openings, with visitors standing beside it on a high plain.

photos.credit: Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of a carved stone lintel with a central frontal figure holding staffs, surrounded by rows of winged attendants.

summary.description: Carved from a single block of stone by the Tiwanaku culture, this monolithic gateway is about 3 m tall and 4 m wide. A frieze above the opening shows a central figure surrounded by dozens of running attendants.
keyFeatures: Monolith of about 10 tons cut from one stone
Central figure in the Staff God pose with 24 rays around its head
48 running attendants, human and bird-headed
At about 3,825 m above sea level near Lake Titicaca
funFacts: When rediscovered by European explorers in the mid-19th century it lay horizontally with a large crack through it.
It is believed that the gate no longer stands in its original place, which remains uncertain.
Its carvings are thought to have astronomical or calendrical meaning.

hints.text: A doorway cut from a single block of stone, about 3 metres tall and 4 metres wide, with a frieze of running attendants above it.
At the centre of the frieze a figure with 24 rays around its head holds a spear-thrower; it was found lying flat and cracked in the 19th century.
It stands among the ruins of an Andean culture near Lake Titicaca, some 3,800 metres above sea level in Bolivia.

architects.name: Unknown Copán Maya builders
architects.bio: The stairway was first built by the Copán king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil in AD 710 and doubled in length in AD 755 by K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil. No individual architect is recorded; the work is credited to the Maya builders and scribes of Copán.

photos.alt: Steep stairway of narrow steps under a canvas awning, with a tall carved stone figure standing in front of it
photos.credit: Photo: Peter Andersen · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Luis Alfredo Romero · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view up a very steep flight of narrow weathered stone steps with carved blocks at the foot and a sliver of sky above.
Close view of a stone step carved with rounded, face-like glyph blocks
photos.caption: Glyph blocks carved on the risers of the steps.
photos.credit: Photo: Hans Birger Nilsen · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

summary.description: Climbing the west side of Structure 10L-26, this staircase is 10 m wide and has 62 steps, first built in AD 710 and doubled in length in AD 755. About 2,200 glyphs on its steps form the longest known Maya hieroglyphic text.
keyFeatures: 62 steps, 10 m wide and 21 m long
About 2,200 glyphs, the longest known Maya text
Life-size seated rulers on every twelfth step
Stela M with its altar at the base
funFacts: The text is still being reconstructed, scrambled when the temple's facade collapsed.
Stela M at its foot bears a portrait of K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil and was raised in AD 756.
Copán was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.

hints.text: A wide staircase of 62 steps climbs the west side of a temple platform in a Maya city.
A large seated figure, thought to be a ruler, sits in the centre of every twelfth step.
Its risers carry about 2,200 glyphs, the longest known text in the Maya script, in the ruins of a Honduran valley near the Guatemalan border.

architects.name: Unknown Inca builders
architects.bio: The citadel was built under the Sapa Inca Pachacuti and continued by his successors Topa Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac. No individual architect is recorded; the work is credited to the Inca masons and the labourers levied from the provinces.

photos.alt: Three tiers of massive fitted stone walls rising above a lawn, with huge blocks in the lowest course
photos.credit: Photo: Esoltas · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: W. Bulach · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Visitors standing before a towering wall of huge irregular boulders fitted tightly together, with a dirt path and grass in front.

photos.credit: Photo: The original uploader was Ljuba brank at Slovenian Wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Stepped terraces of giant polygonal stone blocks with a smaller fieldstone wall set between them, and two people at the top.
Enormous irregular boulders fitted together in a long wall on a dry grassy slope under big clouds
photos.credit: Photo: Lars Falkdalen Lindahl · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

summary.description: On a hill above Cusco, the capital of the Inca, this citadel was built from the 15th century under Pachacuti and his successors. Three huge dry stone terrace walls use some of the largest stones in pre-Hispanic America, fitted without mortar.
keyFeatures: Three massive terrace walls of interlocking stones
No mortar, with rounded corners and walls leaning inward
Stones among the largest in pre-Hispanic America
At 3,701 m above sea level
funFacts: The chronicler Cieza de León reported 20,000 men levied from the provinces, with 4,000 quarrying and 6,000 hauling stone.
After the siege of Cusco, the Spaniards took much of the stone to build the colonial city; mostly the blocks too big to move remain.
Cusco and Sacsayhuamán were listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

hints.text: A citadel of three massive terrace walls on a steep hill on the outskirts of an empire's capital, in the Andes at about 3,700 metres.
Its dry stone walls use huge blocks cut to fit so closely that, in many joints, a sheet of paper will not go between them, with no mortar.
Spaniards pulled down much of it to build their colonial city, and the Inca festival Inti Raymi is held near it every 24 June, above Cusco.

name: Pyramid of the Magician, Uxmal

architects.name: Unknown Puuc Maya builders
architects.bio: The pyramid was built and enlarged by the Maya of Uxmal over some four centuries, from about the 6th century AD. No individual architect is recorded; the work is credited to the Puuc Maya builders of the city.

style: Puuc and Chenes Maya step pyramid

photos.credit: Photo: Anagoria · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall steep-sided oval pyramid of fitted stone blocks with a temple on top and a stepped ruin at its foot, under bright clouds.
Rounded stepped pyramid with temples on its upper terraces behind a long low building with a row of columns
photos.credit: Photo: Rob Young · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: tato grasso · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Smooth curved flank of a large stone pyramid rising to a small temple on top, with green lawn and blue sky around.

summary.description: Rising about 35 metres at the centre of the Maya city of Uxmal, this rounded step pyramid grew over about 400 years from the 6th century. Five temples are stacked within it, and masks of the rain god Chaac cover its upper temple.
keyFeatures: About 35 m high, base about 69 by 49 m
Five temples built one over another
Puuc lower levels with Chenes-style upper temples
Masks of the rain god Chaac on the western stair and Temple IV
funFacts: Its western stairway is placed to face the setting sun at the summer solstice.
Reported heights range from 27.6 to 40 metres.
Hurricane Gilbert damaged the pyramid in 1988, and the west facade needed conservation.

hints.text: A steep, rounded pyramid about 35 metres high, built in five stages with a temple set over the earlier ones.
Hook-nosed masks of the rain god line its western stair, and the city's name means 'thrice-built'.
It is the tallest and best-known structure of a UNESCO-listed Maya city in the Puuc hills of the Yucatán Peninsula.

architects.name: Unknown builders
architects.bio: The names of the carpenters are unknown. A legend says the master builder used a single axe for the whole church and threw it into the lake when he finished, saying there would never be another to match it. The work follows the carpentry traditions of the Russian North.

photos.alt: Dark wooden church crowned by a cluster of onion domes of many sizes, beside a tall bell tower with a tent roof
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Two wooden churches and a bell tower on a grassy shore of a lake, one church wrapped in scaffolding
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands on a small island in a huge northern lake, and its builders used no nails apart from the domes and roof shingles.
Its altar was laid in 1714 on the site of an earlier church struck by lightning, and a legend says its builder threw his only axe into the lake afterwards.
It is a wooden church with 22 onion domes, one of the tallest wooden buildings in Northern Europe, in the Republic of Karelia.

summary.description: On Kizhi Island in Lake Onega, the Church of the Transfiguration rises 37 metres in 22 domes of different sizes, all in wood. Its altar was laid on 6 June 1714, on the site of an older church burnt by lightning, and it forms with a second church and a bell tower the Kizhi Pogost, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990.
keyFeatures: 22 domes covered in aspen shingles
Octagonal log frame with four two-stage side attachments
37 metres high, built without nails apart from domes and roof shingles
Four-tier iconostasis with 102 icons
funFacts: About 180,000 nails hold its 60,000 roof shingles, but the log structure itself uses none.
A legend says the master builder used one axe for the whole church and threw it into the lake when he finished.
It is a summer church: it is not heated and holds no winter services.

architects.name: Aristotele Fioravanti
architects.bio: Born in Bologna into a family of architects and hydraulic engineers, Fioravanti worked in Florence, Milan and Hungary before Ivan III invited him to Moscow in 1475. He built the Dormition Cathedral after studying the Russian church of the same name in Vladimir, mixing Renaissance ideas with Russian tradition.

photos.alt: Large white stone church with five golden domes on a paved square, beside a lower palace with silver domes
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Three golden domes on white drums with narrow windows above arched gables of pale stone
photos.credit: Photo: Jorge Láscar · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: An earlier cathedral on this site was nearly finished when an earthquake brought it down in 1474.
The Russian tsars were crowned here from Ivan the Terrible in 1547 until the last coronation in 1896, and it is the burial place of the Moscow Metropolitans and Patriarchs.
An Italian engineer from Bologna designed it in the spirit of the older cathedral at Vladimir, and it stands on the square inside the Moscow Kremlin.

summary.description: After an earthquake wrecked the first attempt in 1474, Ivan III summoned the Bolognese architect Aristotele Fioravanti, who built this five-domed cathedral between 1475 and 1479, taking the older Dormition Cathedral in Vladimir as his model. It was the mother church of Muscovite Russia and the setting of the coronations of the tsars.
keyFeatures: Five domes, symbolising Christ and the Four Evangelists
White stone walls with arched gables
Light, spacious interior combining Renaissance ideas with Russian tradition
Frescoes and the icons of the Theotokos of Vladimir and Blachernitissa
funFacts: Its five-domed design became a template for numerous churches across Russia.
Ivan the Terrible was crowned here in 1547 as the first Russian tsar.
Under the French occupation it was looted and used as a horse stable.

name: Church of the Intercession on the Nerl
aliases: Church of the Protection of the Virgin on the Nerl

architects.name: Unknown builders
architects.bio: The master builders are unknown. They were probably craftsmen brought from western Russia by Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky, who founded the Vladimir-Suzdal school of white-stone architecture during his reign.

photos.alt: Slim white stone church with a single dark onion dome on a grassy mound above a river
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: White carved church with a dark dome seen through green trees over a still pond
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: A prince commissioned it to mark a victory over the Volga Bulgars and to remember his son who died in the campaign.
It was built in a single season in the 1160s, and its elongated proportions make it look slimmer than it really is.
It stands where two rivers meet near Vladimir, and in spring floods it seemed to float on the water.

summary.description: Andrei Bogolyubsky, grand prince of Vladimir, commissioned this small church in 1165 where the Nerl joins the Klyazma, in memory of his son Izyaslav. It is one of the oldest and best-preserved single-domed churches in Russia and a symbol of the Vladimir-Suzdal school.
keyFeatures: Single dome carried on four interior columns
White limestone walls covered in 12th-century relief carvings
Elongated proportions that make the outline slimmer
Site on a river confluence that floods in spring
funFacts: According to a 1702 source, it was built in one season.
The galleries added in the 12th century were rebuilt in the 18th century and later demolished.
It was meant as the forward gate of the prince's residence at Bogolyubovo.

architects.name: Unknown builders
architects.bio: The builders are unknown. Artisans from many places, from the earlier Bogolyubovo churches to Balkan and Armenian traditions, shaped the building and its carvings for Grand Prince Vsevolod the Big Nest.

drawings.label: Floor plan
drawings.alt: Old printed plan of a nearly square church with an apse of three bays, four interior piers and an octagonal outline of walls around it
drawings.credit: Unknown author, old print · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Cubic white stone church with arched gables, carved upper walls and a small drum with a gilded dome
photos.credit: Photo: Alex Zelenko · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Wall of white stone covered in relief carvings of seated figures, birds, beasts and plants between slender columns
photos.credit: Photo: Tsvetkova · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built as the private church of a grand prince, originally linked to his palace, which no longer exists.
Its white limestone walls carry relief carvings of saints, beasts and plants, with King David, Alexander the Great and Hercules among the figures.
It was finished in 1197 in Vladimir, and it is one of the White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal on the UNESCO list.

summary.description: Built between 1193 and 1197 for Grand Prince Vsevolod III of Vladimir-Suzdal, the cathedral is a compact cube of local white limestone with four interior columns holding up the drum. Its upper walls are covered in shallow reliefs of saints, animals and plants.
keyFeatures: Cubic white limestone body with three bays and zakomara gables
Horizontal arcade frieze at mid-height
Reliefs of animals, plants and figures across the upper walls and drum
Deeply recessed, richly carved windows and doors
funFacts: It was the prince's own church, connected directly to his palace.
The reliefs show King David, Solomon, Alexander the Great and Hercules among other figures.
The most extensive renovation in 1832 moved some exterior blocks and replaced others with new carvings.

architects.name: Unknown builders
architects.bio: The builders are unknown. The cathedral was commissioned by Vladimir of Novgorod and Bishop Luka Zhidiata, and built between 1045 and 1050 to replace an oak cathedral of the late tenth century.

photos.alt: Whitewashed church with thick walls, low rounded apses and five helmet-shaped domes of grey and green metal in evening light
photos.credit: Photo: A.Savin · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: View from a high gallery down a painted nave to a tall wooden iconostasis, with a large iron chandelier hanging on chains
photos.credit: Photo: Дар Ветер · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It replaced an oak cathedral and is the oldest church building in Russia outside the Caucasus still standing.
Its name means Holy Wisdom, in imitation of the great cathedral of Constantinople, and its helmet-shaped domes date from the 1150s.
Novgorodians said that where it stands, there is their city, and it rises within the Kremlin of Veliky Novgorod.

summary.description: Built between 1045 and 1050 and consecrated in 1050 or 1052, this 38-metre, five-domed stone cathedral is the oldest church building in Russia outside the Caucasus. It was the spiritual centre of the Novgorod Republic and came to symbolise the city itself.
keyFeatures: Five helmet-shaped domes, a sixth over the stair tower
Thick whitewashed stone walls
Dedication to the Holy Wisdom of God, after Hagia Sophia
Frescoes mostly from the 1890s
funFacts: Chronicles record Novgorodians being ready 'to lay down their heads for Holy Wisdom'.
The main golden dome was gilded by Archbishop Ioann in 1408.
In 1859 its gallery library of more than 1,500 volumes was moved to the St Petersburg Spiritual Academy.

name: Trinity Cathedral, Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius
aliases: Old Katholikon of the Trinity Lavra

architects.name: Unknown builders
architects.bio: The masters are unknown. The stone cathedral was built in 1422–1423 under the abbot Nikon of Radonezh to honour the monastery's founder, Saint Sergius of Radonezh, in white stone in the early Muscovite manner.

photos.alt: White stone church with a single gilded dome on a tall drum, rounded apses and gilded roof edges
photos.credit: Photo: Mike1979 Russia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Gilded and white domes of a monastery church beside blue domes starred in gold
photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is the oldest surviving building of a monastery founded by one of Russia's most venerated saints.
It was built in 1422 and 1423 to house the relics of that saint, and its walls were painted by two famous icon painters, whose frescoes are lost.
Its five-tier iconostasis holds the famous icon of the Trinity, painted by Andrei Rublev, in the town of Sergiyev Posad near Moscow.

summary.description: The oldest surviving building of the Trinity Lavra, the cathedral was raised in white stone in 1422–1423 under the abbot Nikon to honour Saint Sergius of Radonezh, whose relics lie inside. It is one of the key examples of early Muscovite architecture.
keyFeatures: White stone walls under a single gilded dome
Five-tier iconostasis, mostly from the early 15th century
Frescoes of 1635 reproducing the lost originals
Relics of Saint Sergius of Radonezh
funFacts: The wall paintings by Andrei Rublev and Daniel Chorny of 1425–1427 are lost.
The iconostasis holds both Rublev's original icon of the Trinity and a copy commissioned by Boris Godunov.
The history of the whole lavra begins with the construction of this cathedral.

architects.name: Unknown builders
architects.bio: The designer is unknown. The church, built in 1532 for Grand Prince Vasily III, translated the tent roofs of northern Russian wooden churches into white stone and so broke with the Byzantine tradition.

photos.alt: Tall white church rising from a ground floor with open stair galleries to an octagonal tower and a slender pointed tent roof
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ludvig14 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close view of a tall white tent-roofed church on a grassy hill, with covered galleries and stairs around its base.

photos.credit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: White tent-roofed church seen across a lawn under a stormy sky, with a white gate tower and trees beside it.
Wall of icons in several tiers with a golden central gate, set against whitewashed walls
photos.caption: The interior is small and tall, with a tiered icon wall.
photos.credit: Photo: A.Savin · Free Art License · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built to give thanks for the long-awaited birth of an heir to the throne, the future Ivan the Terrible.
It was the first stone church of its kind, copying a form of northern Russian wooden churches and breaking with Byzantine tradition.
A tall tent roof tops this white church on a hill above the Moskva River, now inside the city of Moscow, and UNESCO listed it in 1994.

summary.description: Built in 1532 on the Kolomenskoye estate to celebrate the birth of a long-awaited heir, the future Ivan the Terrible, this white stone church was the first of the tent-roofed type in stone. Its octagonal tent springs from an octagonal body above a cross-shaped ground floor.
keyFeatures: Octagonal stone tent roof with a small dome on top
Three tiers of kokoshniks
Arrow-shaped window frames and narrow pilasters
Open galleries and stair arcades around the ground floor
funFacts: Its tall form is thought to come from the hipped-roof wooden churches of the Russian North.
It is sometimes called the White Column.
UNESCO inscribed it on the World Heritage List in 1994.

architects.name: Unknown masters (Peter Potapov attributed)
architects.bio: The oldest church, the Smolensky Cathedral, dates from the 1520s to 1560s. Most of the walls, towers and gate churches date from the 1680s, when the convent was renovated for the regent Sofia Alexeyevna in the Muscovite Baroque style, supposedly by a certain Peter Potapov.

photos.credit: Photo: Елена Нечипоренко · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Walled cloister with red and white towers and golden domes reflected in a still pond at sunset, trees along the bank.

photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long white crenellated wall and ornate red and white towers beyond a green pond, with a golden-domed church behind.
White crenellated wall with a corner tower of red and white, and a red gate church with golden domes behind
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Cloister seen over trees: a tall tiered bell tower, a cathedral with silver and gold domes, and a red gate church
photos.credit: Photo: Ivtorov · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was founded in 1524 to give thanks for the capture of a fortress city, and it is the best-known cloister of its capital.
Its blood-red walls and crown-like towers date from the 1680s, when a regent who was later imprisoned here had the convent renovated.
Its name means 'new', to tell it from an older nunnery inside the Kremlin, and its six-tier bell tower stands 72 metres tall.

summary.description: Founded in 1524 by Vasily III after the capture of Smolensk, the convent is probably the best-known cloister of Moscow and has stayed almost intact since the 17th century. Behind a masonry wall with 12 towers stand the old Smolensky Cathedral and the Muscovite Baroque gate churches, refectory and 72-metre bell tower.
keyFeatures: Wall with 12 towers, in white and red
Six-pillared, five-domed Smolensky Cathedral
Two lofty over-the-gate churches
Six-tier bell tower, 72 metres high
funFacts: Its name was chosen to distinguish it from the Old Maidens' Monastery inside the Kremlin.
The regent Sofia Alexeyevna, who paid for the renovation, was later locked up here.
UNESCO proclaimed it a World Heritage Site in 2004.

architects.name: Unknown builders
architects.bio: The monastery grew over centuries from its foundation in 1436 by the monk Zosima. Its most important structures date from the 16th century, under the hegumen Filip Kolychev, and were raised by monks and local craftsmen.

photos.credit: Photo: Александр Байдуков · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Massive boulder wall with round towers and dark onion domes rising behind it, mirrored in still water under a cloudy sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Trasprd · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a walled monastery with corner towers and white churches beside a lake and green grass on a flat island.
Massive boulder wall with towers and white church domes behind it, seen across a quiet harbour
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stone obelisk and small white chapels in the foreground with a fortress tower and domes fading into morning fog
photos.credit: Photo: Александр Байдуков · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was one of the largest Christian citadels of northern Russia, and it repelled attacks by the Livonian Order and the Swedes.
In the 20th century the Soviets turned it into a prison camp, a prototype for the Gulag system.
It stands on islands in the White Sea, a fortified monastery founded in 1436 by the monk Zosima.

summary.description: Founded in 1436 by the monk Zosima on islands in the White Sea, the Solovetsky Monastery became one of the largest Christian citadels in northern Russia, with an economic and political reach across the region. Its most important buildings date from the 16th century.
keyFeatures: Fortified monastery on an island in the White Sea
Walls and towers that withstood sieges
Most important buildings date from the 16th century
Extensive reconstruction ongoing after Soviet use
funFacts: In 1854, three British ships shelled it for nine hours during the Crimean War and left with nothing.
From 1926 to 1939 it was a Soviet prison camp that served as a prototype for the Gulag.
A small brotherhood of monks, about ten, has re-established life there.

architects.name: Unknown Late Roman builders
architects.bio: The builders of this small cruciform chapel are not recorded. It was probably commissioned by the empress Galla Placidia in the years after 425, when Ravenna was the capital of the Western Roman Empire, and it set the pattern for the mosaic-lined churches that followed in the city.

photos.credit: Photo: Ввласенко · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Small cross-shaped brick building with blind arcades, a low tiled roof and a taller central tower, seen across a lawn.
Small cross-shaped brick building with blind arcades, gabled arms and a square tower rising in the middle, on a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: Petar Milošević · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Vault covered in dark blue mosaic with gold stars and a gold cross, beside a band of fruit and leaves
photos.caption: The dome is a starry sky made of glass tesserae.
photos.credit: Photo: Petar Milošević · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: bradhostetler · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Barrel vault covered in blue mosaic with starry rosettes, and a lunette showing a robed figure beside flames and a cupboard.

hints.text: Despite its common name, the empress it is named for was almost certainly not buried here; she died in Rome.
It began as a chapel beside a lost church, and its plain brick walls hide one of the oldest and best-preserved mosaic interiors in Europe.
A starry blue dome, the Good Shepherd and deer drinking at a spring decorate this tiny chapel in a former capital of the Western Roman Empire.

summary.description: Built between 425 and 450 in Ravenna, this small cross-shaped chapel is plain brick outside and covered in glittering glass mosaic inside. It is named for the empress Galla Placidia, who probably commissioned it but was not buried here. It is one of the earliest and best-preserved mosaic interiors in the world.
keyFeatures: Cruciform plan with a central dome on pendentives
Barrel vaults over the four arms
Brick walls with blind arcades
Mosaic dome of golden stars on deep blue
Mosaic of the Good Shepherd among his flock
funFacts: Galla Placidia died in Rome, so the building was never her tomb; the idea dates from the thirteenth century.
The floor has been raised by about five feet since the fifth century to stay above the rising water of the upper Adriatic coast.
It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 together with seven other structures in Ravenna.

architects.name: Unknown Byzantine builders
architects.bio: The builders of the church as rebuilt after 532 are not recorded. The work was ordered by the emperor Justinian I as part of his rebuilding of Constantinople after the Nika revolt, and was repaired and redecorated under Constantine V after the earthquake of 740.

photos.alt: Brick church with a low drum and shallow dome seen across a lawn with autumn trees, another large dome behind it
photos.credit: Photo: Alexxx1979 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Sébah & Joaillier · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Old sepia photograph of a brick church with a ribbed drum and low dome, a lone figure standing in the yard before it.

photos.credit: Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Weathered brick and stone walls with tall grilled arched windows and a small dome rising behind them.
Bare brick interior with a wooden gallery, a semicircular apse and rows of red concert chairs
photos.caption: Today the church is a concert hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Semicircular brick apse with three arched windows and a plain dark cross drawn in the half dome above.

hints.text: Its name means 'Holy Peace', and it was one of three shrines an emperor devoted to a divine attribute.
Unlike nearly every other Byzantine church in its city, it was never turned into a mosque; it served as an arsenal until the 19th century.
It stands in the outer courtyard of a sultans' palace, just beside a far more famous domed church of the same emperor.

summary.description: Hagia Irene is the oldest known church in Istanbul. Justinian I rebuilt it in 548 after the Nika revolt had burned an earlier church, and Constantine V repaired it after the earthquake of 740. It stands in the outer courtyard of Topkapı Palace and, never converted to a mosque, is now a museum and concert hall.
keyFeatures: Domed basilica with a nave, two aisles and galleries
Dome about 15 m wide with twenty windows
Apse mosaic of a plain cross from the Iconoclast period
Bare brick interior with remarkable acoustics
funFacts: Janissaries used the church as an arsenal until 1826.
It is one of only two Byzantine churches in Istanbul never converted into a mosque.
Concerts of the Istanbul International Music Festival have been held here every summer since 1980.

architects.name: Unknown Byzantine builders
architects.bio: The builders of the church are not recorded. The quality of the masonry suggests that workers were brought from Constantinople, possibly under the emperor Basil II, and the mosaics are the work of an unknown artist of the early Komnenian period around 1100.

photos.credit: Photo: George E. Koronaios · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Stone church with a red tiled dome, tall arched windows and a columned porch, among ruins and dark cypress trees.

photos.credit: Photo: Ktiv · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Side view of a small cross-in-square church of banded brick and stone with a low red dome behind a rubble wall.

photos.credit: Photo: Giovanni Dall'Orto · CC BY-SA 2.5 it · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Front of a stone church with a pointed-arched porch on slim white marble columns and a battlemented top.
Round dome with a tiled roof and arched windows rising above walls of pale stone framed in red brick
photos.credit: Photo: Anastassios Baktis · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Dome with a gold-ground mosaic of a bearded Christ in a roundel at its centre, surrounded by patches of bare plaster
photos.caption: Christ Pantocrator looks down from the dome.
photos.credit: Photo: Giovanni Dall'Orto · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It lies a few kilometres from a great capital, on the old Sacred Way to Eleusis, near a laurel grove that gave it its name.
It was founded on the site of a sanctuary of Apollo, and one ancient Ionic column is still built into its wall.
Together with Hosios Loukas and Nea Moni it is a UNESCO site celebrated for the gold mosaics of its dome.

summary.description: Daphni is an eleventh-century monastery on the outskirts of Athens, on the site of an ancient sanctuary of Apollo. Its church is a Greek cross-in-octagon topped by a broad dome and decorated with gold-ground mosaics from around 1100, among the best-preserved of the period. Together with Hosios Loukas and Nea Moni it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
keyFeatures: Greek cross inscribed in an octagon under a broad dome
Squinches carrying the dome over the square bay
Cloisonné masonry of stone blocks framed in brick
Gold-ground mosaics with Christ Pantocrator in the dome
funFacts: Frankish crusaders sacked the monastery in 1205, and Cistercian monks later added Gothic pointed arches to the front of the church.
Columns of the ancient Sanctuary of Apollo were taken to London by Lord Elgin and are in the British Museum.
The name 'Daphni' means 'laurel grove' in Modern Greek.

architects.name: Mimar Hayruddin
architects.bio: A pupil of Mimar Sinan, Hayruddin was an Ottoman architect and engineer under Bayezid II and Suleiman the Magnificent. He is best known for the bridge at Mostar; legend says he doubted that it would stand and prepared for his own funeral on the day the scaffolding came down.

photos.credit: Photo: Hibasi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Single high stone arch bridge over a turquoise river, flanked by towers, old houses and a rocky hillside under cloud.
Single hump-backed stone arch between two fortified towers over a green river, with hills behind
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stone bridge arch rising from the rock at the river's edge, seen from the bank beside a tower and old houses
photos.credit: Photo: Berthold Werner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Bjoertvedt · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Stone arch rising steeply to a fortified tower at its end, with pedestrians crossing and mountains behind.

photos.credit: Photo: miketnorton · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking up at the underside of a great pointed stone arch, with a minaret and old houses framed beneath it.

hints.text: The city around it takes its name from the men who once guarded it.
Its builder is said to have prepared for his own funeral when the scaffolding was removed, fearing it would collapse.
A single hump-backed stone arch over the Neretva, it was shelled and destroyed in November 1993, then rebuilt and reopened in 2004.

summary.description: Commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent and designed by Mimar Hayruddin, the Old Bridge of Mostar was completed in 1566 and was for a time the widest man-made arch in the world. A single steep stone arch protected by two towers, it became a symbol of the city. It was destroyed in 1993 during the Croat-Bosniak War and rebuilt, reopening in 2004.
keyFeatures: Single hump-backed stone arch, about 30 m long and 4 m wide
Crosses the Neretva about 24 m above the water
Fortified Halebija and Tara towers at each end
Limestone abutments instead of foundations
funFacts: The city of Mostar is named after the bridge keepers (mostari) who guarded it.
It is thought to have been built with a mortar made with egg whites.
It was shelled and destroyed on 9 November 1993 and reopened on 23 July 2004.

architects.name: Davud Agha
architects.bio: Chief imperial architect of the Ottoman Empire from 1588, after the death of his teacher Sinan, until his own death in 1598 or 1599. He began the mosque in 1597 and died before it rose far.

architects.name: Mustafa Agha
architects.bio: Imperial architect who in 1660, after the Great Fire, suggested that Turhan Sultan complete the half-ruined mosque as a work of piety. It was finished in 1663 and inaugurated in 1665.

photos.alt: Large grey mosque with a cascade of domes and half-domes and two tall minarets beside a busy square under a cloudy sky
photos.credit: Photo: Jorge Láscar · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Another Believer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Paved courtyard with an ornate domed ablutions fountain at the centre, arcaded galleries around it and a cascade of domes behind.
Prayer hall seen from a gallery, with a red carpet, rings of lamps, blue and green tiled walls and a painted dome
photos.caption: Ringed lamps hang over the red-carpeted prayer hall.
photos.credit: Photo: RramazanŞahin · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: View straight up into painted domes and half-domes, with round calligraphic medallions and rows of small arched windows.

hints.text: Two queen mothers shaped its story: one began it in 1597, and another finished it in the 1660s.
Work stopped in 1603, and the half-built shell was then damaged in the Great Fire of 1660.
It stands at the Golden Horn end of a famous bridge, with a spice bazaar as part of its complex.

summary.description: Begun in 1597 for Safiye Sultan, mother of Mehmed III, and abandoned after his death in 1603, the New Mosque was finished only in 1663 by Turhan Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, and inaugurated in 1665. It stands on the Golden Horn at the southern end of the Galata Bridge, a landmark for anyone crossing into the old city. Its cascade of 66 domes and semi-domes follows the plan of the earlier Şehzade Mosque.
keyFeatures: 66 domes and semi-domes in a pyramidal arrangement
Main dome about 36 m high, carried by four semi-domes
Two minarets
Spice Bazaar built as part of the complex
funFacts: It was first called the Valide Sultan Mosque; 'New Mosque' stuck in popular use after its completion.
Construction took more than half a century and passed through two queen mothers.
The project drew sharp criticism for its cost and for the property confiscated to build it.

architects.name: Garabet Balyan
architects.bio: Armenian court architect of the Balyan family, who served Ottoman sultans for five generations. He worked with his son Nigoğos on the Dolmabahçe Palace and this mosque.

architects.name: Nigoğos Balyan
architects.bio: Armenian court architect, son of Garabet Balyan. Father and son worked as a team on the Dolmabahçe Palace, the Dolmabahçe Mosque and this mosque for Sultan Abdülmecid I.

photos.credit: Photo: Pragdon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Pale stone mosque with a shallow dome and two slender minarets beside the water, a suspension bridge crossing behind it.

photos.credit: Photo: Moataz1997 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Waterfront mosque with ornate carved windows and two tall minarets, a long bridge spanning the strait beyond under grey sky.
Small cream-coloured mosque with two slender minarets at the edge of a pier, with a suspension bridge on the horizon
photos.credit: Photo: Calistemon · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Looking straight up into a painted dome with trompe-l'oeil architecture, cords of a lamp crossing the view
photos.caption: The dome is painted with trompe-l'oeil frescoes.
photos.credit: Photo: Dosseman · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was designed by a father and son from an Armenian dynasty of court architects, who also built a neighbouring palace for the same sultan.
Its stone-carved decoration is unusually ornate for a mosque of its time, mixing Ottoman Baroque with European Neoclassical details.
It stands right on a Bosphorus pier, a favourite view with a suspension bridge to Asia behind it.

summary.description: Built around 1854-1856 for Sultan Abdülmecid I by the Armenian father and son Garabet and Nigoğos Balyan, the Ortaköy Mosque sits at the water's edge on the Bosphorus. It mixes Ottoman Baroque with Neoclassical details and is known for its carved stone decoration. Its view with the Bosphorus Bridge is one of Istanbul's most photographed.
keyFeatures: Single dome over a square prayer hall
Two slender minarets
Richly carved stone reliefs on the facades
Trompe-l'oeil frescoes inside the dome
Imperial apartment for the sultan with a U-shaped plan
funFacts: The Balyans also designed the nearby Dolmabahçe Palace and Dolmabahçe Mosque.
The original brick dome cracked, and a new concrete dome was built before the mosque reopened in 1969.
A restoration completed in 2014 reopened the mosque on 6 June 2014.

architects.name: Thomas Farnolls Pritchard
architects.bio: Born in Shrewsbury and trained as a joiner, Pritchard became an architect and interior designer who specialised in chimney-pieces, decoration and funerary monuments. He is best remembered for proposing the first cast-iron bridge in the world, and died in December 1777, a month after work began.

architects.name: Abraham Darby III
architects.bio: A Quaker ironmaster born in Coalbrookdale, Darby belonged to the family that played a pivotal role in the Industrial Revolution. He was commissioned to cast and build the bridge and was responsible for its ironwork.

photos.alt: A single grey cast-iron arch spanning a wooded river gorge, with a stone abutment at the right
photos.credit: Photo: Colin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Tk420 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Side view of a red-painted cast-iron arch with circles and diagonal braces between stone abutments over a wooded valley.

photos.credit: Photo: Alice Humphreys - transatracurium · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Aerial view of a single-span iron bridge crossing a narrow river between trees, with houses and a road on one bank.
Lattice of iron ribs and rings forming a high arch over a green gorge, with walkers on the deck
photos.caption: Almost 1,700 separately cast parts.
photos.credit: Photo: August Schwerdfeger · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It crosses a deep river gorge in a part of England where coal, iron ore and limestone lay close to the surface.
It was the first major bridge in the world built of cast iron, and its single span lets boats pass underneath.
It gave its name to the village around it and to a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it became a symbol of the Industrial Revolution.

summary.description: Opened on 1 January 1781 across the Severn, this is a cast-iron arch bridge that spans the Ironbridge Gorge with a main span of 100 ft 6 in (30.6 m). It was the first major bridge in the world to be made of cast iron, and its success inspired the widespread use of the material as a structural element.
keyFeatures: Five cast-iron ribs forming a single arch
Main span of 30.6 m, high enough for river boats
Almost 1,700 individual components, each cast to fit
About 385 tonnes of iron
funFacts: The parts were cast individually to fit each other rather than to standard sizes, so identical-looking pieces differ by several centimetres.
The architect Pritchard died only a month after work began; the ironmaster Abraham Darby III was responsible for the ironwork.
It was closed to vehicles in 1934, and pedestrian tolls were collected until 1950.

architects.name: Giuseppe Mengoni
