architects.bio: Born in 1829, Mengoni designed the Galleria in Milan, the first monumentally scaled iron and steel arcade in Italy, in a Renaissance Revival style. He also designed the Palazzo di Residenza of the Bologna Savings Bank.

photos.credit: Photo: Paolobon140 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall triumphal-arch entrance in a cream stone palace front opening onto a busy square, with a glass vault visible inside.

photos.credit: Photo: Daniel from Glasgow, United Kingdom · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Octagonal crossing of a glass-roofed arcade seen from above, with painted lunettes, mosaic floor and visitors below.
Crowded arcade with cream-coloured facades rising to a huge glass and iron dome and barrel-vaulted roofs
photos.caption: Two glass-vaulted arcades meet under a glass dome.
photos.credit: Photo: C messier · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: acediscovery · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking up between two ornate cream facades at a long barrel vault of iron ribs and glass ending in a dome.
Weathered glazed dome with a small lantern on top, seen from a rooftop walkway, with a Gothic pinnacle in the distance
photos.credit: Photo: Alex Para · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a covered shopping street linking two of the most famous landmarks of a great Italian city.
Two glass-roofed arcades cross in an octagon under a glass dome; the ironwork came from a French workshop.
It is nicknamed the drawing room of its city, and it is named after the first king of a unified Italy.

summary.description: Designed in 1861 and built between 1865 and 1877, this is Italy's oldest active shopping arcade. Two glass-vaulted arcades intersect in an octagon crowned by a glass dome, and the whole connects Piazza del Duomo with Piazza della Scala.
keyFeatures: Four barrel vaults of glass and iron, about 14.5 m wide
Central glass dome, about 37.5 m across inside
Octagonal crossing with four floor mosaics
Ironwork by the French firm Henry Joret, glass by Saint-Gobain
funFacts: It is often nicknamed il salotto di Milano, Milan's drawing room.
It was the direct progenitor of the modern glazed shopping mall and gave the word galleria to arcades elsewhere.
Biffi Caffè opened here in 1867 and Borsalino in 1883.

architects.name: Jacques Ignace Hittorff
architects.bio: Born in Cologne, Hittorff moved to Paris in 1810 and studied at the Académie des Beaux-Arts. He combined advanced structural use of cast iron with conservative Beaux-Arts classicism in a career that ran from the Restoration to the Second Empire.

photos.alt: Giant arched window with a clock and a row of crowned statues above a colonnade, on a pale stone facade
photos.credit: Photo: Velvet · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long train shed with slender iron columns and trusses, lit platforms, waiting trains and travellers beneath a wooden-slatted roof.
Trains and a platform seen from above under a high iron-framed shed roof, with a steel bridge in the distance
photos.credit: Photo: James Petts from London, England · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a terminus on the north side of a European capital, and it serves the trains to the Channel and beyond.
Its stone facade is built around a triumphal arch, topped with statues of the cities the railway served.
It is Europe's busiest railway station and the Paris terminal of the Eurostar.

summary.description: Built between 1861 and 1865 for the Chemin de Fer du Nord company on a design by Jacques Ignace Hittorff, it replaced a smaller terminal. Its stone front, shaped like a triumphal arch, hides a great iron shed, and sculptures represent the cities the company served.
keyFeatures: Facade built around a triumphal arch in stone
Cast-iron structure of the main shed
Allegorical sculptures of the cities served
U-shaped terminus plan
funFacts: The station is Europe's busiest railway station.
The iron pillars inside were made at Alston & Gourley's ironworks in Glasgow, the only foundry in Europe then large enough for the job.
The facade of the first station of 1846 was moved to Lille, where it survives as part of the Lille-Flandres station.

architects.name: Decimus Burton
architects.bio: One of the foremost English architects and landscapers of the 19th century, Burton was the foremost Victorian architect in the Roman Revival, Greek Revival and Regency styles. He was a founding fellow of the Royal Institute of British Architects.

architects.name: Richard Turner
architects.bio: An iron-maker who built the early Palm House at the Belfast Botanic Gardens, designed by Charles Lanyon, before building the one at Kew. He knew the problems of heating, ventilation and structure in greenhouses.

photos.alt: Huge curved glasshouse of white iron ribs and glass panes beside a formal flower garden with stone beasts
photos.credit: Photo: Deror avi · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long curved glasshouse with a taller central dome seen across lawns and flower beds under a cloudy blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Tilman2007 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Glass and white iron conservatory with a central dome and curved wings, behind pink roses and dry grass in clear sun.
Looking up through palm fronds to a vaulted roof of slender white iron ribs and glass
photos.caption: Wrought iron and glass above the palms.
photos.credit: Photo: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall palms rising inside a glasshouse, their fronds reaching toward slender curved iron ribs and glass panes.

hints.text: It was built in a famous botanical garden beside a river in west London to grow tropical palms.
It was the first greenhouse built on this scale, and the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron.
It was completed in 1848, and it houses the oldest pot plant in the world.

summary.description: Built between 1844 and 1848 in the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, the Palm House is a large glasshouse that specialises in tropical and subtropical plants. It was the first greenhouse of this scale and the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron.
keyFeatures: Curved frame of wrought iron with glass panes
First greenhouse built on this scale
Upper walkway among the palm branches
Neoclassical style preferred by Burton
funFacts: It houses the oldest pot plant in the world, a cycad moved here in 1848.
Who really designed it was disputed: Burton drew sketches and finished the design, but Turner was primarily involved.
In 2025 Kew announced a five-year renovation to start in 2027.

architects.name: Giulio Romano
architects.bio: A pupil of Raphael, Giulio Romano was a painter and architect whose stylistic deviations from High Renaissance classicism help define the sixteenth-century style known as Mannerism. Engravings after his drawings spread Italian style across Europe.

photos.credit: Photo: FrDr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Low cream palace front with a central pedimented entrance of round arches and tiled roof, behind a gravel path and clipped hedge.
Long rusticated wall with free-standing columns, niches and a pedimented arched doorway beside a lawn
photos.credit: Photo: Marcok · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Courtyard front with three rusticated arches between columns, seen over a lawn and a brick path
photos.caption: The facades are less symmetrical than they look.
photos.credit: Photo: Marcok · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Errem · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: View through a loggia of paired columns and arches with painted vaults, out to a garden and a long arcaded wing.

photos.credit: Photo: Giulio Romano · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Illusionistic painted ceiling of swirling clouds and tumbling figures around a circular temple opening at the centre.

hints.text: It was built as a palace of leisure for a ruler, on the edge of marshes just outside his city walls, on the site of the family stables.
Its walls bend the rules of classical architecture, with columns and details placed in irregular, playful ways.
Its frescoed halls include one where giants seem to fall around the walls, painted for the Gonzaga family of Mantua.

summary.description: Built between 1524 and 1534 for Federico II Gonzaga, Marquess of Mantua, as a palace of leisure, Palazzo del Te is the acknowledged masterpiece of Giulio Romano and a classic example of Mannerism. The shell, a square house around a cloistered courtyard, went up in eighteen months, and a team of painters and plasterers then spent ten years decorating it.
keyFeatures: Rusticated walls with flat pilasters
Irregular spans between the columns
Frescoes in the Sala di Psiche, the Sala dei Cavalli and the Sala dei Giganti
Casino della Grotta around a grotto and loggetta
funFacts: The facades are not as symmetrical as they appear, and the spans between the columns are irregular.
Emperor Charles V visited in 1530 and raised his host to Duke of Mantua.
In 1630 imperial troops sacked the palace over three days, leaving an empty shell.

architects.name: Giorgio Vasari
architects.bio: A painter, architect, art historian and biographer, Vasari wrote Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, the ideological foundation of Western art-historical writing. He was a Mannerist painter highly regarded as both painter and architect.

photos.alt: Long courtyard framed by two matching arcaded wings with a bridge-like arch across the far end
photos.credit: Photo: de:Benutzer:Thomas.mies · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Ingo Mehling · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Panorama of a river front with a ground-floor arcade, a central triple-arched bridge-like block and ochre palace walls.

photos.credit: Photo: Petar Milošević · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Very long gallery corridor with a painted coffered ceiling, tall windows on one side and white marble statues along the walls.
Long narrow street between two matching arcaded palace wings, with a medieval tower and a red dome at the far end
photos.credit: Photo: Armin Kleiner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was begun in the sixteenth century by a ruling family to house the offices of the government in one place.
Its long, narrow U-shaped courtyard, open to a river at one end, is treated as the first regularised streetscape of Europe.
Today it is one of the largest and most visited art museums in the world, famous for its Italian Renaissance collection.

summary.description: Begun in 1560 for Cosimo I de' Medici to bring the city's offices (uffizi) together, the building has a long, narrow courtyard that opens to the Arno through a Doric screen. Work continued under other architects and was completed in 1581, and the top floor became a gallery for the Medici collections.
keyFeatures: Long, narrow courtyard framed by matching loggias
Continuous cornices stressing the perspective length
Doric screen opening the courtyard to the river
Octagonal Tribuna completed in 1584
funFacts: Architectural historians treat its courtyard as the first regularised streetscape of Europe.
The Medici collections passed to the city of Florence under the "family pact" negotiated by Anna Maria Luisa, the last Medici heiress.
It officially opened to the public in 1769 and became a museum in 1865.

architects.name: Filippo Brunelleschi
architects.bio: An architect, designer, goldsmith and sculptor, Brunelleschi is considered a founding father of Renaissance architecture and the first modern engineer. He is most famous for the dome of Florence Cathedral.

photos.alt: Long pale building with a loggia of slender columns and round arches, blue roundels above each column and a bronze equestrian statue at the right
photos.credit: Photo: Ricardalovesmonuments · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: MenkinAlRire · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Oblique view across a wide square of a long pale building with a loggia of round arches on slender columns.
Golden evening light on a loggia of round arches on slender columns, with blue roundels of swaddled babies in the spandrels
photos.caption: Roundels of swaddled babies in the spandrels.
photos.credit: Photo: Txllxt TxllxT · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: edited by MenkinAlRire · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Quiet cloister court with slender stone columns, round arches on two levels and a tiled roof above a wooden door.

hints.text: It began as a charitable institution paid for by one of the wealthiest guilds of a great Italian city.
Its nine-bay loggia is considered the first pure Early Renaissance structure, with round arches on slender columns.
Blue roundels with babies in swaddling clothes decorate its arcade, because it was the city's foundling hospital.

summary.description: Commissioned in 1419 from Filippo Brunelleschi by the Silk Guild of Florence, this foundling hospital has a nine-bay loggia that faces the Piazza della Santissima Annunziata. It is regarded as the first pure Early Renaissance structure, with round arches springing from Composite columns in grey pietra serena against white walls.
keyFeatures: Nine-bay loggia of semicircular arches
Column height equal to the width of each bay, making each bay a cube
Pietra serena set against white walls
Glazed blue terracotta roundels of babies
funFacts: Only the first phase (1419–1427) was under Brunelleschi's direct supervision, and the hospital formally opened in 1445.
The roundels of babies were added around 1490 by Andrea della Robbia; Brunelleschi meant them to be blank.
A wheel for anonymous abandonment of babies worked here until the hospital closed in 1875.

architects.name: Joseph Gire
architects.bio: French architect born in Le Puy-en-Velay who was prolific in Brazil and Argentina. In Rio de Janeiro he also designed the Hotel Glória and the Copacabana Palace.

architects.name: Elisário Bahiana
architects.bio: Rio-born architect and professor, known for Art Deco work and landscaping. He later worked in São Paulo, including on the reconstruction of the Viaduto do Chá.

photos.alt: Tall pale tower of twenty-two storeys with a stepped, finned crown, rising beside a plaza and a bronze statue on a column
photos.credit: Photo: Antonio Donioli · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Gilgarcias · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Tall cream tower with rows of small windows and a stepped, finned crown, seen from a corner beside trees and a glass building.

photos.credit: Photo: Tânia Rêgo/Agência Brasil · CC BY 3.0 br · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Slender cream skyscraper with a stepped top rising above a wide, sunny plaza and low buildings under a deep blue sky.

photos.credit: Photo: Tânia Rêgo/Agência Brasil · CC BY 3.0 br · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking steeply up the face of a pale skyscraper with regular rows of windows and a stepped crown against dark blue sky.

hints.text: Built in the late 1920s in then-novel reinforced concrete, its 22 floors made it the tallest building in Brazil.
It was raised for an evening newspaper and later housed the radio station whose auditorium shows defined Brazil's radio age.
Its French co-architect also designed a famous Copacabana beach hotel; it stands on a square beside the port of Rio de Janeiro.

summary.description: Built between 1927 and 1929 on Praça Mauá beside Rio's port, this 22-storey, 102-metre tower was the tallest building in Brazil until São Paulo's Martinelli surpassed it. Its facade and common areas show Art Deco influence, and its reinforced-concrete frame gave a big push to Brazilian engineering.
keyFeatures: 22 floors, about 102 metres tall
Reinforced-concrete structure
Art Deco facade ornament and stepped crown
Close to North American skyscraper models rather than European ones
funFacts: It was the headquarters of the Rio evening newspaper that gave it its popular name.
Rádio Nacional broadcast from here at the height of the Radio Era, with famous singers performing in its auditorium.
The structural calculations were by engineer Emílio Baumgart, who later worked on the Ministry of Education and Health.

name: Igreja e Convento de São Francisco
aliases: Church and Convent of São Francisco
Igreja de São Francisco de Salvador
Church and Convent of Saint Francis

architects.name: Unknown Franciscan master builders
architects.bio: The architect of the church is not known for certain; the cloister is credited to Francisco Pinheiro. Friars and master masons of the Franciscan order built it, supervised by Manoel Quaresma and then Friar Hilário da Visitação, in the Portuguese colonial tradition.

photos.credit: Photo: Wellington Da Costa Gomez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Sandstone church front with two towers topped by pyramid roofs and a scrolled central gable, under a clear blue sky.
Sandstone church front with two tiled towers, a scrolled central gable and a stone cross in a cobbled square
photos.credit: Photo: Fabio Gomes · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: BrunoEspindola84 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Church nave densely covered in gilded carving, with a geometric painted ceiling and a golden altarpiece at the far end.

photos.credit: Photo: Paul R. Burley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Close detail of weathered sandstone pilasters and carved cornices beside a tall green panelled wooden door.

hints.text: Its facade of local sandstone, with Mannerist echoes, faces a square marked by a large stone cross in a World Heritage historic centre.
A Franciscan convent built here in 1587 was destroyed by the Dutch; the present one was begun in 1686 and finished in the 18th century.
With about 55,000 azulejo tiles, it holds more than any other church in Latin America, and its interior is famed for gilded carving.

summary.description: The Franciscans arrived in Salvador in 1587; after the Dutch invasions destroyed their first convent, work on the present one began in 1686 and the church was completed in 1723. Built of Bahian sandstone, it is a landmark of colonial Baroque in Brazil, with a three-aisled nave unusual for Franciscan churches of the Northeast.
keyFeatures: Bahian sandstone walls, pilasters and facade
Three-aisled nave with three side chapels on each side
About 55,000 azulejos, the most of any church in Latin America
Largo do Cruzeiro square with a large stone cross in front
funFacts: It was listed as a historic structure by the national heritage institute in 1938.
With the adjacent Third Order church it is one of the Seven Wonders of Portuguese Origin in the World.
The Third Order church next door was built in parallel, between 1702 and 1870.

name: Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Candelária
aliases: Church of Our Lady of Candelária

architects.name: Francisco João Roscio
architects.bio: Military engineer born on Madeira who worked in southern Brazil and briefly served as interim president of the captaincy of Rio Grande de São Pedro. He drew the plans for the new church in the 1770s.

style: Portuguese colonial Baroque with Neoclassical and Neo-Renaissance elements

photos.credit: Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Twin-towered stone church front with a grey dome behind its pediment, standing across a fountain roundabout between office blocks.
Twin-towered church front of dark granite and pale plaster with a triangular pediment and a pale dome behind
photos.credit: Photo: Rodrigojordy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Richly painted and gilded arches under a dome with arched windows and murals in the corners
photos.credit: Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Looking up into a ribbed dome painted with robed figures and angels, with arched windows and a skylight at the top.

hints.text: Tradition says a small chapel was vowed here in the early 1600s by a couple whose ship nearly sank in a storm.
Its main facade is Portuguese colonial Baroque with neoclassical touches, while the interior was redone in Neo-Renaissance marble and painting.
Its white Lioz stone dome, finished in 1877 and shipped from Lisbon, was the tallest structure in Rio de Janeiro; it closes a great downtown avenue.

summary.description: Planned by military engineer Francisco João Roscio, the church was begun in 1775 and inaugurated, still unfinished, in 1811. Its dome was completed only in 1877, and the interior was redecorated from 1878 in the Neo-Renaissance style, so the building combines several periods.
keyFeatures: Baroque facade with neoclassical elements and twin towers
Latin-cross plan with a dome over the transept and three aisles
Dome and eight statues in white Lioz stone made in Lisbon
Neo-Renaissance interior with Italian marble and paintings by João Zeferino da Costa
funFacts: The plan may have been inspired by the Mafra convent church and the Estrela Basilica in Portugal.
The bronze doors (c. 1901) are by Portuguese sculptor António Teixeira Lopes.
It was the site of the 1984 Diretas Já rally, attended by over a million people.

architects.name: Carl Friedrich Gustav Waehneldt
architects.bio: Prussian-born architect who worked in Rio de Janeiro. Besides the palace, he designed the Palacete do Gavião, made changes to the Candelária church and won the 1852 competition for the Teatro Provisório.

photos.credit: Photo: Donatas Dabravolskas · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Symmetrical pink three-storey palace front with a stone base, balustraded balconies and bronze eagles along the roofline.
Pale pink three-storey mansion with balustraded balconies and dark bronze eagles on its roofline, seen from a street corner
photos.credit: Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Grand salon with gilded wall panels, painted arches, chandeliers and a large mirror above a green sofa
photos.credit: Photo: Boaventuravinicius · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Long wooden meeting table with leather chairs in a room with painted wall panels, a chandelier and a herringbone floor.

hints.text: It was built from 1858 as the town residence of a Portuguese-born coffee magnate, a baron, in a Rio seaside neighbourhood.
From 1897 until 1960, when the capital moved to Brasília, it was the seat of the federal government and presidential palace.
In 1954 President Getúlio Vargas shot himself in a third-floor bedroom here; it now houses the Republic Museum.

summary.description: Designed in 1858 by German architect Carl Friedrich Gustav Waehneldt for the Baron of Nova Friburgo, the mansion was built between 1858 and 1867 and became Brazil's presidential palace in 1897. Portuguese Wikipedia classes it as an example of late-19th-century Brazilian Neoclassical architecture.
keyFeatures: Neoclassical urban mansion between Rua do Catete and Flamengo beach
Bronze allegorical statues on the roofline, replacing original iron eagles
Gardens attributed to landscape designer Auguste Glaziou
Richly decorated salons now part of the Republic Museum
funFacts: Brazil declared war on Germany here in 1917, and on the Axis in 1942.
Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli, the future Pope Pius XII, was hosted here in 1934.
It was long known as the Palace of Nova Friburgo, after its first owner.

architects.name: Augusto Frederico de Lacerda
architects.bio: Engineer from a Bahian family firm. The original lift was conceived and built by the Lacerdas from 1869; the Art Deco towers of 1930 came from a later renovation whose designer is not named in the sources consulted.

photos.alt: Slim cream tower with vertical slotted windows and a glazed top, linked by a bridge to a second tower on the hillside above a street
photos.credit: Photo: Paul R. Burley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: EvertonCostaFoto · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Slim cream tower with a glazed top platform, seen from a stone quay with a small weathered boat in the foreground.
View from the upper tower platform over a turquoise bay with boats, a fort and a sculpture in a fountain below
photos.credit: Photo: Paul R. Burley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It is a public urban lift, and pioneered the idea: it links a lower port district to the historic upper city on a cliff.
It rises 72 metres in two towers, four cabins of 27 passengers each making the 30-second trip; it was hydraulic before electricity in 1906.
A 1930 renovation gave its towers an Art Deco look; at the top you overlook the Bay of All Saints and a famous crafts market.

summary.description: Opened in 1873 as a hydraulic lift joining Salvador's lower city to the upper city, it was electrified in 1906 and given its present Art Deco towers in 1930. The 72-metre lift has four cabins and one tower that pierces the stone slope.
keyFeatures: 72 metres tall, two towers
Four cabins of 27 passengers, 30-second ride
Art Deco styling from the 1930 renovation
Links the lower city to the upper city
funFacts: It was named after Antônio de Lacerda, director of the Commercial Association of Bahia.
It carried more than 33,000 passengers a day in 2019.
It was listed as national heritage by IPHAN on 7 December 2006.

name: Biblioteca Nacional do Brasil
aliases: Biblioteca Nacional do Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Francisco Marcelino de Sousa Aguiar
architects.bio: Military engineer born in Salvador who graduated in engineering in 1876. He was mayor of the Federal District from 1906 to 1909 and designed the Army Central Hospital in a few days at the request of Floriano Peixoto.

style: Eclectic, mixing Neoclassical and Art Nouveau elements

photos.credit: Photo: Halleypo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: View from above of a large ochre palace-like building with a columned portico, a green copper dome and red tile roofs among trees.
Ochre-yellow palace-like building with a columned portico, sculpted pediment and green copper dome, beyond a tree-lined street
photos.credit: Photo: Antonio Donioli · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Photo: Eugenio Hansen, OFS · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
photos.alt: Corner of a cream and ochre neoclassical building with arched upper windows, a pedimented portico and a green dome.
Grand double staircase with red carpet, wrought-iron balustrades and bronze lamp-bearers leading to a doorway with a bust
photos.credit: Photo: Julio imagenations · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its cornerstone was laid in 1905 and it opened in 1910, on the centenary of the institution it houses.
Its collection began with a royal library moved from Lisbon after the 1755 earthquake; it now holds about nine million items.
Considered by UNESCO the largest library in Latin America, it stands on Rio's Cinelândia square beside a famous theatre and the fine-arts museum.

summary.description: Designed by military engineer Sousa Aguiar, the building rose on Cinelândia square after the cornerstone of 1905 and opened on 29 October 1910. Its style is eclectic, with neoclassical and Art Nouveau elements and ornament by artists such as Eliseu Visconti and the Bernardelli brothers.
keyFeatures: Eclectic facade with neoclassical and Art Nouveau elements
Ornament by Eliseu Visconti, Henrique and Rodolfo Bernardelli, Modesto Brocos and Rodolfo Amoedo
Grand interior staircase and stained-glass ceilings
Forms an ensemble with the Teatro Municipal and the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes
funFacts: UNESCO considers it the largest library in Latin America and the seventh largest in the world.
The collection began with about 60,000 volumes of the Portuguese royal library brought in 1810-1811.
Eliseu Visconti designed the library's emblem in 1903, before the building was finished.
